# MUSICAL TREATISE
<note>original: "Syntagmatis Musici"</note>
## BY MICHAEL PRAETORIUS C.
<note>The "C." stands for Creutzbergensis, indicating his birthplace in Creuzburg.</note>
# VOLUME TWO
## ON INSTRUMENTATION.
<note>original: "De Organographia"</note>

->In Which<-

### The nomenclature, tuning, and characteristics of all musical instruments—ancient and modern, foreign, barbarian, rustic, and unknown, as well as domestic, artistic, lovely, and familiar—are found, together with their accurate drawings and true likenesses:

->As Well As<-

## A Reliable Description of Ancient and Modern Organs,
manual and pedal keyboards, bellows, specifications, and various types of stops; also how to tune regals <note>a small portable organ with reed pipes</note> and harpsichords <note>original: "Clavicymbel"</note> purely and easily; and what must be observed during the delivery of an organ, together with an attached, detailed index:
**Not only quite useful and necessary for organists, instrumentalists, organ and instrument makers, and all those devoted to the Muses, but also very pleasant and delightful for philosophers, philologists, and historians to read.**

->**Along with a detailed index.**<-

---

->Printed at Wolfenbüttel by Elias Holwein, Printer and Woodcutter to the Prince of Brunswick. Published by the Author.<-

### In the Year of Christ, 1619.

--- Page 4 ---
<meta>Continuity established with previous discussion of biblical musical instruments; catchword "sen/ wel" suggests a transition from a previous description of trumpets.</meta>

it was such that one could hold them in one hand, as can be seen in Judges chapter 7, verse 20. Regarding their form and shape, however, there is no surviving information; likewise, what kind of sound they produced—whether it was a <term>unisonus</term> <note>a single, unchanging pitch</note> or whether one could produce variations or different tones upon them, as is done nowadays on our trombones or trumpets. It appears, however, that variations could be played on them, because a distinction is made between **simple blowing** and **sounding the trumpet**.

**Simple blowing** occurred either with one trumpet, when the princes and leaders were to assemble, or with both, when the congregation was to gather before the door of the Tabernacle. **Sounding the trumpet** <note>original: "Trommeten," likely referring to a rhythmic or melodic signal</note>, however, occurred either during the feasts and New Moons, or in times of war when the camps were to break or when moving into battle. Numbers 10, verses 3, 4, 5, 6, 9, 10.

Some wish to claim that the trumpets used to announce the Jubilee or Year of Release (Leviticus chapter 25, verse 10)—from whose resonance it is called the "Resonance Year" <note>original: "Hall-Jahr," a German play on "Jubilee" relating to the sound or "echo" of the horn</note>—were said to have been made from the horn of a ram. Although others believe that while they indeed had such a form and shape, they were made of silver or other metal.

**Pipes** <note>flutes or reed instruments</note> are indeed mentioned in 1 Samuel chapter 10, verse 5; 2 Samuel chapter 6, verse 5; 1 Kings chapter 1, verse 40; in the Psalms; and many other places in Scripture. They were used at the anointing of kings (1 Kings chapter 1, verse 40), at banquets (Isaiah 5, verse 15), and at funerals (Matthew 9, verse 23). But there is no mention at all of the material from which they were made, much less their form and shape, how many holes they had, or how many tones they produced.

King David not only organized a famous, well-appointed, and populous <term>Capellen</term> <note>a musical ensemble or chapel choir</note> in Jerusalem, but also invented many instruments and had them made from ebony, which was brought from Ophir and had not been seen in Palestine before this time—

<meta>This page continues the discussion of ancient musical instruments, specifically those used in the biblical era by King David and King Solomon.</meta>

...ments, which were stringed instruments played by striking, as seen in 2 Chronicles chapter 29, verse 27. Among these is also the harp, mentioned in 1 Kings chapter 10, verses 11 and 12, which was plucked with the fingers, as in 2 Samuel chapter 6, verse 5.

And that David invented many instruments, and also had them manufactured, is testified by the Holy Scripture in 1 Chronicles chapter 23, verse 5; chapter 25, verse 7; and 2 Chronicles chapter 29, verses 26 and 27; as well as by *Josephus in book 7 of the Antiquities of the Jews.* <note>Flavius Josephus was a 1st-century Romano-Jewish historian.</note> Several of these are mentioned here and there in the Psalms, but merely by their names; from this, neither their physical design nor their **intonation** <note>The specific pitch or tuning system used</note> can be understood, nor how one string was tuned against another in an *eight-stringed instrument* <note>original: "Octa-Chordo"</note> or a *ten-stringed instrument* <note>original: "Decachordo"</note>, and so forth. However, King David’s chapel <note>The royal musical ensemble or "Kapelle"</note> was four thousand persons strong and arranged in such a way that there were two hundred and eighty-eight directors among them, divided into twenty-four choirs. In each choir, twelve persons were employed, among whom were three thousand, seven hundred and twelve other musicians, which amounts to more than one hundred and fifty persons for each choir. All of these performed music on the instruments that King David had commissioned, according to 1 Chronicles chapter 23, verse 5 and chapter 25, verse 7.

Solomon not only maintained such a *chapel* further, but also likewise had harps and psalteries made from ebony <note>original: "Hebenholtz"</note> which had been brought from Ophir, as noted in 2 Chronicles chapter 9, verses 10 and 11.

*Jerome in his Letter to Dardanus, Josephus,* and *Polydore Vergil in book 1, chapter 15 of "On Discovery"* <note>original: "de inventione"</note> write that the zither <note>original: "Cither"</note> among the Hebrews had twenty-four strings, and its shape was a *triangle* or a Greek *Delta-shape* <note>original: "Deltoton," referring to the triangular letter Delta</note>, from which some of our people derive the modern harp. Then there is yet another instrument, which *Josephus* calls a *Cynyra* <note>A type of lyre</note>; it had ten strings and was played with a *plectrum* <note>A small tool for plucking strings</note>. And yet another, which he calls a *Nablum* <note>A Phoenician or Hebrew harp/lute</note> with twelve strings, which was struck with the fingers. However, it is not recorded how they were shaped or tuned.

--- Page 6 ---
<meta>Continuity note: This page continues the discussion of ancient musical instruments, specifically addressing why Jewish instruments were not described in detail and comparing them to those of the pagans. Catchword from previous page: "It be-"</meta>

The reason why the **instruments** are not actually described in Judaism is perhaps because they were known to all Jews, and it was unnecessary to write much about familiar things. Furthermore, they did not wish to grant or **share** <note>original: "Communiciren"</note> those **instruments**—which they used in the performance of true divine service in the Temple to the honor of the Eternal and Almighty God—with the superstitious pagans for their idolatry and misuse, lest "pearls be cast before swine," as the saying goes.

Regarding pipes and stringed instruments in paganism, we have somewhat more information from **historians**, **poets**, **philologists**, and **musicians**, such as how many holes the pipes had or how many strings the stringed instruments possessed. Some pipes were composed of seven tubes joined together, of which **Virgil** speaks: "A **PIPE** <note>original: "FISTVLA"</note> constructed of seven unequal hemlock stalks," which are nothing other than our seven **keys** <note>original: "Claves"</note>: A. B. C. D. E. F. G. Or the seven **musical voices common among the moderns**: **Ut, Re, Mi, Fa, Sol, La, Ni**. Or the newly invented system of the **Belgians**: **Bo, Ce, Di, Ga, Lo, Ma, Ni**. Some pipes had only four holes, which **M. Varro**, as an <term>eyewitness <note>Greek: αὐτόπτης (autoptes)</note></term>, saw in the Temple of Marsyas, as he writes in book 3 of *On the Latin Language*. Some pipes, called **Spondaic**, had holes equidistant from one another; the **Dactylic** ones, however, had unequal spacing, according to **Scaliger, book 1, chapter 20 of *Poetics***. The **left-handed Phrygian pipe** <note>original: "Tibia Phrygia sinistra"</note> had two holes, while the **right-handed** one had only one, as **Servius** testifies in his commentary on the 9th book of the **Aeneid, verse 618, citing Varro**.

The **Tyrrhenians** <note>An ancient Italian people, often identified with the Etruscans.</note> had a type of pipe composed of two tubes. The small tube at the bottom was blown into, from which the wind went into the larger one and moved the water contained therein, thus giving off a great harmony, according to **Scaliger, book 1, chapter 20 of *Poetics*** and **Julius Pollux, book 4**.

<summary>The author explains the lack of detailed descriptions for Jewish Temple instruments as a measure to prevent pagan misuse and provides a technical comparison of various Greek, Roman, and Phrygian pipes and tuning systems.</summary>
<keywords>Temple instruments, Jewish music, pagan music, Virgil, Varro, Phrygian pipes, Tyrrhenian water organ, musical notation, solmization</keywords>

--- Page 7 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of the historical origins of musical instruments, transitioning from wind-driven mechanisms to stringed instruments and their mathematical foundations.</meta>

<term>Vitruvius</term> <note>Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, a Roman architect and engineer of the 1st century BC</note> also describes in Book 10, Chapter 13 of his work *On Architecture* the instrument called the <term>Hydraulicum</term> <note>The water organ, which used water pressure to regulate air flow</note>, which is said to have been invented by <term>Ctesibius</term> <note>An inventor from Alexandria</note>, as noted by <term>Pliny</term> in Book 7, Chapter 37; <term>Ramus</term> in Book 1 of his *Mathematical Commentaries*; and <term>Turnebus</term> in Book 1 of his *Miscellany*. From this instrument, our modern organ undoubtedly later originated.

Regarding <term>Stringed Instruments</term>, the <term>Lyre</term> was formed in the shape of a sled (as <term>Caelius Rhodiginus</term> testifies in Book 9, Chapter 6 of his *Ancient Readings*, citing <term>Ammianus Marcellinus</term>). The strings were originally made of linen threads, but were later made from gut, according to <term>Scaliger</term> in Book 1, Chapter 48 of his *Poetics*. In number they were only four, either corresponding to the number of the four elements, or the four seasons of the year; or perhaps in honor of the number four, which was held as a sacred number by the <term>Pythagoreans</term> <note>Followers of the philosopher Pythagoras who believed numbers were the essence of all things</note>, by which they also swore an oath, as <term>Pythagoras</term> testifies in his *Golden Poem*:

> By him who gave to our soul the <term>Tetractys</term> <note>original: "τετρακτὺν" - a triangular figure of ten points arranged in four rows, symbolizing the organization of the universe</note>,
> The fountain of eternal nature,

and as can be seen more extensively in the works of <term>Macrobius</term>, <term>Aulus Gellius</term>, <term>Suidas</term>, and others.

Or perhaps it was in honor of the <term>Muses</term>, of whom there were said to be only four in the beginning; or according to the number of the four <term>Pythagorean proportional harmonic numbers</term> 1, 2, 3, 4. Within these, all the ancient <term>Consonances</term> <note>Musical intervals that sound pleasing together</note> are contained, such as the <term>Unison</term>, <term>Fourth</term>, <term>Fifth</term>, <term>Octave</term>, <term>Twelfth</term>, and <term>Fifteenth</term>. The first and last strings sounded an <term>Octave</term> apart; the two middle strings sounded a <term>Whole Tone</term> apart from each other, but formed a <term>Fourth</term> or <term>Fifth</term> against the outer strings, as can be clearly seen from these <term>Harmonic numbers</term>: 6, 8, 9, 12. However, this <term>Music</term> was in the beginning very simple...

...they remained so until the time of **Orpheus**, when the number of strings reached **seven**, corresponding to the number of the seven planets, or according to the seven daughters of **Atlas**. Among these was **Maia**, the mother of **Mercury**—who is said to have first invented the lyre—as **Polydore Vergil** <note>original: "Polyd. Virgil." - an Italian scholar of the Renaissance who wrote a famous history of "first inventions"</note> testifies in Book 1, Chapter 15 of *On Discovery* <note>original: "de invent."</note>.

Afterward, other instruments with many strings were invented, such as the <term>Epigonium</term> <note>A stringed instrument of ancient Greece</note> by **Epigonus of Ambracia** with 40 strings; the <term>Simicum</term> with 35 strings, which **Julius Pollux** and **Gioseffo Zarlino** mention in the preface to the first Dialogue of *Harmonic Demonstrations* <note>original: "Demonstrat. Harm:"</note>; and the <term>Magadis</term> <note>An ancient harp-like instrument</note> with 20 strings, which **Athenaeus** mentions in Book 13.

In **Palestine**, **Asia Minor**, and **Greece**, there are no longer any traces <note>original: "Vestigia"</note> of any ancient instruments. For **Muhammad**, in order to propagate his tyrannical rule, devilish sect, and crude, inhuman barbarism, forbade in his entire land not only the liberal arts—which serve to promote friendliness—but also everything that serves for joy, such as wine and string music. In their place, he ordained a "devil’s bell" and a "rumble-drum" <note>original: "Rumpelfaß" - likely a disparaging reference to Ottoman percussion</note> with a snarling and screeching <term>Shawm</term> <note>original: "Schalmeyen" - a loud, double-reed woodwind instrument</note>, which are still held in high regard by the **Turks** and used at weddings and joyful feasts, as well as in war. For when the children of the **Turkish Emperor** or other great lords are to be circumcised, such a procession is organized:

First, two **Turks** ride ahead; one with a kettledrum <note>original: "Heertrummel"</note>, the other with a **shawm**. Following them are several well-equipped riders, and after these, another two musicians similar to the first. Following this, an ox with gilded horns and hung with fragrant leaves is led, which a large... <note>The text cuts off here; the next page begins with "number" or "multitude"</note>

a number of riders follow. After them come musicians and again an ox, similar to the first. These are followed by several distinguished gentlemen and riders, then a crowd of well-adorned Janissaries <note>Elite infantry units that formed the Ottoman Sultan's household troops and bodyguards.</note> on foot, among whom is the Lord's son, who is to be circumcised. Finally, many musicians with drums and shawms <note>A medieval and Renaissance wind instrument, the precursor to the modern oboe.</note> follow them all the way to the church <note>The author likely means a mosque, but uses the familiar Christian term.</note>.

When a Christian has also become a Mameluke <note>A term used here for a convert to Islam; originally referring to a member of a specific military caste.</note> and a Turk, and has allowed himself to be circumcised, they place him upon a beautiful horse and lead him through the entire city with shawms and drums. This "rag-music" is held in high regard among the Turks even to this day, while our music, by contrast, is utterly despised by them. For instance, when Francis I, King of France, sent a large and magnificent musical instrument—which required several men to carry, much to the amazement of the Turks—along with several select artists and musicians well-practiced in music, as a special gift of honor to the Turkish "bloodhound" Suleiman <note>Suleiman the Magnificent, who began his reign in the year of Christ 1520, or the year 926 of the Turkish Hegira (the Islamic calendar).</note>, it was at first dear and pleasant to the Turkish Emperor. However, soon afterward in Constantinople, when the people came running in crowds to hear such foreign, lovely musicians and gained a particular delight and love for this art, the Turkish Emperor became worried. He feared that his people might cast off their coarse barbarism through this and become more friendly—or, according to his pretext, "soft and effeminate." Therefore, he ordered such a magnificent instrument to be broken into pieces and burned with fire, and he sent the Frenchman's musicians back home.

But because a detailed account of this can be found in the <term>First Volume of the Musical Treatise</term> <note>original: "Primo Tomo Syntagmatis Musici," referring to the encyclopedic work by Michael Praetorius.</note>, I deem it unnecessary to provide further reminders of it here.

<meta>The catchword "Stim-" from the previous page likely refers to "Stimmen" (voices or stops), indicating a discussion on musical parts or organ registers.</meta>

instruments / as well as their strings, holes, and intonation, there is little to no instruction available / therefore I have endeavored, according to my simple ability, to bring to light in this **Second Volume** not only the sketches and likenesses of the artistic and lovely instruments currently in use in Germany, Italy, France, and England: but also their intonation, and how high or low they can be used. From this, not only can instrumentalists see how wind and stringed instruments are to be tuned and used together / but also the Cantors <note>The leaders of church music and choirs</note> in the arrangement of Concert-Music <note>original: "Concert-Music"; referring to music for mixed ensembles of voices and instruments</note> might see which voices are suited to this or that instrument because of their depth or height.

I have also wished to include the likenesses of foreign, barbarian, and rustic instruments / which are used partly in Moscow, Turkey, and Arabia / and partly in India and America / so that they might be known to us Germans, not indeed for practical use, but for the sake of knowledge.

Furthermore, because not much is found in historical records regarding organs / I have also wished to include as much as I could learn about ancient organs and their structure / and how from the design of the ancients, these current New Organs have arisen from year to year / regarding the pipework and many types of stops <note>original: "Stimmen"; in this context, the different sets of pipes in an organ</note> set to various foot-tones <note>The pitch level of an organ stop, e.g., 8-foot or 4-foot</note> / as well as the bellows / windchests / manual and pedal keyboards, etc. Then also, by way of a **Corollary** <note>original: "Corollarii"; an appendix or additional deduction</note>, I have wished to include how the Regal <note>A small portable organ with reed pipes</note> and Harpsichord <note>original: "Clavicymbel"</note> are to be tuned purely and easily / what is especially to be observed in the delivery of an organ / and also the specifications of several notable organs.

Since Your Honorable Worships and Excellencies are particularly great patrons of music and hold it in high, dear, and worthy regard; just as you have always had distinguished people in your highly praised school / such as **Georg Rhau** <note>A famous 16th-century cantor and printer in Wittenberg</note> / who in his time already [composed] a Mass with 12 voices— <note>original: "Stim-"; the text cuts off mid-word</note>

Composed parts, performed music in St. Thomas Church <note>The famous Thomaskirche in Leipzig, later home to J.S. Bach</note> before a large assembly, and thereby earned great applause / also afterwards, around the year of Christ 1530, he published a special **Practical Music** <note>original: "Musicam practicam"; the study of musical performance and composition as opposed to abstract theory</note> in two books / which is still cited by the Italians today: Furthermore, Johannes Galliculus, who was so experienced in practice / that around the year of Christ 1520, he published a special treatise **on the composition of song** <note>original: "de compositione Cantus"</note> in public print: To pass over others after these for the sake of briefness / mention is made with all honor and fame of the highly experienced and excellent mathematician, musician, and chronologist, Mr. Sethus Calvisius of blessed memory / who not only attained an immortal name for himself in matters of chronology and music / but also instructed the excellent man Master Johannes Lippius in such a way that he advanced far in music / and could have published many further writings for the benefit of our common Fatherland / had he not been taken away from this life by an early death / whose place has now been filled by a likewise noble practical musician and composer, Johann Hermann Schein <note>Schein was one of the most important German composers of the early 17th century</note>. 

Thus I am also of the opinion / that the ingenious mathematician and music theorist, Heinrich Baryphonus <note>A Latinized name for Heinrich Pipegrop</note> from Wernigerode of the Cherusci <note>A reference to an ancient Germanic tribe, often used by scholars of this era to denote their regional heritage</note>, currently a musician and Cantor in Quedlinburg, will honorably follow the aforementioned excellent Calvisius, especially regarding what concerns the **Theory** of music / and will shortly bring to light his **Works on Music Theory** <note>original: "Opera Theorico-Musica"</note>, with which the German nation will be notably served / and for which many noble people already wait with longing.

And because until now great favor, a well-disposed will, and kindness have been shown by Your Reverence and Lordship <note>original: "E. Hochw. vnd Herrligk."; a formal honorific address to a high-ranking patron</note> toward my lowly, undeserving person / for which I have not yet been able to find a fitting opportunity to show myself grateful. Thus I have been of the mind / that I would present myself with this very small work <note>original: "Opusculo"</note> to Your Excellency, as one who would gladly be grateful, if only he were able—

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Dated the 19th of June, on which day now more than 1,294 years ago, the Council of Nicaea <note>The first ecumenical council of the Christian church, held in 325 AD</note>, which was summoned by the Christian Emperor Constantine the Great and held by 318 bishops against the cursed heresy of Arius <note>Arius taught that Jesus was a created being, subordinate to God the Father; his views were condemned at Nicaea</note>, took its beginning. # To all Organists, Instrumentalists, Organ and Instrument Makers, and those who practice and love <term>Instrumental Music</term> <note>original: "Musicam Instrumental"</note>, not only of the <term>German</term> <note>original: "Teutscher"</note> but also of other nations.

**W**iſhing you <note>The large decorative initial "W" begins the word "Wünschet," meaning "wishes"</note>—the Author, along with proper greetings and due respect for your various stations—his service, luck, blessing, and all welfare: And he requests in a friendly and helpful spirit that everyone take this, his well-intentioned work, in the best possible light. He has brought this work together with no small effort and expense, drawing from other proven writings and <term>accounts</term> <note>original: "Relationibus"</note> as well as from his own diligent research and experience. 

It should not be perceived or criticized as if he intended to make this art common, or to reveal it to every ignorant <term>fumbler and criticker</term> <note>original: "Hümpl- vnd Schimpler," derogatory terms for unskilled amateurs or musical charlatans</note> in our German mother tongue. Indeed, such a thing has already been improperly attributed and reproached to him by several "highly learned wise-acres." 

Yet, this work is certainly no <term>Sacred Rites of Vesta</term> <note>original: "Sacra Vesta," referring to the Roman goddess of the hearth whose mysteries were guarded</note>, nor those of the <term>Mother of the Gods</term> <note>original: "Matris Deorum," referring to Cybele</note>, which the <term>profane common people</term> <note>original: "prophanum vulgus"</note>, as the <term>Poet</term> <note>Likely a reference to Horace’s "Odi profanum vulgus"</note> says, must pass by. Nor is it the <term>Mastery of the Philosopher’s Stone</term> <note>original: "Magisterium Lapidis Philosophici"</note>, which the authors of <term>more secret philosophy</term> <note>original: "Secreterioris-Philosophia," i.e., Alchemy</note> wish to hold as a special <term>mystery</term>. Nor are these the hidden <term>principles</term> <note>original: "rationes"</note> and causes in nature why the <term>Islands of the Nymphs</term> <note>original: "Nympharum Insulae"</note> in Lydia, at the sound of a pipe, move from the land into the sea and move in a crosswise fashion as if they were leading a dance, and afterwards return to their place on the shore—as <term>Marcus Varro</term> <note>A prolific Roman scholar (116–27 BC)</note> testifies, claiming to have seen it with his own eyes.

The Author also knows very well, without needing any reminder, that he published the <term>First Volume</term> <note>original: "Primum Tomum," referring to Volume I of Syntagma Musicum (1614/15)</note> in the Latin language, which the other <term>Volumes</term> <note>original: "Tomi"</note> should rightfully have followed in like form. However, he had sufficient reasons to publish this second and also the third <term>Volume</term> in the German language. This is because every language has not only its particular <term>idioms</term> <note>original: "Idiomata"</note> of speech, but also its own distinct <term>technical terms</term> <note>original: "Terminos"</note> currently in use among <term>Italians</term> and <term>Germans</term>, which cannot easily be translated with proper and clear Latin <term>expressions</term> <note>original: "dictionibus"</note> and <term>words</term>. Consequently, the discourse would become much more obscure and unintelligible rather than clearer—especially since the majority of organ and instrument makers, organists, and instrumentalists are not proficient in the Latin language.

<meta>The previous page established that the author is writing in the German vernacular to make musical knowledge accessible, despite criticism from academic "wise-acres" who believe such things should remain in Latin.</meta>

Thus, the author has intended in this work—as in all his others—to serve the common Fatherland of the **German Nation** with the talent and gifts graciously bestowed upon him by God the Lord. He wishes to leave a well-intentioned memory for **posterity**, however much longer this transitory world, now nearing its end, may remain. Namely: which various **musical instruments** <note>original: "Musicalische Instrumenta"</note> are currently in use, praise be to God, in Imperial, Royal, Electoral, and Princely chapels, as well as in other churches, for the honor of God and the blessed encouragement of our hearts.

It would be highly desirable if we could know today, and have for our use, exactly which **musical instruments** and **church organs** <note>original: "Organa Ecclesiastica"</note> existed before and during the time of David and Solomon, and thereafter—and how each was specifically shaped, tuned, and constructed according to its kind. Unfortunately, however, no such records have been left in any **antiquities** <note>original: "Antiquiteten"</note>; therefore, the **instrumental music** <note>original: "Musica Instrumentalis"</note> of the ancients remains very little known to us—indeed, entirely unknown. One finds in several libraries a book printed in Basel in the year of Christ 1511, in quarto <note>This refers to Sebastian Virdung's *Musica getutscht*, the first printed book on musical instruments</note>, in which some of the ancient as well as some of the current instruments are **sketched** <note>original: "abgerissen"</note>. But such a work is not actually that old, and furthermore, the use and properties of the illustrated instruments cannot be particularly well understood from it.

Therefore, the author hopes the aforementioned <term>Zoili</term> <note>A "Zoilus" is a term for a nitpicking or envious critic, named after Zoilus of Amphipolis, a Greek grammarian known for his harsh criticism of Homer</note> will reconsider and have a better change of heart. They should consider how many heart-warming things and excellent arts have been published and brought to light by prominent physicians, surgeons, mathematicians, geometers, painters, and others skilled in the **Liberal Arts**, thereby significantly serving posterity. They should likewise view his **labors** <note>original: "labores"</note>, intended for the best and for the common good, with better consideration and reflection. 

He is also quite willing to allow other, more prominent people—who for many years have looked quite deeply into the **antiquities** not only of musicians but also of historians and philosophers—to take this opportunity to significantly improve these **humble sketches** <note>original: "schlechte delineationes"</note> and slight instructions, and to bring them to light more clearly and perfectly. To others who are just beginning, however, he intends only to have given a little occasion for further research and reflection. And if he has indeed **erred** <note>original: "halluciniret," literally "hallucinated" or wandered in mind</note> or gone astray in one thing or another, whether in his first works or these current ones, or has set down or written too much or too little: he does not doubt that reasonable hearts—those who do not act out of passion, hatred, or **envy**...

### 1. On the dignity and excellence of the Organ. pages 82 to 89

Wherein, among other things, it is mentioned that it would be desirable for organists—who devote themselves to this noble art with particular earnestness, zeal, and diligence—to be provided with better pay and maintenance, and that they should not be held in lower or more contemptuous regard than the lowest craftsman. This is especially true because in the time of King David, such <term>churchmen</term> <note>original Latin: "Ecclesiastici"</note> and <term>spiritual musicians</term>, <term>Levites</term>, and <term>priests</term> existed, and they were ordered and esteemed next to the priests, just as <term>preachers</term> and <term>pastors</term> are today. And I am of the unwavering opinion that if King David (who was, above all others, a singular lover, patron, and protector of <term>musicians</term> <note>original Latin: "Musicorum"</note>, indeed a chief among all <term>chapel masters</term> <note>original German: "Capellmeistern"</note> and <term>musicians</term>) could have heard and possessed such an excellent organist as are now found in several places, he would not have known how highly he should <term>extol</term> <note>original Latin: "extolliren"</note> and exalt him. Yet, at this present time, many—and indeed good—organists must make do with an annual salary of 50, 40, 30, or even fewer Thalers. Because of this, I cannot wonder enough how such good people are often able to support themselves with a wife and children and manage their coming and going. And since people listen with particular delight and love when a nimble organist performs and brings forth spiritual Latin and German psalms and songs on the organ beautifully, gracefully, and lovely (whereby the heart, as if with joy, <term>rejoices</term> <note>original Latin: "Iubiliret"</note> within itself with special devotion and attentiveness, and is encouraged and driven toward the following sermon): therefore, all and every authority, city council, church elder, and congregation of every place should rightly see to it and be mindful that such servants of the church might be held in greater respect and provided with a better <term>living allowance</term> <note>original Latin: "Competentz"</note>, salary, and maintenance.

->I humbly request that this reminder of mine<-

<meta>This page follows the technical discussions of organ building and pitch, moving into the practical and social consequences of musical discord within the church service. It emphasizes the need for cooperation between the Organist, the Cantor (choir leader), and the instrumentalists.</meta>

and they should conduct themselves peacefully in unanimity, meeting one another with choir-measured harmonic intonation and resolution <note>original: "Final," referring to the concluding note of a musical phrase.</note>, so that the music is not thrown into confusion, God and the Christian congregation are not offended, and they do not bring harm upon themselves. For if an **Organist** does not maintain the proper range <note>original: "Ambitum," the compass or span of notes in a piece of music.</note>, but instead transposes the song against the **Cantor’s** <note>The Cantor was the official in charge of the choir and the musical direction of the church service.</note> wishes by a second or a third <note>original: "per Secundam oder Tertiam." This means shifting the pitch up or down by one or two steps on the scale.</note>, it subsequently ends up either in the heights in a squeaking and shrilling, or down low in a grumbling and booming. By this, not only is the nature and character of the mode <note>original: "Modi." In the 17th century, music was based on "modes" rather than just major or minor scales, each believed to provoke specific emotions.</note> changed, which alters the emotional effects <note>original: "affectus"</note> it should move, but the music—as far as both the singers and instrumentalists are concerned—is also thrown into confusion. 

For if the Cantor is skilled in music, he certainly will not follow the Organist in this; rather, because a Cantor can usually find and grasp the correct choir-tone <note>original: "Chor-Thon." This was the standardized pitch used by the church choir, which often differed from the pitch of secular instruments.</note> by a clef, or a choir-pipe, or even by his own voice, he will begin anew—after the organ has finished playing—in the other and correct choir-measured key <note>original: "Chormessigen Clavij"</note>. This is not only vexing to hear in the church, but can also easily give cause for confusion among the students. For because the previous organ key and range are still fresh in the students' memory, it rarely passes without confusion, or at the very least begins with great difficulty until one becomes accustomed to the newly struck tone and key and lets the one given by the organ depart from the mind and memory. 

To say nothing of the fact that such a thing is also quite shameful for the instrumentalists, the town and art-pipers <note>original: "Stadt- vnd Kunstpfeiffer." These were professional guild musicians employed by the city to play for civic and church events.</note>. For if any Cantor follows the Organist in the wrong key and begins the singing before the town pipers arrive and start with him—or before they first blow into the **cornett** <note>A woodwind instrument with a trumpet-like mouthpiece, very popular in the Renaissance and Baroque for doubling choral parts.</note> or **trombone** <note>original: "Posaun"</note> and give the Cantor the correct choir-measured key—they cannot proceed, especially on the cornetts or violins, which are tuned specifically to the choir and the correct key. This is because transposition by a second or third is not well known to them, seeing as it is sour and difficult enough for some to transpose a song by a fourth or a fifth; thus they create an outright confusion, or otherwise produce miserable work.

In the face and before the holy ears of GOD and the Christian congregation, however, they profane and desecrate the public worship not a little with such ill-sounding inconsistency and hostile music; they grievously offend the LORD God as a God of order, and they also disgrace themselves, much to the vexing annoyance of Christian, devout hearts.

## II.

Since it has also come to my attention that my Latin works <term>Opera|Latin for 'works,' referring to published musical collections.</term> published four years ago—such as the *Song of the Mass*, *Song of Hymns*, *Song of Greatness*, and *Song of Blessing* <note>original: "Missodia, Hymnodia, Megalodia vnd Eulogia." A massive collection for large ensembles of singers and instruments.</note>, shall be quite willingly and gladly provided and delivered without any charge by me and my household to those who desire them—provided that they write with the prior authorization of the pastors or churchwardens of that place. However, let no one presume to demand them in a frivolous manner...

## III.

Since I have treated certain matters—especially in the **Third Volume** <note>referring to 'Syntagma Musicum III,' his major theoretical treatise.</note>—which some **Musicians** and City **Cantors** might initially **judge unfavorably** <note>original: "sinistrè judiciren"</note> before they properly understand them, perhaps even **mocking and disapproving** <note>original: "Cavilliren vnd improbiren"</note> of one thing or another, or interpreting and explaining it in this way or that: I therefore ask once more that if a **doubt** or reservation should arise anywhere: they might notify me in writing or in person and hear my opinion on the matter. 

However, should I meanwhile depart from this world through death according to **GOD’s** will, I do not doubt (as I have also requested of my friends) that other good people will be found in *Dresden, Halle, Leipzig, Quedlinburg*, and other places who are well-acquainted with such a new manner. Should any **opposing writings** <note>original: "Contraria Scripta"</note> be published against me, these people would be able to **defend my opinions and views** <note>original: "Sententiam vnd Opiniones defendiren"</note> and present them somewhat more clearly and extensively to the world.

For I intend hereby only to provide a modest guide and impetus, and as it were, to lay the **preamble** <note>original: "Praeambulum"</note> and the first foundation stone, upon which other more excellent **Musicians** <note>original: "Musici"</note> may further **continue** and complete the structure according to their best ability. Since something more and better can be discovered from day to day, they may fully **complete** and supplement whatever might still be **desired** <note>original: "desideriret"</note>. This is especially because I may not be able to bring several matters and treatises to a full conclusion due to weakness or other accidents—including, among others, a work on **thorough-bass** <term>General-Baß|Also known as Basso Continuo, a system of musical notation where a keyboardist improvises an accompaniment over a given bass line.</term>, the delivery of organs, and several more (which were partly **promised** in my **Works** <note>original: "Operibus"</note>, and of which a good beginning has already been made, having also **conferred** on these new developments with several distinguished Musicians who will well remember it).

Therefore, let the dear Musician and lover of Sacred Music be favorably pleased and willing to bear with me (as one who initially applied himself to the **other liberal arts** <note>The "Artes Liberales" were the traditional university subjects like grammar, logic, and rhetoric; Praetorius suggests he came to professional music later in life.</note> and attained the **practice of Music** very late) and with those **Musical Works** <note>original: "Operibus Musicis"</note> which have been prepared within sixteen years (solely through God’s grace and gift). Some of these have been promoted to print at my own expense, while others are still held back for **revision** <note>original: "ad revisionem"</note>. And because of my manifold weaknesses, constant travels, and other frequent hindrances, these works could not come forth so **elaborately and perfect in every part** <note>original: "elaboratum & ex omni parte perfectum"</note>; I ask that you take this in the best spirit and help to excuse it **in Christian good faith** <note>original: "pro candore"</note>. If it is not all perfectly successful, it is nonetheless well-intentioned and from the heart.

May the pious, dear, and faithful **GOD** now grant His help so that—just as we have begun in this transitory life to arrange the heavenly prayers and songs of praise of the Holy Patriarchs, Prophets, Apostles, and other spirited, godly Christians with various choirs (at times not **without confusion** <note>original: "absq; Confusionibus"</note>) and to strike them up with stammering tongues—so also in the future, in the approaching eternal life and heavenly, imperishable being, at the joyful wedding of our heavenly Bridegroom **JESUS CHRIST**, we may stand before the Throne of the Lamb with the heavenly **Singers** <note>original: "Cantoribus"</note> and **most perfect Musicians**, all the Holy Angels and Archangels. There, we shall hold a constant, everlasting choir and **alternate through various Choirs** <note>original: "alternatim per Choros varios"</note> with our cry of praise and joy. We shall, as it were, **perform in the concerted style** <term>Concertiren|In this period, "concerting" referred to the "concertato style," where different groups of voices or instruments interact, compete, and contrast with one another.</term> to laud and prize God the Lord, the triune and undivided Holiness, and with the Cherubim and Seraphim, sing the most lovely and precious **concerted** songs: the threefold **Holy, Holy, Holy** <note>original: "Sanctus, S. S. Heilig"</note>

<meta>This page begins the main body of the Second Volume of Michael Praetorius's *Syntagma Musicum*, known as *De Organographia*. ## Part One
### This is
# THE SECOND VOLUME.

->Concerning the General or Common Description of Musical Instruments (as they are<-
->currently in use): And then also concerning their Names, Classification, and<-
->complete distinctions.<-

## I.

AS FAR AS the description of musical instruments is concerned, they are described as the artistic works of noble and deep-thinking artists, who invented them through diligent reflection and industrious practice, prepared them from suitable materials, and shaped them with proper and proportioned forms according to art; through these, they produce a beautiful *harmony* <note>original: "harmoniam"</note> or pleasing sounding-together, and are used for the spreading of God's honor, as well as for the lawful and becoming pleasure and delight of mankind.

## II.

But regarding the classification of such musical instruments, one cannot appropriately distinguish them from one another except by their tone and sound.

Firstly, *regarding the qualitative generation* <note>original: "quo ad qualitativam generationem"</note>: namely, how and by what movement of the instruments and the human limbs that same noise and sound is produced.

Secondly, *regarding the quantitative measurement* <note>original: "quo ad quantitativam mensurationem"</note>: when we consider the sound and tone of the instruments according to how long it lasts, or how high and low it can be produced.

## III.

Concerning now the tone or tuning of musical instruments, *regarding their qualitative generation*; there are some instruments which through

the air is made to ring and resound: Namely, when the air is guided into their artfully made passages, and they thereby give forth a well-sounding ring: And they are called *wind instruments* <note>Greek original: "ἐμπνευστά" (empneusta)</note>, blowing-in or blowing-on instruments.

### IV.

However, there is still a distinction here: for some are made to sound through the help of **natural air**; but some are blown into by **human breath**.

### V.

The first kind are the instruments which—when the wind or air is let into the pipes by the raising of the bellows—are caused to ring or sound by the striking of the keyboard: Such as,
->The pneumatic organ <note>original: "Organum pneumaticum"</note>.<-
->The positive organ <note>original: "Positivum"</note>.<-
->The portable organ <note>original: "Organum portatile"</note>, a small organ which can be played<-
->while being carried.<-
->The regal <note>original: "Regale," a small portable organ with reed pipes</note>.<-
And these one could call **piping instruments**.

### VI.

But those which are blown into by human breath are called *Inflatilia* <note>Latin: "wind instruments"</note>, blowing instruments. And of these, there are some which are blown and sounded by the mouth alone, without any movement of the instrument; such as,
->The trumpet <note>original: "Tuba"</note>.<-
Some, however, in addition to the blowing of human breath, are simultaneously pulled with the hands or directed with the fingers; and these either have no holes, such as,
->The trombone <note>original: "Buccina seu Trombone"</note>.<-
whereby the lower tubes or slides <note>original: "Züge"</note> must be pulled out and in, now one way, now another, with one hand or a grip;
Others, however, have holes which, when one blows into them, are now pressed shut with the fingers and now left open again, according as the tone in the song requires it.

### VII.

These instruments which have holes are, furthermore, of three kinds. The first

### VIII.

Regarding the first group, which have holes only in the front and no thumb-holes in the back, these are of two types: For some have a bag attached to them, such as,
->The bagpipe <note>Latin: *Tibia utricularis*; German: *Schafforgel* or *Schäfferpfeiffe*—literally "shepherd's organ" or "shepherd's pipe"</note>.<-

### IX.

->The cornett <note>Latin: *Cornu*; Italian: *Cornetto*; German: *ein schwarzer krummer Zinck*—a "black curved cornett" made of wood covered in leather</note>.<-

->The crumhorn <note>Latin/Italian: *Cornamuse*; German: *Krumbhörner*—literally "crooked horns" due to their J-shape</note>.<-

### X.

Thirdly, those which have holes in the front, back, and also alongside on the sides, and are pressed closed with the palms of the hands <note>Because these instruments have multiple bores or very thick walls, the hands must cover more than just the front holes</note>, are these:
->The rackett, sordun, double-recorder, and shryari <note>German: *Schreypfeiffen*—literally "screeching pipes," a loud, capped-reed instrument</note>.<-

### XI.

And so these are the wind instruments <note>Greek: "ἔμπνευσα" (*empneusta*); Latin: *Inflata*</note>. Now follow those which are called non-wind instruments <note>Greek: "ἄπνευσα" (*apneusta*)</note> and specifically percussion instruments <note>Greek: "κρουστὰ" (*krousta*); Latin: *percussa*</note>.
These are those which are struck with special wooden sticks or other things; and these are again distinguished; for some have no strings <note>Greek: "ἄχορδα" (*achorda*)</note>, while some do have strings <note>Greek: "ἔγχορδα" (*enchorda*)</note>.

### XII.

Those which have no strings are made to ring and sound solely through hitting or knocking: And this is done,
1.  By iron or wooden mallets or small sticks, such as:
    **The kettledrum or drum.** <note>original: *Tympanum*</note>
    **The triangle.** <note>original: *Crepitaculum*</note>
    **The xylophone.** <note>original Latin: *Clavitympana*; German: *Strohfiedel*—literally "straw-fiddle," a folk instrument where wooden bars were laid on bundles of straw.</note>
2.  By clappers or small pellets, such as:
    **Church bells.** <note>original: *Campanæ*</note>
    **Small bells.** <note>original: *Tintinabula*</note>
    **Cymbals.** <note>original: *Cymbala*</note>
    **Rattles.** <note>original: *Sistra*</note>
    **Jingle bells.** <note>original: *Nolæ*, *Schellichen*</note>

### XIII.

The instruments which are called **stringed** <note>original Greek: *enchorda*; Latin: *fidicinia*</note> or instruments with strings: some of these have gut strings, made from the intestines of animals and especially from sheep; others, however, have metal strings, prepared from steel, silver, iron, brass, or other materials.

### XIV.

Those which have gut strings produce a lovely **harmony** <note>original: *Concent*—a term for the sounding together of multiple parts</note>, of which 1. some are played and controlled solely with the fingers, such as:
**The lute.** <note>original Latin: *Testudo* (literally "tortoise," referring to the bowl shape), *Chelys*</note>
**The theorbo, which is like a large bass lute.**

**The quintern.** <note>original: *Quinterna*—a small guitar-like instrument</note>
**The harp or psalter.** <note>original: *Arpa*, *Psalterium*</note>
2.  Others, however, are touched and stroked with a horsehair bow at the same time, such as:
    **The lira or lirone.** <note>original: *Lyra, Lyroni*—referring here to the Italian *Lira da braccio* or *Lira da gamba*</note>
    **The large lira.** <note>original: *Arci-violate lyre*</note>
    **The viola da gamba.** <note>literally "leg viol"</note>
    **The violin, rebec, or small fiddles.** <note>original: *Violino, Rebechino, Fides, Fidicula*</note>
    Otherwise called **the arm viol** <note>original: *Viol de bracio*</note> or **the viola bastarda.** <note>A specialized, mid-sized viol used for virtuosic, improvisatory playing</note>

## **The Trumpet Marine, a Tromba Marina.** <note>original Latin/Greek: *Chorus seu Tympanischiza*; German: *Trumscheidt*. A long, triangular-bodied bowed instrument that produces a brassy sound through a vibrating bridge.</note>

This is an instrument of considerable length / almost like a beam / upon which the four **strings** are tuned with a bow / and it gives a resonance / just as if there were four trumpets / and clarions were blown along with them. Concerning this, see also in the 2nd part.

3. There is yet another instrument / on which the keys are struck at the same time / and the **strings** are vibrated with a wheel / instead of a bow / namely:

### **The Peasant Lyre, or the common Hurdy-Gurdy.** <note>original Latin: *Lyra Rustica, seu pagana*; German: *gemeine Lyra*</note>

## XV.

These **instruments** / which were just recounted / have (as was said) **gut strings**. Now follow those which are strung with **metal strings** (drawn from silver / iron / steel or brass). And these same are made to ring or are struck;

1. Only with the bare fingers / such as /
->**Pandora, Penorcon, Orpheoreon, Irish Harp.** <note>These are various types of large, wire-strung plucked instruments popular in the late Renaissance.</note><-

2. Some, however, with a small quill / such as:
->**The Cittern.** <note>original Latin: *Cithara*; German: *Cither*</note><-

3. In some, the strings are struck with raven feathers / which are inserted into the wooden jacks <note>original: *Tangenten*. While we use "tangents" for clavichords, here the author refers to the plucking mechanism of the harpsichord family.</note> / such as:
->**The instrument specifically so-called, the Virginal, the Spinet,**<-

## XVI.

And all these **instruments** recounted so far can be called **primary** <note>original: *prima*</note> / to distinguish them from those following / which, as **derived from the first** <note>original: *â primis orta*</note>, are as it were composed from the preceding / such as. 1. **The Claviorganum**, which is an instrument / where not only are the pipes [sounded] by the bellows / but also the strings by the quills / by the striking of the keys / are made to ring / and thus give off a lovely sound.

2. **The Jaw Harp** <note>original Latin: *Crembalum*; German: *Brummeisen*</note> / for which / if it is to be made sounding / the human breath / just as in the other wind instruments / must also assist / and it must be struck at the same time with a finger. And in such a way these instruments could be called **Mixed** <note>original: *Mixta*</note> or blended.

### XVII.

And this is thus the consideration of the sound or tone of musical instruments, **regarding their qualitative generation** <note>original Latin: *quo ad qualitativam generationem*</note>, as to how and in what form the same is put into action and produced.

Furthermore, we must also consider that very same sound or tone **regarding its quantitative measurement** <note>original Latin: *quo ad quantitativam mensurationem*</note>, according to its proportions.

And this first, 1. **with respect to duration** <note>original Latin: *respectu longitudinis*. Here meaning the stability or "length" of time an instrument stays in tune.</note>, whether the tone remains constant and stable or not. 2. **with respect to breadth** <note>original Latin: *respectu latitudinis*</note>, which **instruments** can **imitate, represent**, and bring to light all voices and **tones** <note>original Latin: *tonos*</note>: which, however, only allow a few voices to sound, and which produce only a single tone. 3. **with respect to depth, or elevation and depression** <note>original Latin: *respectu profunditatis vel elevationis & depressionis*</note>, which instruments can be forced and brought beyond their natural tone, and which cannot.

### XVIII.

Now considering first the tone of musical instruments **with respect to duration** <note>original Latin: *respectu longitudinis*</note>, we find that: 1. Some **instruments** **keep** their tone constantly and do not easily change it, even if they are struck and used steadily and daily: such are all those which we have called "clapping and striking instruments," and hereafter also several whistling [wind] instruments, such as the **Pipe Organ** <note>original Latin: *Organum*</note>, an organ and **Positive organ** <note>A small, playable pipe organ without pedals.</note>.

2. In some, however, the tone is quite easily and often changed and put out of tune: such as among the wind instruments which are blown with the mouth, the **Bagpipe** <note>original Latin: *Tibia utricularis*; German: *Sackpfeiffe*</note>, and almost all stringed **instruments** which are strung either with **metal strings** <note>original: *Erzsaiten*</note>, such as the **Cittern, Pandura, Penorcon, Orpheoreon, Irish Harp** <note>original Latin: *Cithara, Pandura, Penorcon, Orpheoreon, Arpa Hybernica*</note>: or with **gut strings**, such as the **common harp** <note>original Latin: *Arpa communis*</note>; **Lute** <note>original Latin/German: *Testudo, Lautte*</note>; **Theorbo, viols, violins**, fiddles, **Lyre**, etc. Although **instruments** strung with gut strings go out of tune much sooner than those with metal strings, because the former (depending on the weather) expand or contract much more easily and sooner than the steel and brass strings, and therefore become changeable all the more quickly.

3. Some, however, stand in the middle, which do not keep such a completely constant tone as the first group, yet are not so very easily displaced as the others; such as the **Kettledrum** <note>original Latin: *Tympanum*</note>, **Regal** <note>A small portable organ with reed pipes.</note>, **Clavichord, Harpsichord, Spinet.**

### XIX.

Secondly, when we [consider] the tone and sound of musical instruments—

# ON THE DESCRIPTION OF INSTRUMENTS.

<meta>Catchword: different</meta>

Looking at instruments **with respect to breadth** <note>original Latin: *respectu latitudinis*</note>, that is, how many tones or voices each instrument can produce, there are:

1. Some instruments are **all-voiced** <note>original Greek: *πάνφωνα* (panphona); Latin: *Omnivoca* or *omnisona*</note>. These are full-voiced instruments which can represent and produce all the voices of any song or, as is commonly said, can play all the parts. I call these **Foundation Instruments** <note>original: *Fundament Instrumenta*</note> because they are used to provide the harmonic foundation for a singer, or are otherwise played alone. These include: the Organ, Regal <term>Regal: a small portable organ with reed pipes</term>, Harpsichord, Virginal, Lute, Harp, Double Cittern, Pandora, Penorcon <term>Penorcon: a rare, bass-range string instrument similar to a bandora</term>, and the like.

2. Some, however, are **many-voiced** <note>original Greek: *πολύφωνα* (polyphona); Latin: *Multi* <gloss>voca / sona</gloss></note>, which do not produce all, but only several voices. These include the Small Cittern, the Small *Lyra da braccio*, and the *Lyra da gamba*.

3. Some are **single-voiced** <note>original Greek: *μονόφωνα* (monophona); Latin: *uni-* <gloss>voca / sona</gloss></note>, which assist the harmonic ensemble with only one voice. These include all instruments that are blown with the mouth, such as: Trombones, Cornets <term>Zincken: early woodwind instruments with a cup-shaped mouthpiece, often called cornetts</term>, Flutes, Shawms <term>Schalmeyen: loud, double-reed ancestors of the oboe</term>, and the like; as well as some stringed instruments like Violins <note>original German: *Geigen*</note> and the like. In the **Third Volume** <note>referring to *Syntagma Musicum* Vol. 3</note>, these are called **Ornamental Instruments** <note>original: *Ornament Instrumenta*</note>.

->XX.<-

Finally and thirdly, when we consider the tone and sound of the instruments **with respect to depth** <note>original Latin: *respectu profunditatis*</note>, or **according to their rising and falling** <note>original Greek: *κατ' ἄρσιν & θέσιν* (arsis and thesis)</note>, as musicians are accustomed to saying: specifically, which instruments can be drawn or forced higher or lower in pitch. Namely:

1. Some instruments cannot easily be forced or brought beyond their natural tone. These include all stringed and percussion instruments, as well as some wind instruments, particularly the pipe-like instruments.

2. However, some instruments—when played by a famous and experienced artist and musician—can be brought quite well somewhat higher or lower through the help of the lips, by adjusting the mouth and the breath. Each of these instruments will now be discussed here in greater detail hereafter.

# ON THE DESCRIPTION OF INSTRUMENTS.

### Chapter I.

## How the words **Instrument** and **Instrumentalist**, **Accord**, **Sorts**, and **Falsetto** voices, in pipes and other instruments, are to be understood.

To avoid all error that might arise from the inconsistent use of the words **instrumentalist** and **instruments**, it is first to be known here: That although the common man understands and pronounces the word or name **instrument** very **specifically** <note>original: *specialiter*</note> (namely, referring to a **harpsichord** <note>original: *Clavicymbel*</note>, **symphony** <note>likely a virginal or small keyboard instrument in this context</note>, **spinet**, **virginal**, and the like; as well as the name **instrumentalist**, as referring only to one who can strike <note>i.e., play</note> such a aforementioned **harpsichord** or **symphony**, or "play" it as they say in the Netherlands): yet such a thing cannot be permitted and is incorrect.

For because the **noun "instrument"** <note>original: *nomen instrumenti*</note> is quite **general** <note>original: *generale*</note>, and must be **referred** <note>original: *referirt*</note> and applied to all **musical instruments**, **especially single-voiced ones** <note>original: *præsertim univoca*; instruments that play only one melodic line at a time</note>, or **ornamenting instruments**, as they are called **in Volume Three**, such as cornetts, trombones, flutes, violins, and whatever other names they may have; it cannot be so narrowly constrained, nor **specifically** <note>original: *in specie*</note> **referred** to a single **all-voiced instrument** <note>original: *instrumentum omnivocum*; one capable of playing many voices or polyphony simultaneously, like a keyboard</note> alone. And therefore, those who can play the **symphony** or **harpsichord** must not be called **instrumentalists** in the general sense, but rather **organists** **to distinguish them** <note>original: *ad differentiam*</note>.

And although the organ—(because of its excellence, and because, as found in the more detailed report in the 1st point of the following treatise on old organs, almost all other **musical instruments** are contained within it)—is called an **organ** <note>original: *organum*</note>, or an instrument of all instruments: yet it will not do to use the word "instrument" in that way here, because it would create great **confusion** and inaccuracy. Since in all Imperial, Royal, Electoral, and Princely **chapels** <note>original: *Capellen*; musical ensembles or courtly musical establishments</note>, all those who can perform their **parts** on **single-voiced instruments** <note>original: *instrumentis univocis*</note>—that is, on simple instruments that have and carry only one voice, be they wind or stringed, cornetts or violins, etc.—whether on many kinds or only a few, are called by the name **instrumentalists**; while those appointed to the organ, **regal**, and **symphonies** are called **organists**. **In Italy**, those who are able to **practice** and **perform** their craft thoroughly on all **musical** instruments, both **all-voiced** and **single-voiced**, are called **universal**; however, very few of them are found <sig>B ij</sig> <meta>catchword: will be.</meta>

...to be played. Since a **craftsman** <note>original: *Artifex*</note> in these matters strives much more toward practicing <note>original: *præktiren*</note> something substantial on a single instrument, or at most on two, so that he might be **unique** <note>original: *singular*</note> and **excel** <note>original: *excelliren*</note> above others; rather than it being said of him, "**a little of everything, nothing of the whole**" <note>original: *ex omnibus aliquid, de toto nihil*</note>, a fault which is otherwise quite common among us Germans.

An **Accord** <note>original: *Accort*; in this context, it refers to a "consort" or a complete set of instruments of the same family</note> is a complete **set of voices** <note>original: *Stimmwerck*</note> of pipes, bassoons, and other instruments; wherein from the lowest bass and the largest pipes, one follows after the other in sequence, up to the smallest **soprano** <note>original: *Discant*</note> pipes.

**Sorts** <note>original: *Sorten*</note>, however, refers to just one single type of pipe within that same Accord; these can be more clearly identified in the table placed after Chapter 4.

**Falsetto voice** <note>original: *FalsetStimme*</note> in a pipe or other instrument is the term for that which can be achieved and "forced out" by a skilled master beyond the natural high or low range of any wind instrument.

# ON THE DESCRIPTION OF INSTRUMENTS <note>original: *DE ORGANOGRAPHIA*</note>

### Chapter II.

## Regarding the proper pitch of organs and other instruments, 
## and how it is used sometimes higher, sometimes lower, in different countries and places: Likewise, what difference exists between "Choir Pitch" and "Chamber Pitch": 
## Also, how high and low the human voice can be raised and brought.

It is only right that not only an **instrumental musician**, but also every composer and music director <note>original: *Capellmeister*</note> should know how high and low every **musical instrument**—the wind instruments as well as the stringed instruments—can be pushed and used, so that they may be guided accordingly in composition and otherwise. For a composer must take diligent care that he does not, through his composition, drive the instrument higher than it is by nature capable of doing; otherwise, a **human voice** must necessarily be placed with it so that one can help the other, which would otherwise not be needed.

In the same way, it is necessary for every organist to know how to distinguish one voice <note>meaning a "stop" or rank of pipes</note> from another in the organ, and especially what is meant by a pitch of 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 16, 24, or 32 feet, so that one may be guided accordingly when changing the stops.

Although many others may have more and better knowledge of these matters than I do myself, I have nevertheless—for the sake of those unpracticed in these things who have frequently requested it of me—not wished to refuse to record something here for further reflection.

Initially, it is important to know that the pitch varies greatly in organs as well as in other **musical instruments**; for because "concertizing" <note>playing together in mixed ensembles</note> and making music with all kinds of instruments together was not common among the ancients, wind instruments were made and tuned very differently by instrument makers—one high, the other low. For the higher an **instrument is tuned in its own manner and kind** <note>original: *in suo modo & genere*</note>—such as cornets <note>original: *Zincken*</note>, shawms, and soprano violins—the more fresh they sound and resonate. Conversely, the deeper the trombones, bassoons, **bassanelli**, **bombards** <note>original: *Bornbardoni*</note>, and bass violins are tuned, the more solemn and magnificent they appear. Therefore, it causes a **musician** much trouble when the organs, **positive organs**, **harpsichords**, and other wind instruments are not simultaneously set to one and the same proper pitch.

However, the Choir Pitch <note>original: *Chor Thon*; the standard pitch for church music</note> was originally a full tone lower and deeper among the ancients than it is now, which can be seen in old organs and other wind...

...instruments still to be found: And thereafter, from year to year, it was raised so far as it is now in use in Italy and England, as well as in the princely chapels of the German lands. Although the English pitch on instruments is still somewhat—though very little—lower, which can be perceived in their cornetts, **shawms**, or **oboes** (as they call them) that are manufactured there.

There have been some, however, who have dared to raise our current pitch by yet another semitone. While it is not my place to correct this, in my opinion such a height is very uncomfortable for the **vocal singers** <note>original: *Cantoribus vocalis Musicae*</note>, especially for the altos and tenors, and often nearly impossible to reach. Therefore, one should rightly let it remain at the aforementioned pitch; for even as it is, it is frequently found to be too high, not only for the vocalists but also for the instrumentalists of stringed instruments, such as **violins** <note>original: *Violini de Bracio*</note>, **violas da gamba**, as well as lutes, pandoras, and the like. For they must be exceptional strings to withstand such high tension. This is why, when one is in the middle of a performance, the top strings <note>original: *Quinten*; the highest-pitched string on a violin or lute was often called the 'quint' or 'chanterelle'</note> snap away, and the performance lies in the dirt <note>an idiomatic expression meaning the performance is ruined or comes to a halt</note>. To ensure that the strings can better stay in tune, such stringed instruments must commonly be tuned a tone lower, and then necessarily performed a second lower with the other instruments <note>the players must transpose their music down a step to match the lower-tuned strings</note>. While this seems difficult to inexperienced instrumental musicians, it helps the vocalists and singers greatly to perform a tone lower for their voices.

For this reason, I am extremely well-pleased with the distinction made in Prague and several other Catholic chapels, where the pitch is divided into **Choir Pitch** <note>original: *ChorThon*</note> and **Chamber Pitch** <note>original: *CammerThon*</note>. For there, the current common pitch, to which almost all our organs are now tuned, is called **Chamber Pitch** and is used only for the table and in banquets <note>original: *Conviviis*</note> for merriment; this is then most convenient for instrumentalists, regarding both wind and stringed instruments.

**Choir Pitch**, however, which is a whole tone lower, is used only in the church. This is done, firstly, for the sake of the vocalists, so that they—since the greatest and most frequent labor in the church rests upon them (especially in Catholic chapels, where the singing lasts a long time due to the many psalms and other parts)—may better manage with their voices and not become hoarse so quickly because of the high pitch. Secondly, because the human voice, when it moves in the middle and somewhat lower range, is much more pleasant and lovely to hear than when it must shout and scream at the top of its capability. Therefore then

# ON THE DESCRIPTION OF INSTRUMENTS <note>original: *DE ORGANOGRAPHIA*</note>

...then, <note>original: *propter alias etiam multifarias commoditates, suavitatem singularem et concentus benè susceptos*</note> **on account of various other conveniences, a singular sweetness, and well-received harmonies**, it would not be a bad thing if all organs were tuned and set a tone or a second lower. However, this is now quite impossible to change in our German lands, and therefore we must surely remain with the usual **Chamber Pitch** <note>original: *Cammerthon*</note> (which at this time in most places is called **Choir Pitch** <note>original: *Chor-Thon*</note> and is regarded as such).

In England in former times, and in the Netherlands still today, they have tuned most of their wind instruments a **minor third** <note>original: *tertiam minorem*</note> lower than our current Chamber Pitch, so that their *F* is our *D* in Chamber Pitch, and their *G* is our *E*. Just as the excellent **instrument maker** in Antwerp, **Johannes Bossus**, tuned most of the **harpsichords** <note>original: *Clavicymbeln*</note> and **virginals** <note>original: *Symphonien*</note>, as well as the **pipework** built into them, to that same pitch.

And it is indeed true that in this lower pitch, one can give and provide the harpsichords a lovelier and more charming resonance (as knowledgeable instrument makers know) than when they are measured according to Chamber Pitch; just as the flutes and other instruments sound lovelier in such a low pitch than in the "correct" pitch, and bring with them almost an entirely different quality to the ear (since they do not scream so harshly in the high register).

But such instruments are very inconvenient to use in **full ensemble music**; and we shall now have to remain only with the two previously mentioned, namely **Choir Pitch** and **Chamber Pitch**.

Nevertheless, in Italy and in other **Catholic chapels** in **German lands**, the aforementioned lower pitch at the **lower third** is very much in use. For some Italians take no pleasure in high singing—and not without reason—opining that it has no grace, and that the text cannot be properly understood; one crows, screams, and sings in the high register just like the **grass-maids** <note>original: *Graßemägde*; a derogatory comparison likely referring to the unrefined, shrill singing of rural laborers in the fields</note>. Therefore, it is sometimes the custom that they perform the **Hypo-Ionian mode** <note>a specific musical scale or "mode" starting on C</note> from *C*, and when the same is transposed **by a fifth** <note>original: *per quintam*</note> into *F*, they perform it yet another third lower from *D* with organs, **positive organs**, and accompanying instruments. Even though this mode, perhaps better than any other, could be performed **by human voices** <note>original: *humanis vocibus*</note> **without further transposition**, this is nevertheless arranged in this way solely for the sake of the vocalists and singers. In the same manner, the **Hypo-Dorian mode** is also performed a third lower from *E*. Such **transpositions** <note>original: *Transpositiones*</note> certainly seem somewhat bitter and disagreeable at first to an organist as well as to other instrumentalists; but if one does not let the effort grieve him, but rather practices with diligence for a time...

...practices and exercises himself therein, it is and will become quite easy for him, indeed almost a pleasure to practice and perform. <note>original: *practiciren vnd præstiren*</note>

Now, when the **Chamber Pitch** <term>Cammer Thon: The standard performing pitch used in royal chambers and for instrumental music, which Praetorius notes was often higher than older standards.</term> customary at this time is given to an organ by the **organ builder** and the entire instrument is tuned accordingly, then in most organs that are not built too small or meagerly, the lowest **C** in the **Principal** <note>The "Principal" is the core set of pipes that provides the foundational sound of the organ.</note> stop of the **Manual Keyboard** is of 8 feet. This pitch then corresponds exactly with the proper **harpsichords** and **spinets**, and is called **Equal** <note>original: *AEqual*</note> by the organ builders, because it corresponds in depth and height with the human voice; as can be understood further and more extensively in the following Table No. IV. For this **C** is the true depth of a proper bass singer in a Princely Chapel, when he can naturally produce it with a full and whole voice. Some can descend even lower (though somewhat unclearly) down to **AA** and **GG**. But they cannot descend lower, even though they often try to force themselves to reach the **F** <note>original: *assequiren*</note>; however, it is a completely imperfect sound and tone.

Yet, in former times at the court of his Princely Serenity in **Bavaria** at Munich, during the time of the excellent and world-renowned musician **Orlando di Lasso** (where the musical establishment is said to have been quite strong, numbering some 90 persons: 12 bassists, 15 tenorists, 13 altists, 16 choirboys, 5 or 6 castrati <note>original: *Capunern oder Eunuchis*</note>, 30 instrumentalists, and so on), there were, among others, three bassists—two brothers named Fischer and a peasant's son named Grasser—who could reach the low **F** according to **Choir Pitch** <term>Chor Thon: The standard pitch for church music, which could vary significantly from city to city.</term> (which in **Chamber Pitch** is the **E** of 13 feet) <note>Praetorius cites 13 feet here, which is an unusual measurement compared to the standard 12-foot or 16-foot pipe lengths, likely indicating a specific regional pitch variance.</note> very strongly and with a full voice; yet in the high register they could go no further than f, g, or a. Likewise, one in Rome named **Cæsaron** was found with a similar voice and strength. In the high register, most bassists can reach c' and d', and indeed even f'—as could, among others, the former Neapolitan monk Carolus Cassanus (who served in various Electoral and Princely Chapels in Germany) quite purely, strongly, and with a full voice, alongside the low notes, reaching **G in Chamber Pitch**. Common bassists in schools, however, can seldom reach below the **F** of 6 feet or the **E** with true natural strength, and in the high register some cannot ascend <note>original: *ascendiren*</note> very far beyond a.

How high and low a tenor, altist, eunuch, or soprano <note>original: *Discantist*</note> can approximately reach with their voice is shown in the following table. It is enough if a tenor can reach c' and an altist f' in **Chamber Pitch**; if he can reach higher, it is all the better and more praiseworthy for him.

### Chapter III.

## UNIVERSAL TABLE
# Of all wind and stringed instruments,
->Wherein are found<-

### 1. SIGNS.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'D' featuring scrolling foliage.</image-desc>The **Signs** or **Clefs** <note>original: *Claves signatæ*</note>, as they are drawn at the beginning of all songs and compositions / to distinguish one voice from another.

### 2. KEYS IN THE TABLATURE SCALE.

The keys <note>original: *Claves*</note> set according to **organ tablature** <term>Tablature: A form of musical notation indicating instrument fingering or specific keys rather than just pitches on a staff. Organ tablature used letters to represent notes.</term>, according to which one can most conveniently orient oneself for all musical instruments. Because nearly six octaves are contained therein / I could not think of any other way to present or prescribe this / so as to distinguish one clearly from the other. In this way I have often considered / how the lowest **pedal keys** from 8 to 16-foot pitches <note>Organ pipe pitch is measured in feet; an 8-foot pipe produces the standard pitch, while a 16-foot pipe sounds an octave lower.</note> might be marked. And although it would not be so very absurd / or rather to place two large letters like **CC**, **DD** (just as the ancients did in their scale, and I have also kept here in the signs, having placed two small letters above) close together at the bottom: Yet this finally pleased me better / that the large letters should be marked and placed somewhat thicker and fuller / and also with a little stroke at the bottom, thus: <gloss>C</gloss> <gloss>D</gloss> etc. marked and placed.

<meta>catchword: 3. Foot-</meta>

<summary>Praetorius discusses the powerful singing voices of castrati in courtly chapels before introducing a "Universal Table" for all instruments. He explains his specific notation system for organ tablature, focusing on how to clearly label different octaves, especially the low pedal notes.</summary>
