<header>ON THE DESCRIPTION OF INSTRUMENTS.</header>

### 3. Feet.

In this Table at Number 3, the names and number of **Feet** <term>Feet: A measurement used by organ builders to designate the pitch of a stop. An 8-foot pipe produces the standard pitch, while a 4-foot pipe sounds an octave higher, and a 16-foot pipe sounds an octave lower.</term> are indicated / according to how organ builders use the term / by which they aptly name the stops and keys <note>original: *Claves*</note> in the pipes / according to their tone and sound / in height and depth / and bring them to an easy understanding / pronunciation and naming / and thus can better distinguish one tone from another. And because such a distinction is urgently necessary to observe in other musical instruments <note>original: *instrumentis Musicis*</note> as well as in the human voice / and is not unhelpful to recognize / and since no other more convenient name can be found for it; I have retained this word (**Feet**) here / and have found it necessary to use it.

### 4. HUMAN VOICE.

Regarding the **human voice** <note>original: *VOX HUMANA*</note>, a necessary reminder was given in the preceding chapter.

---

### Chapter IV.

Furthermore, in this Table, as well as in the following detailed report and explanation, the following will be shown more extensively:

1. How many various kinds and sorts are found together in every **consort** <term>Consort: A "Stimmwerck" or family of instruments of different sizes (e.g., soprano, alto, tenor, bass) designed to be played together.</term> of instruments / and in a full ensemble <note>original: *Accort*</note>.

2. Also / how deep and how high every wind instrument can be brought in its natural tone / (which the **white notes** indicate; ) and what **falsetto voices** <term>Falsetto voices: Extended notes beyond the "natural" range of an instrument or voice, achievable only by highly skilled performers.</term> / above and below / can be brought about by a practiced and experienced instrumentalist beyond the nature and property of each instrument. Which falsetto voices / because not everyone can always attain or reach them either with the human voice <note>original: *humana voce*</note> or on wind instruments / I have marked with **black notes**.

3. How many strings or **courses** <term>Courses: A "Chor" or pair of strings tuned to the same note, common on instruments like the lute or cittern.</term> the stringed instruments have / and how high or deep one string must be pulled and tuned from the other.

4. Alongside this, it is to be known here in general above all things: That in this entire work throughout / the instruments and voices are calculated and distributed not according to **Choir Pitch** / but according to **Chamber Pitch** <term>Pitch Standards: In the 17th century, pitch was not standardized. "Chorthon" (Choir Pitch) was often higher and used in churches, while "Cammerthon" (Chamber Pitch) was the standard for courtly and instrumental music. Praetorius advocates for Chamber Pitch here as the more universal reference.</term> (as it / as previously mentioned / is very well and rightly distinguished by some). Because **Chamber Pitch** is the most common / and almost all instruments / both stringed and wind / as well as the organs of the present time / are directed and tuned to this **Chamber Pitch**.

### VII. Recorders and Pipes
<note>original: *Flautti: plockpfeiffen* (recorders) and *Schwägel* (a small three-holed pipe used with a drum).</note>

| 1. Type | 2. | 3. | 4. | 5. | 6. | 7. | 8. |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Great Bass** | **Bass / Tenor / Alto** | **Basset / Tenor / Alto / Cantus** | **NB. Bass / Cantus** | **Tenor / Alto / Cantus** | **Exilent** <note>The smallest recorder, also called a *Garklein*.</note> | | |
| <margin>f</margin> | <margin>c</margin> | <margin>g</margin> | <margin>f</margin> | <margin>c</margin> | <margin>g</margin> | | |

<note>The diagram above maps the various sizes of recorders onto musical staves. The notes are written in diamond-shaped "white notation" common in the Renaissance and early Baroque.</note>

**Note Well.** This flute—as well as the transverse flute <term>transverse flute: a flute held horizontally, as opposed to the vertical recorder</term> in this pitch—can be used not only for the **Discant** <note>Soprano range</note>, as I have placed it here, but also for the **Tenor** an *octave* lower. As it is commonly held by several instrumentalists, they believe that this type of recorder and transverse flute possesses the true sound and **tone** of a Tenor; and that its lowest **key** <note>original: *clavis*—referring here to the lowest finger-hole or note</note> produces the Tenor C or D, and thus gives off its sound at the **four-foot pitch** (according to the **organ-maker’s scale** <term>organ-maker’s scale: a system where pipe length determines pitch; an 8-foot pipe produces standard pitch, 4-foot is an octave higher, and 2-foot is two octaves higher</term>). 

And to tell the truth, I was also of the same opinion at first, because it is very difficult to recognize and distinguish this by ear. But when one allows this pitch to be **tuned** <note>original: *intoniren*</note> against the pitch of organ pipes, and carefully takes heed of one against the other with a diligent ear, it is revealed to be only a true **Discant**, where the key of C or D sounds at the **two-foot pitch**. 

The same situation also applies to the **Bass** and other flutes that belong to such a **consort** or **set of instruments** <note>original: *Accort oder Stimmwerck*</note>. In these sets, the very large and the small bass flutes sound no differently than if they were an octave lower—as if the lowest key in the one Bass flute sounded B or C at eight feet, and in the very large flute D or F at twelve feet. Yet, in reality, the sound and tone of these large bass flutes extends no further than to six feet, and the other to **four-foot pitch**.

<summary>This page illustrates the pitch ranges of recorders and flutes, correcting a common misconception by clarifying that they actually sound an octave higher than many musicians of the time perceived.</summary>

<note>original: *Theorba* — A large member of the lute family developed in Italy. It features a very long neck and two pegboxes: one for the strings played on the fingerboard and another for the long, open bass strings (diapasons) that provide a rich lower register.</note>

### 26. Quintern
<note>original: *Quinterna* — A small, high-pitched instrument of the lute family, often seen as a relative or ancestor of the guitar. It typically had four or five courses of strings.</note>

### 27. Mandora
<note>original: *Mandürichen* — A "little mandora." This was a small, treble lute with a pear-shaped body, usually played with a plectrum or the fingers for fast, melodic lines.</note>

### 28. Bandora
<note>original: *Bandoer* — A large, bass-range instrument with wire strings and a scalloped, festooned body shape. It was often used in "broken consorts" (ensembles of different types of instruments).</note>

### 29. Penorcon
<note>original: *Penorcon* — A rare instrument similar to the bandora but with a slightly wider neck to accommodate more strings, though shorter in length.</note>

### 30. Orpharion
<note>original: *Orpheoreon* — Named after the mythical musician Orpheus, this instrument featured wire strings but was tuned like a lute, allowing lute players to play wire-string repertoire easily.</note>

**Signs.**
<note>original: *Signa.* — These symbols on the left of the musical staves represent the clefs (G, C, and F clefs) used to define the pitch range for each instrument's strings.</note>

# Trombones.
<note>original: *Tromboni, Posaunen.*</note>
->(See Illustration Column VIII in the *Sciagraphia*)<-
<note>The *Sciagraphia* is the appendix of woodcut illustrations that accompanied Praetorius's book.</note>

The trombone (Latin: *Tuba ductilis, oblonga* <note>original: "extended, oblong tube"</note>; Italian: *Trombone, Trombetta*) exists in four different types or varieties.

1. **Alto or Soprano Trombone:** *Trombino, Trombetta picciola* <note>original: "little trumpet"</note>, on which a <term>soprano part</term><note>original: *Discant*. The highest vocal or instrumental range.</note> can be played very well and naturally. However, the <term>harmony</term><note>Here meaning the resonance and tonal quality.</note> is not as good in such a small body as it is when a high range is reached on the standard common trombone through a good <term>embouchure</term><note>original: *Ansatz*. The way a player applies their mouth to the mouthpiece.</note> and practice.

2. **Common Standard Trombone:** *Tuba minor, Trombetta*, or *Trombone piccolo*, on which one can naturally reach from high <term>f</term><note>f1</note> down to <term>E</term><note>E2</note>. With a good embouchure, one can naturally achieve two more notes above and below, and thus play an alto part quite well.
Although some—including the famous master in Munich, Phileno—have progressed so far through extensive practice on this instrument that they can sound the low <term>D</term><note>D2</note> and the high <term>c'', d'', e''</term> in the soprano range without particular difficulty or strain. Furthermore, I heard one Erhardus Borussus in Dresden (who is said to be staying in Poland currently); he had mastered this instrument so thoroughly that he could reach the height of a <term>cornett</term><note>original: *Zincke*. A curved woodwind instrument with a trumpet-like mouthpiece, famous for its agility.</note>, namely the high <term>g''</term> <note>original: *sol re ut*</note>. He could also reach the depth of a <term>bass trombone</term><note>original: *Quart-Posaun*</note>, reaching the low <term>A</term><note>A1</note> with such fast <term>coloratura</term><note>original: *Coloraturen*. Rapid, ornamental musical passages.</note> and leaps <note>original: *saltibus*</note>, as if playing on a <term>bastard viol</term><note>original: *Viol de Bastarda*. A virtuosic string instrument known for playing complex, jumping divisions.</note> or a cornett. This can be seen to some extent at the end of the fourth Canzona in this third part.

3. **Bass Trombone:** *Tuba major, Trombon grande, Trombone majore* <note>original: "Large or Great Trombone"</note>. Some of these are a fourth lower, and some a fifth lower than the common or standard trombone, and exactly an octave below the alto trombone. A player who is skilled and agile on the standard trombone can also easily progress on this one; he must simply imagine that everything he plays is a fifth higher, and when the <term>flat sign</term><note>original: *Signum ♭*</note> is marked, he should visualize it as if it were the note <term>F</term>.

<margin>
Bass
Trombones
</margin>
<note>original: *Quart-Posaunen*</note>
<image-desc>Musical notation showing transposition: The top staff in bass clef shows a series of notes with a flat (B-flat, A, G, F), while the bottom staff shows how they correspond to the standard trombone's positions (F, E, D, C).</image-desc>

For this reason, it might more appropriately be called a "Fifth-Trombone." However, it should be noted here that because bass trombones vary—some being larger than others—the <term>slide positions</term><note>original: *Züge*</note> will also fall differently.

<meta>catchword: 4. Octave- [trombone]</meta>

<summary>This page describes the varieties of the trombone family, focusing on the alto, common standard, and bass (Quart) trombones. Praetorius highlights the impressive technical range and agility achieved by virtuoso players of his era.</summary>
<keywords>Trombone, Alto Trombone, Bass Trombone, Phileno, Erhardus Borussus, embouchure, coloratura, musical range, instrument construction</keywords>

--- Page 60 ---
<meta>This page continues the catalog of wind instruments, specifically the largest variety of trombone, and begins the discussion of the trumpet. It maintains the technical detail regarding instrument construction and pitch found in the previous section.</meta>

<header>ON THE DESCRIPTION OF INSTRUMENTS.</header>

4. **Octave Trombone**: <note>original: *Tuba maxima*, *Trombone doppio*, or *la Trombone all Ottava basso*</note> the "greatest trumpet" or "double trombone" was very rarely found in earlier times. However, there are two types of them that I have seen. The first is exactly twice as long as the common, standard trombone, without any extra loops of tubing. Therefore, in its slides and other parts, it is exactly the same as the standard trombone, except that it produces a tone an octave lower. It naturally reaches the note <term>E</term>, but with a good <term>embouchure</term> <note>original: *Ansatz*; the way a player applies their mouth to the mouthpiece</note> it can also reach <term>D</term> and <term>C</term>. This particular type was made four years ago by a master wind-player named *Hans Schreiber*. A drawing of it can be found in the *Sciagraphia* <note>The book's illustrated appendix</note>, Columns VI and VII.

The second type is not quite twice as long, but it has slightly thicker tubes and also uses <term>crooks</term> <note>original: *Krum-Bügel*; detachable lengths of tubing used to change the instrument's pitch</note>, through which the low range is achieved. These have already been in use in several court chapels for many years.

This musical instrument, the **Trombone**, is particularly useful above all other wind instruments in all kinds of ensembles and concerts. This is because it can be adjusted to all pitches, made slightly higher or lower, not only by adding or removing <term>crooks</term> <note>original: *Cromette*</note> and other extension pieces <note>original: *Polette*</note>, but also through the breath and the mouth. Even without adding these curved crooks, a practiced and experienced artist can force the instrument to play <note>original: *per tonos & semitonia*</note> in whole and half steps at his pleasure using only his embouchure and the mouthpiece. This cannot be done on other instruments where the holes must be controlled by the fingers.

## Chapter VI.
# The Trumpet.

<image-desc>Ornate decorative initial T with floral scrollwork and vine motifs.</image-desc>The Trumpet: <note>original: *Vulgo Taratantara, seu Tuba, Instrumentum in curvum ex ære argentovè, cujus sonitu milites, equiq; ad prælium inflammantur; à tubis id est, canalis concavitate nomen habens: Italis Tromba*</note> Commonly called the *Taratantara* or *Tuba*, it is a curved instrument made of brass or silver, whose sound inflames soldiers and horses for battle; it takes its name from *tubis*, that is, the hollowness of a canal; called *Tromba* by the Italians. It is a magnificent instrument when played by a master who can control and rule it with skill. It is truly a wonder that on this instrument—without any slides such as those used to control trombones—one can produce almost all the notes in the high register one after another, including some half-steps, and can achieve all kinds of melodies. And although until now trumpeters have based their fundamental or bass note in <term>D</term> according to <term>Chamber Pitch</term> <note>original: *Camerthon*; the standard pitch used for secular music</note>, which the...

<meta>catchword: Field-</meta>

<summary>This page describes the rare Octave Trombone, noting two distinct construction styles, and introduces the Trumpet as a noble military and melodic instrument capable of high-register scales despite lacking slides.</summary>

<keywords>Octave Trombone, Hans Schreiber, crooks, embouchure, trumpet, Chamber Pitch, brass instruments, instrument construction</keywords>

--- Page 61 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of the trumpet, specifically focusing on recent modifications to its length and pitch to match standard ensemble tuning. It then transitions into the seventh chapter, which begins a detailed technical description of the recorder family.</meta>

<header>ON THE DESCRIPTION OF INSTRUMENTS.</header>

Field Trumpets <note>original: *FeldtTrumter*</note> were formerly kept in their original state. However, only a few years ago, at several princely and noble courts, they have been lengthened in their dimensions or have had <term>crooks</term> <note>original: *Krumbbügel*; curved pieces of tubing</note> attached to the front. This tunes their bass a tone lower into C, in the <term>Hypoionian Mode</term> <note>original: *Ad Modum Hypojonicum*; a specific musical scale</note>, which then matches <term>Choir Pitch</term> <note>original: *ChorThon*; the standard pitch for church music at the time</note>. Regarding this, Glareanus also writes in his *Dodecachordon* <note>original: *Dodecachordo*, book 2, chapter 27; a famous 16th-century music theory book</note>:
> <note>original Latin: "Tubarum sonitus hodie inter Modi Hypojonici limites constat, integra omnibus Chordis diapente, sed diatessaron extremis potissimum."</note> The sound of trumpets today remains within the limits of the Hypoionian mode; there is a full fifth for all notes, but a fourth especially at the extremes.

Some, however, prefer that they be brought a half or whole tone lower into B-flat <note>original: *B*</note>.

Some have trumpets manufactured that are wound together like a posthorn or a snake; however, these are not equal to the others in resonance. One also finds very long trumpets, tightly and densely wound together from bark <note>original: *Past*</note>, with which the shepherds from the Vogtland and Switzerland (called the *Wästerwälder*) wander around the cities seeking their livelihood. (Illustrations of all these can be found in *Sciagraphia*, Column VIII).

### Chapter VII.
## Flutes / Recorders.
->(in Sciagraphia: Column IX.)<-

Recorders (in Latin <term>Fistula</term>, called <term>Flauto</term> by the Italians and <term>Recordor</term> by the English) have seven holes in front and one in back for every size in the set <note>original: *Corpore*</note>. Even though there are two holes side-by-side at the very bottom, they both produce the same tone. They are only placed that way because some instrumentalists use their left hand at the bottom, while others use their right. Therefore, one of these two holes must be plugged with wax.

The largest recorders normally <note>original: *Ordinarie*</note> produce no more than 13 tones; in the small ones, however, one can have 14 tones, depending on how good they are. <term>Beyond the ordinary range</term> <note>original: *Extraordinariè*</note>, certain skilled instrumentalists can ascend four tones higher, or even seven tones higher than the aforementioned 13 or 14. These are called <term>Falsetto voices</term> <note>original: *FalsetStimen*</note>, as was indicated above in Chapter 1.

How many different sorts and ranges there are of recorders, and of all the other instruments mentioned in this treatise, can be understood from the previously provided Table and in Chapter 1. However, for further instruction, I have also included the eight varieties of recorders here.

### ON THE DESCRIPTION OF INSTRUMENTS.

1. **Little recorder** <note>original: *Klein Flötelin*</note>; a <term>fifteenth</term> <note>original: *Quintadecima*</note>, that is, two octaves higher than a <term>cornetto</term>.
2. **Descant recorder** <note>original: *DiscantFlöt*</note> a fourth lower.
3. **Descant recorder** a fifth lower than the first type.
4. **Alto recorder** <note>original: *AltFlöt*</note>; an octave lower than the first type.
5. **Tenor recorder** <note>original: *TenorFlöt*</note>; a fifth lower than the fourth type.
6. **Basset recorder** <note>original: *BassetFlöt*</note>; another fifth lower; these have a <term>key</term> <note>original: *Schloß*</note> or <term>fontanelle</term> <note>a protective wooden cover over the brass key mechanism</note> at the bottom.
7. **Bass recorder** <note>original: *BasFlöt*</note>: A fifth lower than the sixth type.
8. **Great Bass recorder** <note>original: *GroßBasFlöt*</note>; an octave lower than the sixth type or set.

And such a complete **consort** <note>original: *Stimmwerck*</note> can be obtained from Venice for approximately 80 **Thalers** <note>a silver coin used throughout Europe</note>. Related to these is the **pipe** <note>original: *Schwiegel* or *Eckpfeiffel*, also called the *StamentienPfeiff*</note>: this has only 2 holes in the front and one in the back. It is equal in length to a transverse flute but is voiced like a recorder. It is used by some **Englishmen** with the left hand, accompanied by a **small drum** or **tabor** (see Column 9): it ascends from g' up to g'' and a'' and even higher. Some are a fifth deeper, from g to f' and a'. It is truly to be wondered at that one can reach such high and wide ranges with only three holes, which otherwise cannot be achieved on instruments with 6 or 7 holes.

Just as one also has very small little recorders—about three or four inches long (see Col. 9)—which have three holes in the front and one in the back, and in the same manner almost two octaves can be achieved on them. Both the three-holed pipe and such small recorders must be controlled at the bottom opening with a finger <note>to produce certain notes by partially closing the end of the tube</note>. The **Stamentien pipe** is 20 inches long; the tenor is 26, and the bass 30 inches.

Additionally, I must necessarily point out that initially, when arranging **concerts**, the **recorder choir** <note>original: *Flöten Chor*; Italian: *Choro da flauto*—that is, when several instrumentalists with recorders are organized into a choir, as will be further explained in the third volume</note> was not a little difficult for me. This is because one very rarely finds such recorders that are perfectly in tune with each other, especially because—as will follow in Chapter 44—even the **organs** in some churches, which are easily affected by heat and cold, are found to be lower in pitch in winter and higher in summer. It would therefore be necessary to have two sets of wind instruments available, where one set or consort was tuned a half **semitone** <note>original: *Semitonium*</note> apart from the other. Therefore, this remedy occurred to me: that I divide the recorders in the middle, between the mouth and the finger-holes, and [fit] the uppermost piece...

...have it made two fingers longer, so that one can insert it into the lower part as far as one wishes or as is necessary, making the pipes longer or shorter. In this way, one can immediately help such a flute, whether it needs to be <term>higher</term> <note>original: *jünger* (literally "younger"); used here to mean a higher pitch</note> or <term>lower</term> <note>original: *gröber* (literally "coarser"); used here to mean a deeper, lower pitch</note>. And although some famous instrument makers were of the opinion that the flutes might become out of tune in some holes because of this, they later found no fault with it themselves, except for this: that some [flutes] did not want to "speak" <note>respond or sound</note> quite as well in the highest register.

Just as a **Cornetto** <note>original: *Cornet*</note> can be adjusted by pulling the mouthpiece further out or pushing it deeper in.

### Chapter VIII.
### Transverse Flutes.
->(in the Book of Illustrations, column IX.)<-

The Transverse Flutes (called **Traversa** or **Fiffaro** by the Italians) have six holes in the front and none in the back. They naturally produce 15 notes or tones, and four <term>falsetto</term> <note>overblown</note> tones above that, making 19 tones in total, just like a **Cornetto**.

The same situation applies to the **Recorder-flutes** <note>original: *Dolzflötten*; these were flutes designed with a recorder-like block but often held transversely</note> (which are otherwise called **Transverse Recorders**), except that these are voiced and blown like a **Recorder** <note>original: *Plockflötten*</note>.

To this category also belongs the **Swiss Pipe**, otherwise called a **Field Pipe** <note>original: *Schweitzerpfeiff* or *Feldtpfeiff*; essentially a military fife</note> (in the Illustrations, column XXIII). It has its own unique fingerings, which do not agree at all with the transverse flute, and it is used solely alongside the soldiers' drums.

---

### Chapter IX.
### The Cornetto.
->(in the Book of Illustrations, column VIII.)<-

Cornettos <note>Italian: *Cornetti*; and perhaps the Latin *Buccinae* or *Cornua* (Horns)</note> are of two kinds: **Straight** and **Curved** <note>original Latin: *Recti* and *Curvi*</note>. Of the **Straight** Cornettos, there are again two types:

1. **Straight Cornetto** <note>original: *Cornetto diritto*</note>: this is a straight cornetto onto which a separate mouthpiece must be placed.

<sig>E ij</sig>
<meta>catchword: 2. Cornetto</meta>

<summary>Praetorius describes methods for tuning wind instruments using adjustable joints and introduces the transverse flute family, including the fife and the 'sweet' recorder-flute. He begins a classification of cornettos, distinguishing between straight and curved varieties.</summary>

<keywords>tuning slides, pitch adjustment, transverse flute, fife, Swiss pipe, recorder-flute, cornetto, cornetto diritto, Bassanelli, instrument construction</keywords>

--- Page 64 ---
<meta>This page continues the classification of the cornetto family from the previous discussion on recorders and flutes, detailing the different sizes and timbres of cornetts before introducing the shawm and pommer (bombard) family in Chapter 10.</meta>

<header>ON THE DESCRIPTION OF INSTRUMENTS</header>

2. **Mute Cornett** (*Cornetto muto*); in these, the mouthpiece is turned out of the same piece of wood as the cornett itself (column 13). Their resonance is very soft, quiet, and lovely to hear; for this reason, they are also called "silent cornetts."

3. **Curved Cornetts** (*Cornetto Curvi*); these are the black, curved cornetts. 
All cornetts, without distinction, naturally produce 15 tones, from <term>a</term> up to <term>aa</term>. However, some can quite easily reach <term>gg</term> and sometimes even <term>ff</term> at the top, while at the bottom they can manage <term>g</term> and <term>f</term> in <term>falsetto</term> <note>original: *falset*; here referring to the "underblown" notes below the instrument's natural range</note>.

4. **Twisted Cornett** (*Corno* or *Cornetto torto*), otherwise called the **Cornon**, is a large cornett shaped somewhat like an 'S'. it is a fifth lower than a regular, common cornett. Although some believe this instrument produces no more than 11 natural tones or voices with no falsetto above them, the reality is different; it produces 15 tones just like the common cornetts. However, because the resonance is quite unpleasant and "horn-like" <note>original: *hornhafftig*; likely meaning a coarse or braying quality</note>, I am of the opinion that a trombone should be used in its place.

5. There are also very small cornetts, the **Cornettino**, which are a fifth higher than the regular common cornetts and cornetts, and are not unpleasant to hear.

---

### Chapter X.
## Pommers, Bombards, and Great Bombards: Shawms.
->(in the Book of Illustrations, column XI.)<-

> **Deep-sounders**, or "Buzzers," as the Greeks might call them, are long pipes which, when blown with great effort and exertion, emit a deeper, thicker sound. <note>original Latin: *Bombyces, sive Bombi Græcis etiam vocari queunt longæ tibiæ, quæ difficulter magnaq; cum contentione flatus impulsæ sonum crassiorem edunt.*</note>

**Pommers** (in Italian **Bombardo**, or **Un Bombardone**; the French call it **Houtbois**; the English **Hoboyen**) undoubtedly take their name *from the buzz* <note>original: *à bombo*; from the Latin *bombus*, meaning a humming or buzzing sound</note>, due to their humming and booming. All of them, the small as well as the large, are called by the name **Bombard** or **Pommer**. In Italian, the Great Bass Pommer is called **Bombardone**; the regular Bass is called **Bombardo**. The **Tenor**, which also has four <term>keys</term> <note>original: *Schlösser* (locks); refers to the brass fontanelles or keys that extend the range</note>, can also be used as a bass in an emergency because its keys allow it to reach the <term>G</term> in the bass register; for this reason, it is called the **Bassert**. This is followed by the **Nicolo**, which is the same size and pitch as the Bassert, except that it has only one key and therefore can only reach down to <term>c</term> in the tenor and no lower (column 13). The **Alto Pommer**, which is nearly the same size as the **Shawm** <note>original: *Schalmeyen*; the soprano of the family</note>, except that it has a key...

<summary>This page concludes the description of the cornetto family, including the mute, curved, and "horn-like" twisted varieties, before transitioning to the shawm (Pommer/Bombard) family, explaining their terminology and various sizes from alto to bass.</summary>

<keywords>mute cornett, curved cornett, cornon, cornettino, pommer, bombard, shawm, Bassert, Nicolo, musical range, instrument construction</keywords>

--- Page 65 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of the woodwind family from Chapter 10, specifically focusing on the naming of the shawm and the technical challenges of tuning and transposing when playing in ensembles of various sizes.</meta>

# ON THE DESCRIPTION OF INSTRUMENTS

...key and is a fifth lower, is called the **Small Bombard** (*Bombardo Piccolo*). Only the highest soprano instrument, which has no brass key, is called the **Shawm** (called *Piffaro* by the Italians and *Gingrina* in Latin <note>original: *Italis Piffaro, Latinis Gingrina*</note>, named after the cackling sound it makes, just like a goose, whose natural cry is a "honk" or "cackle" <note>original Latin: *gingrire*</note>).

In pitch, most shawms are a whole tone higher than **cornetts and trombones.**

It should be noted here: that since ancient times and even now, most wind instruments—such as **recorders, pommers, shawms, crumhorns, etc.**—have been built and tuned in sets or consorts where each size is a fifth apart from the next. For this reason (as I noted in the previous table for instruction), one can always use three together: one as the bass, the others as the tenor and alto. (For these two parts, tenor and alto, can always be played on instruments of the same size and build). The third size can then be used for the <term>Cantus</term> <note>the highest or soprano part</note>. 

However, when a fourth instrument is added to the group, the composition must be arranged accordingly. The <term>Hypo-Ionian mode</term> <note>a specific musical scale starting on C</note> should not be transposed a fifth up from "natural" B into F-flat, but rather a fourth lower into G-sharp, resulting in a <term>cantus fictus</term> <note>music using notes outside the standard scale, requiring accidentals</note>. Or, if a song is already written in F-flat, one must transpose it a whole tone (or a "second," as some call it) higher. This works out quite perfectly, especially on the **pommers and shawms.** 

But if one wishes to add a fifth instrument—either very high or very low—it is quite difficult to get them to tune together. This is because the highest instrument is separated from the lowest (as seen in the table) by five fifths—namely, by a seventeenth (which is the same as a <term>ditone</term> or major third plus two octaves). This is very difficult to harmonize. 

Even though this can be achieved if the music is specifically written for it and great care is taken, it would nevertheless be wise to advise an instrument maker to always produce—alongside the standard soprano and tenor pipes—another pipe that is one tone lower. In this way, the instrument would be tuned only a fourth, rather than a fifth, higher than the one below it. Then, one could successfully harmonize and tune five different sizes of these instruments together. This is already practiced by some, though it is still rare. The **Great Bass Pommer** is 10 feet and 1 inch long; this can be seen in the *Book of Illustrations* <note>original: *Sciagraphia*</note> in columns VI and VII, where it can easily be measured.

E iij

### Chapter 11.
## Bassoons: Dulcians.
->(in the Illustrations, column 10)<-

**B**assoons and Dulcians <note>original: *Fagotten vnd Dolcianen*</note> (called *Fagotto* and *Dolcesuono* by the Italians) are for the most part referred to by these names interchangeably. Otherwise, some maintain that the true Dulcians are those which the English call the **Single Curtal**. In their depth and resonance, these are similar to the basset shawm <note>the *Basset-Pommer*, a medium-low member of the shawm family</note>, except that the Dulcian—as well as the Bassoon—possesses a quieter and softer resonance than the shawms. For this reason, perhaps because of their loveliness, they are called Dulcians, as if to say "Sweet-sounding" <note>original Latin: *Dulciſonantes*</note>. 

This quality arises because the bodies of the shawms are built to their full length and are entirely open at the bottom. In the Bassoon, however, the length of the body is doubled over <note>the tube is folded back on itself</note> so that the hole where the resonance emerges is at the top. Occasionally (though not in all, as some remain entirely open), this opening is covered and then pierced again with small holes—much like certain organ stops I will discuss later in Part IV. Because of this, the resonance cannot be nearly as strong, but must sound somewhat quieter and lovelier. In the same way, the principal and trombone-style pipes in an organ—because they possess their full length and <term>scale</term> <note>the ratio of a pipe's diameter to its length, which determines its tonal character</note> throughout—sound much more strongly and brightly than the stopped pipes and other stopped reed stops <note>stops where the top of the pipe is capped</note>. This is based on the very same principle mentioned above.

On the **Choral Bassoon** <note>original: *Choriſt-Fagott*</note>, the lowest <term>key</term> <note>original: *clavis*</note> is **C**; on the **Double Bassoon**, it is **F**. However, it should be observed that there are two types of Double Bassoons. One reaches the **F** just like the great Bass Shawm and is called the **Quint-Bassoon** <note>refer to column 7 of the illustrations</note>. The other is the **Quart-Bassoon**, which can only reach down to **G**. Therefore, the latter is most conveniently used in "hard" music <note>original: *Cantu duro*, music using B-natural</note>, while the former is best for "soft" music <note>original: *Cantu molli*, music using B-flat</note>. It is very convenient if one can have both types in an ensemble, for <term>semitones</term> <note>half-steps in the scale</note> cannot be changed or achieved as easily through the keys as they can with the fingers.

The master craftsman who made the **Octave-Trombones** is currently at work on a great **Contrabassoon** <note>original: *Fagotcontra*</note>. This instrument is to be a fourth lower than the Double Bassoon, and thus an octave lower than the Choral Bassoon; it should produce and sound the **C** of the sixteen-foot pitch. If he succeeds, it will be a magnificent instrument, the likes of which has never been seen before, and it will be a wonder to behold. This is especially true since organ builders sometimes find it difficult to properly and purely produce the lowest two keys, **D** or **C**, at the sixteen-foot pitch even in the large trombone stops. Time will tell.

### Chapter 12
## Sordunes

->(in the Illustrations, column 12)<-

**S**ordunes <note>original: *Sordun*; in Italian, *Sordoni*; some also call them Dulcians</note> are almost equal in resonance to the *CornaMusen* <note>a straight-bore woodwind with a reed cap</note> or soft crumhorns. Although the lowest bass of the sordunes is barely half as long in its body <note>original: *Corpore*</note> as the double bassoon, it can nonetheless produce a tone just as deep. This is indeed something to marvel at, especially since the body is doubled over only once, similar to the bassoons. Lodovico Zacconi <note>an Italian musical theorist (1555–1627)</note> also calls this instrument the *Sordono*. They have twelve holes that can be seen, and some have two additional keys <note>original: *Schlösser*</note>, making fourteen holes in total. Beyond this, there is a hole at the bottom for moisture to escape, and another at the top from which the sound <note>original: *Harmony*</note> emerges. The largest and deepest is 2 feet and 5 inches long.

I have, however, seen another instrument that had the same length, proportions, and everything else as this bass sordune, but in its resonance it was no deeper than the tenor of these sordunes; it was called a **Short Instrument** <note>original: *Kort Instrument*</note>. I have not yet been able to figure out where this difference originates, nor have I been able to obtain information about it from others.

---

**T**he aforementioned Zacconi has also described another similar instrument which he calls the *Doppioni*. Despite my great efforts, I have not yet been able to see one for myself. It may perhaps be the same as Number 7 in column 12 of the illustrations, or perhaps of the same type as the sordune or *CornaMusa*, as can easily be gathered from its tone and range as found in the table.

**R**acketts <note>original: *Racketten*</note> are very short instruments, as can be seen and measured in the Illustrations, column 10. But because the internal channel <term>bore</term> <note>the hollow tube inside the instrument through which the air travels</note> or pipe winds around nine times, it is just the same as if the body...

# ON THE DESCRIPTION OF INSTRUMENTS

[If the] body <note>original: *Corpus*</note> were nine times as long, they would produce as deep a resonance as the largest **Bombard** <note>a large, deep-toned member of the shawm family</note> or **Double Bassoon**; although some **Bass Racketts** are found which are even a minor third <note>original: *Semiditonum oder tertiam minorem*</note> deeper, so that they reach the **D** and thus possess a 15-foot tone. I myself have specified one, and recently had it made, which reaches down to the **C** of a 16-foot tone <note>This refers to a pitch so deep that it would normally require a pipe 16 feet long</note>; and in its depth, it is equal to the largest pipes in the **Principal ranks** <note>original: *Principal Wercken*; the primary pipes of a pipe organ</note>. The body is no more than 11 inches long. They have many holes, but no more than eleven are for use; and it rarely produces a **falsetto** <note>here meaning "overblown" or higher register notes</note>, since it cannot produce more tones than the number of holes allows—unless it is played very well and a master handles it, in which case it may do a bit more. Regarding their resonance, they are very quiet, almost as if one were blowing through a comb <note>a historical comparison to a buzzing, kazoo-like quality</note>, and they have no particular charm <note>original: *gratiam*</note> when a full consort <note>original: *Accort oder Stimmwerck*</note> of them is played together. However, when **Bass Viols** <note>original: *Violn de Gamba*</note> are used with them, or when one is played alone by a master alongside other wind or stringed instruments in a **Sinfonia** <note>original: *Simphony*</note> and **Harpsichord** <note>original: *Clavicymbel*</note>, etc., it is a lovely instrument, particularly pleasant and good to hear in the bass.

And it should also be noted here that the **Sordunes**, **Short Instruments**, **Racketts**, **Corna Muse**, **Crumhorns**, and **Schryari** cannot produce any more tones than the number of holes allows. But the **Bombards**, **Shawms**, **Bassoons**, **Dulcians**, and **Bassanelli** can all be played several tones higher (just as the previously provided table shows) and can be naturally intonated <note>meaning they can "overblow" to reach higher octaves</note>.

## Chapter 15.
# Crumhorns.
->(in the Illustrations, column 13.)<-

The **Crumhorns** <note>original Latin: *Lituus*; Italian: *Storti* or *Cornamuti torti*</note> are not blown with a bare reed; rather, just like the **Corna Muse**, **Schryari**, and **Bagpipes**, they have special **capsules** <note>reed caps</note> over the reeds. Because of this, one can force them less and cannot help them much in adjusting the tone <note>The player's lips do not touch the reed, so they cannot vary the pitch or dynamics as easily</note>. At the back they have one hole, at the front six, and above these, two more holes at the bottom; thus they could be played two or three tones deeper. However, special keys and brass **levers** <note>original: *Claves*</note> (as are found on some) would have to be made for this; otherwise, it cannot be reached or grasped with the fingers.

<summary>Praetorius describes the remarkable Rackett, which produces a 16-foot organ pitch from an 11-inch body, and begins a technical description of the Crumhorn and its reed-cap mechanism.</summary>
<keywords>Rackett, Bombard, 16-foot tone, consort, Crumhorn, reed cap, woodwind anatomy, pitch range</keywords>

However, the bottom two holes must necessarily remain open; otherwise, the entire instrument would not have a proper, full resonance, and the seventh hole at the bottom would then produce a deeper tone than it rightfully should and must.

In this manner, an organ maker must often help the large and even small reed stops <note>original: *Schnarrwercken*; reed pipes in an organ that produce a buzzing or "snaring" sound</note> achieve the correct intonation by using holes (though this practice is not highly praised) when they do not want to speak or sound properly. Yet, as mentioned before, they produce no more notes or tones than they have holes and keys.

### Chapter XVI.
## CORNAMUSE.
->(See the *Sciagraphia* <note>The *Sciagraphia* is the volume of detailed woodcut illustrations accompanying this treatise.</note>, Plate VII)<-

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'D' with floral and scrollwork patterns.</image-desc>
The **Cornamuse** are straight and have a single tube, not a double one, much like the **Bassanelli**. However, they are closed at the bottom and have several small holes around the sides through which the resonance escapes. In sound, they are exactly like **Crumhorns** <note>original: *Krumbhörnern*; woodwind instruments with a capped reed and a characteristic curved shape</note>, except that they sound quieter, lovelier, and very soft. Therefore, they could rightly be called "quiet, soft Crumhorns" (just as the **Mute Cornetts** <note>original: *Cornetti-muti*</note> are quiet versions of the **Zink** <note>also known as the cornett, a wooden instrument with a finger-holes and a trumpet-style mouthpiece</note>). They have no keys <note>original: *Schlösser oder Claves*</note> at all. They are tuned to **Choir Pitch** <note>original: *Chorthon*; a historical pitch standard often used for church music</note>; that is, one tone lower than our standard **Cornett** or **Chamber Pitch** <note>original: *Cammerthon*; the higher pitch standard typically used for secular or chamber music</note>.

---

### Chapter XVII.
## BASSANELLI.
->(See the *Sciagraphia*, Plate XII)<-

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'B' with intricate floral and architectural patterns.</image-desc>
**Bassanelli** take their name from the master who invented them (**Giovanni Bassano**, a distinguished instrumentalist and composer in Venice). They run straight through, with a single tube, and are open at the bottom. They have only one brass key and are played with reeds <note>original: *blossen Röhren*; referring to the double reed</note> just like **Bassoons** <note>original: *Fagotten*</note>, **Pommers** <note>original: *Pommern*; members of the shawm family</note>, and **Bassetts**, and are almost equal to them in resonance, yet much quieter. The **Cantus** <note>the soprano or highest-pitched member of the family</note>, which is the smallest, is particularly suited to serve as a tenor in **Concerts** <note>meaning a "broken consort" or an ensemble of mixed instrument families</note> when one wishes to use all kinds of instrumental voices among them...

...if one wishes to use them, they are very pleasant to hear; for they are perfectly in tune and sound exactly as a tenor flute would. ### Chapter XVIII.
### SCHRYARI.
->(See the *Sciagraphia* <note>The *Sciagraphia* is the volume of detailed woodcut illustrations accompanying this treatise.</note>, Plate XII)<-

The **Schryari** (in German, "screaming pipes" <note>original: *Schreyerpfeiffen*</note>) are strong and fresh in sound; they can be used on their own or alongside other instruments. They have holes on the back as well as the front. In length and stature, they are almost exactly like the **Cornamuse**, except that they have much stronger resonance because they are simple and open at the bottom. And although the treble <note>original: *Discant*</note> version is covered at the bottom, it nonetheless has many side holes through which the wind can escape. However, they cannot produce more notes or pitches than the number of finger holes allows.

### Chapter XIX.
### Bagpipes.
->(See the *Sciagraphia*, Plates V, XI, XIII)<-

There are many types of **Bagpipes** <note>called *Tibia Utricularis* in Latin and *CornaMusa* in Italian</note>.

1. The **Bock** <note>literally "Billy-goat," likely named for the goat-skin bag</note>, which has only one large, long horn as a drone <note>original: *Stimmer*; a pipe that plays a continuous sustained note</note> and is pitched at a deep C. Some are even a fourth lower in GG and are rightly called the "Great Bock."

2. The **Shepherd’s Pipe** <note>original: *Schaperpfeiff* or *Schäfferpfeiffern*</note>; it has two pipes for drones, tuned to B-flat and F. These Shepherd's pipes are mostly out of tune in the upper finger holes; in my opinion, this happens because they have no thumb hole on the back. The other types, however—such as the **Bock**, the **Hümmelchen**, and the **Dudey**—have a hole on the back, which allows them to be better controlled and brought to pure intonation.

3. The **Hümmelchen** <note>literally "Little Bumblebee," referring to its quiet buzzing sound</note>; it also has only two drones, tuned to F and C.

4. The **Dudey** <term>Dudey; a small bagpipe with three drones</term> however, has three small pipes for tuning: <term>F</term>, <term>B-flat</term>, and <term>low B-flat</term>. 

In the Archbishopric of Magdeburg, I have seen a special kind of **bagpipe** which is somewhat larger than the **Shepherd’s Pipe** <note>original: *Schäfferpfeiffen*</note> and is pitched a third lower. It also has two drones, but features two chanter pipes at the bottom—one for the left hand and the other for the right. Each chanter pipe has three holes on the front and one thumb-hole on the back. In this way, one can play the notes <term>g a b c'</term> with the left hand and <term>D E F G a</term> with the right, allowing one to skillfully produce a duet <note>original: *Duum*</note> or a two-part piece <note>original: *Bicinium*</note>. A drawing of this can be found in the *Sciagraphia* <note>The volume of woodcut illustrations accompanying this work</note>, Column V.

Additionally, a small bagpipe or **Hümmelchen** <term>Hümmelchen; literally "little bumblebee," a small bellows-blown bagpipe</term> has been brought out of France (Column XIII), where the wind is supplied and controlled through a small set of bellows using only one arm.

Furthermore, a certain person (mentioned previously in Chapter 5) has looked into these matters so deeply that he constructed an entire consort <note>original: *Stimmwerck*; a set of instruments in different sizes from the same family</note> consisting of five such bagpipes which are controlled with bellows. On these, one was intended to be able to perform a song with 4 or 5 voices; however, I do not find such a harmony to be particularly pleasing.

Regarding the **REGAL** <term>Regal; a small, portable organ that uses reeds instead of pipes to produce a buzzing sound</term> (which also belongs in part to this section, as it is a wind instrument and must be controlled by air), a report shall be given later at Number 43 near the "Strohfiedel" <note>literally "straw-fiddle," a type of xylophone</note>, shortly before the treatise on organs. Its drawing is to be found in Column IV.

### ON THE DESCRIPTION OF INSTRUMENTS.

1. **Viol de gamba** <term>Viol de gamba; literally "leg viol"</term>: 2. **Viol de braccio**, or **de brazzo** <term>Viol de braccio; literally "arm viol"</term>: These are named according to how they are held. The first type is held between the legs, as **gamba** is an Italian word meaning "leg" and **le gambe** means "the legs." Because these instruments have much larger **bodies** <note>original: *corpora*</note> and longer necks, the strings also have a longer length; thus, they produce a much lovelier **resonance** <note>original: *Resonanz*</note> than the **arm viols** <note>original: *de braccio*</note>, which are held upon the arm. These two types are distinguished by professional musicians in the cities in this way: they call the **viols de gamba** simply **Viols** <note>original: *Violen*</note>, while the **viols de braccio** are called **Fiddles** or **Polish Fiddles** <note>original: *Geigen* or *Polnische Geigeln*</note>. This is perhaps because this type is said to have first come from Poland, or because excellent, masterful artists of these fiddles are found there.

The **Viols de Gamba** have 6 **strings** and are tuned in **fourths**, with a **third** in the middle, just like the six-course lutes. When the English **play music** <note>original: *musiciren*</note> alone on these instruments, they occasionally make everything a **fourth** or even a **fifth** deeper. They count and hold the lowest **strings** of the small **bass** as **D**; the **tenor** and **alto** as **A**; and the **cantus** <term>Cantus; the highest or soprano part</term> as **e**. Otherwise, as can be seen in the table above, each is tuned a **fifth** lower (when calculated according to **chamber pitch** <term>Cammerthon; the standard pitch used in secular/court settings</term>): namely, the **bass** at **GG**; the **tenor** and **alto** at **D**; and the **cantus** at **A**. In such a **consort** <note>original: *Stimmwerck*</note>, this produces a much more pleasant, magnificent, and glorious **harmony** than when one stays in the standard pitch. (A drawing of these is in the **Sciagraphia, Column XX.**) <note>Sciagraphia: The volume of woodcut illustrations accompanying this book.</note>

The large **viol de gamba** (called **Violono** by the **Italians**, or **Contrabasso da gamba**, the drawing of which is in **Sciagraphia, Column VI.**) is tuned by most players **by fourths** <note>original: *per quartam*</note> all the way through; I do not find this method at all bad. I also believe that it does not matter much how someone tunes their **fiddles** or **viols**, as long as they can **perform** <note>original: *præstiren*</note> their part accurately, purely, and well.

There are many who think themselves quite special in these matters, and some organists are inclined to look down on others because they do not use this or that specific **fingering** <note>original: *Application*</note>. In my opinion, however, this is not worth talking about. Whether someone runs up or down the scales with their index, middle, or back fingers—indeed, even if they could use their nose to help—if they make everything sound fine, pure, accurate, and pleasant to the ear, it does not matter much by what means or method they achieve it.

**NB.** <note>Latin abbreviation for 'Note Well'</note> Regarding all these bowed instruments which are strung with strings made of **gut** <note>original: *Dermern*</note>: the notes in the preceding table indicate only how high or low each string is tuned, and not how high one can **ascend** <note>original: *ascendiren*</note> on the instrument using the fingers and frets. This is something...

### ON THE DESCRIPTION OF INSTRUMENTS.

->F iij<-

...is not unknown to every instrumentalist. However, in the case of wind instruments, such things necessarily had to be indicated.

The ancients had three types of these **viols de gamba** <term>Viol de gamba; "leg viol"</term>, as can be found in the works of **Agricola** <note>Martin Agricola (1486–1556), an important German music theorist</note>: for some were strung with three strings; some with four; and some (as seen in *Sciagraphia*, Plate 24) <note>original: *Sciagr. Col. xxiv.* refers to the collection of illustrations accompanying this treatise</note> were strung with five strings. More concerning this can be seen above in the **Universal Table** <note>original: *Tabella universali*</note>.

Because the small strings on the very large bass fiddles—or **violones** <term>Violone; a large, deep-toned member of the viol or violin family</term>—can rarely withstand the tension due to the great length and distance between the top nut and the bridge:

A musician in Prague has given this matter further and deeper thought. He commissioned the construction of a bass fiddle where, among the six strings (counting from the largest), each successive string is given a shorter length. Thus, the smallest string is nearly a whole **foot** <note>original: *Schuch*; a historical unit of measurement</note>—specifically 12 inches—shorter than the largest. To achieve this, he did not only place the large bottom bridge at a slant or **obliquely** (similar to a **penorcon** or **orpheoreon**) <note>Wire-stringed instruments of the cittern family with scalloped fingerboards and slanted bridges</note>, but also slanted the top nut downward. Consequently, the frets had to become so uneven that they could no longer be reached with the fingers. Therefore, it was necessary to invent a solution: a cover was made over the entire neck, similar to common **hurdy-gurdies** <note>original: *Bawer leyren*; literally "peasant lyres"</note>. Near the end, six small five-sided blocks were placed next to each other, which one presses just like the **keys** <note>original: *Clavier*</note> on a hurdy-gurdy, thereby pressing and touching the correct fret for each string.

On these small blocks or **keys**, if I may call them that, there were strong brass wires—just like the brass keys on the large **pommers** <term>Pommer; a powerful, double-reed instrument of the shawm family</term>—which reached high enough for each to hit its required fret. Because each string maintains its proper length and tension, and the **violone player** <note>original: *Violonista*</note> does not have to move his hand so far back and forth to find the notes, but instead has the **keys** or frets right next to one another to press, this is a very fine **invention** <note>original: *Invention*</note>.

However, one thing displeases me: instead of wooden pegs at the head, iron tuning pins were made. On the outside, these have a notched wheel which, just like in **clocks and timepieces** <note>original: *Vhren vnd SchlagSeegerlein*</note>, is held back or moved forward by a steel spring. If only a single notch is released or tightened, the string immediately **ascends** or **descends** by two **commas** <term>Comma; a tiny interval in musical tuning, here implying a jump that is too large for fine tuning</term>. Therefore, in my opinion, it cannot be tuned perfectly or used easily in **accord** with other instruments.

Yet, this could be easily remedied if the notches in such [wheels were made smaller...]

...small wheels <note>original: *Räderlin*; these are the metal gears mentioned on the previous page</note> were filed as closely and precisely as possible together, then by allowing them to move just one notch at a time, the distance of the sound or tone would not be noticeably stepped. Thus, the strings could be tuned into every instrument more purely and accurately. Therefore, this method would be much better and more stable than the common tuning pegs <note>original: *Wörbel*; standard wooden friction pegs</note>, because in this form they cannot slip or give way at all.

### NB. <note>Latin: *Nota Bene*; "Note Well"</note>

Recently, two very large **Sub-Bass** Viols de Gamba <term>Viol de Gamba; "leg viol," a fretted string instrument</term> (the illustration of which can be found in Plate 5) have also been manufactured. With these, one can use the other large double-basses for the tenor and alto parts, and use the small bass viol de gamba in place of the treble <note>original: *Discants*</note>. I have also composed a concert piece for different choirs (*Praise the Lord, O Jerusalem*) <note>original: *Lauda Hierusalem Dominum*</note>—which, with God’s help, will shortly be published in the ninth volume of **Polyhymnia** <note>A massive collection of Praetorius’s Lutheran church music</note>—set for 17 and 21 voices according to my humble ability. In this piece, the five voices of that specific choir must all be played an octave lower <note>original: *in Octava inferiore*</note>.

However, because that choir, with so many large fiddles, tends to hum and murmur together too much—just as on an organ, if one includes the thirds and fifths in the deep bass register on the manual using a coarse **Principal** or a 16-foot **Stopped Flute** <term>Gedactenflöte; a "stopped" organ pipe that sounds an octave lower than its length suggests</term>—I have found that it is much more pleasant and lovely to use the standard bass viol de gamba for the upper and middle voices, and the very large **Sub-Bass** in the lower octave for the bass part. In this way, it is heard from a distance like a deep **Sub-Bass** <term>Untersatz; the largest, deepest-sounding pipes in an organ's pedal division</term> in an organ.

Regarding this, I must also remind the reader: if one wishes to have a part played along on these large Sub-Bass fiddles or on the **Octave Trombone** <note>original: *OctavPosaun*; a contrabass trombone</note>, the bass part must be rewritten. The F-clef <term>𝄢</term> should be placed on the middle line, and the lowest notes should all be set an octave higher, just like a low tenor. It then becomes quite easy and convenient for the instrumentalist, as if he were otherwise playing his part on a tenor instrument; for such very deep instruments stand exactly an octave below the true tenor.

# ON THE DESCRIPTION OF INSTRUMENTS.

## *The 21st Chapter.*
# VIOLA BASTARDA.
->(See Illustrations, Plate XX.)<-

<image-desc>A large decorative historiated woodcut initial 'D' depicting human figures and ornate vine-like scrollwork.</image-desc>
This is a type of Viol da Gamba <term>Viol da Gamba; literally "leg viol," a fretted string instrument held between the knees</term>, and is tuned exactly like a tenor Viol da Gamba (which can also be used for this purpose if necessary). However, the body <note>original: *Corpus*</note> is somewhat longer and larger. I do not know if it received its name because it is, as it were, a "bastard" of all the voices; for it is not bound to any single vocal part. Instead, a skilled master takes the madrigals, or whatever else he wishes to play on this instrument, and seeks out the fugues and harmony with great diligence through all the voices—now high up in the soprano <note>original: *Cant*</note>, now down in the bass, now in the middle from the tenor and alto. He adorns the music with leaps <note>original: *saltibus*</note> and diminutions <term>diminutions; a style of ornamentation where long notes are broken down into many fast, decorative notes</term>, and treats it in such a way that one can clearly hear almost all the voices with their fugues and cadences. For the benefit of those unfamiliar with this, I intended to include two or three examples at the end of this third part; however, I will save them for the Appendix of the Third Volume, titled *Instructions for Musicians* <note>original: *Instructionem pro Symphoniacis*</note>.

These Violas Bastarda are tuned in many different ways, as can be seen in the table, and in many other ways besides, according to how the master has composed and arranged the song.

Now, in England, something even more special has been invented: beneath the six common gut strings, eight other steel and twisted brass strings lie upon a brass bridge (just like those used on the bandoras <term>bandora; a wire-strung plucked instrument with a scalloped body</term>). These must be tuned exactly and very purely in unison with the upper strings. Now, when one of the upper gut strings is touched with the finger or the bow, the lower brass or steel strings resonate at the same time by agreement <note>original: *per consensum*; referring to sympathetic resonance</note>, trembling and vibrating so that the sweetness of the harmony is thereby increased and broadened.

From this, it is visible and tangible to find that the harmony of consonances <note>original: *Consonantiarum*; musical intervals that sound pleasing together</note> is planted entirely within nature. For if a string is sounded on a viol in a room, chamber, or elsewhere, and a lute or cittern <term>cittern; a wire-strung instrument similar to a mandolin</term> is lying on the table or hanging on the wall, the string on that lute or cittern which is [exactly] <meta>the word 'gar' (exactly/entirely) from the bottom of the page indicates the start of the next page's sentence</meta>...

# ON THE DESCRIPTION OF INSTRUMENTS.

...sounds just as pure and equal to the note that is played on the Viol with a bow. This can be observed and experienced all the more certainly and accurately if a small piece of straw <note>original: *Strohehalmlin*</note> is placed upon those Lute or Cittern strings.

Brass and steel strings feel such sharp harmonies much sooner and more strongly than gut strings, so that they not only move but also resonate and produce a sound at the same time. This often happens on the large Bass Viol da Gamba: when the very low GG on the bottom string is played sharply with the bow, the string above it, which is tuned exactly an octave to that G, moves and resonates along with it. Indeed, experience proves even more: when an organ builder, during the installation and assembly of a new organ, is inserting and tuning one pipe after another up on the windchest <note>original: *Gerüste*</note>, and wants to find quickly where a specific pipe is among all those lying in a row, he simply has the octave of that pipe played from the organ keyboard. Immediately, he can find the matching octave among those on the chest by touching them one by one and feeling for the vibration <term>vibration; here referring to sympathetic resonance where one object vibrates in response to the sound frequency of another</term>. For that specific pipe moves and trembles so much from the sound and tone of the other in the organ that one can actually grasp and feel it.

### Chapter 22.

## VIOLINS HELD ON THE ARM.

->(See Illustrations, Plate XXI.)<-

<image-desc>Large decorative woodcut initial 'V' with floral and foliate scrollwork.</image-desc>Viola, Viola da braccio: also called *Violino da braccio*. It is otherwise known as a *Geige* <note>original: *Geige*; a general German term for bowed string instruments</note>, though common folk call it a fiddle. It is named *da braccio* <term>da braccio; Italian for "of the arm," distinguishing these from the "da gamba" or leg-viols</term> because it is held upon the arm.

The Bass, Tenor, and Discant versions of these (the latter being called a *Violino*, or *Violetta picciola*, or also a *Rebecchino*) are strung with four strings. However, the very small little fiddles (shown in Plate XX, No. 1) are strung with only three strings—called a *Pochetto* <note>original French: *Pochette*; a small "pocket" fiddle used by dance masters</note> in French—and all of these are tuned in fifths. Since these are known to everyone, it is unnecessary to write or indicate much more about them, except to mention that when they are strung with brass and steel strings, they produce a quieter and almost more lovely resonance than others.

Different types of these can be found in the Illustrations at Plate XXI and also in the table provided previously.

## Chapter 23.

### L Y R A.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'A' featuring foliage and a small figure.</image-desc> Here, we are not speaking of the peasant’s or wandering women’s Lyre <note>original: *Leyre*; referring here to the Hurdy-gurdy</note>, which is turned with a handle and where the keys <note>original: *Claves*</note> are touched with the left hand: the illustration of which can be seen in the *Illustrations of Instruments* <note>original: *Sciagraphia*</note>, Plate XXII. Rather, we speak of the Italian Lyres, of which there are also two kinds.

1. A Large Lyra <note>original: *Lironi perfetto*, *Arcè violyra*; or, as the aforementioned Ludovico Zacconi calls it, *Arce-viola telire*. Its illustration is in the *Illustrations of Instruments*, Plate XVII.</note>. In its structure, it is similar to the Bass of the Viols da Gamba, though the body <note>original: *Corpus*</note> and the neck <note>original: *Kragen*</note> are considerably wider because of the many strings. For some have 12, some 14, and some even 2 more outside the neck, thus 16 strings, upon which all Madrigals <note>original: *Madrigalia*</note> and compositions can be performed, in both the chromatic <note>original: *genere Chromatico*</note> and diatonic <note>original: *Diatonico*</note> styles. This produces a fine harmony. However, at times the highest or the lowest voice—just as on the small Citterns—is left out; therefore, a Bass and a Soprano <note>original: *Discant*</note> can and must be used quite conveniently alongside it.

2. The Small Lyra is similar to the Tenor Viols held on the arm <note>original: *Violen de bracio*</note>: hence it is also called the *Lyra da braccio*. It has 7 strings, two strings lying outside the neck and the other five lying on the neck. Upon this, one can perform three-part pieces <note>original: *Tricinia*</note> and other things, almost like a Cittern. Its illustration is in the *Illustrations of Instruments*, Plate XX.

### Chapter XXV.

## THE THEORBO.

->(illustrated in the *Visual Index*, Plates V. & XVI.)<-
<note>original: "Sciagraph. Col. V. & XVI." Referring to Praetorius’s own collection of woodcut illustrations.</note>

The **Theorbo** is not very different from a large bass lute, except that it has more strings—namely 14 or 16 courses <note>A "course" is a pair of strings tuned in unison or octaves, though the theorbo's lowest strings were often single.</note>—and besides the main neck upon which the frets lie (which, as mentioned before, is called the fingerboard), it has another longer neck. It is designed solely for accompaniment (because, due to its size and the wide stretching of the fingers required, no complex flourishes or diminutions <note>melodic decorations where long notes are broken into faster patterns</note> can be performed on it; rather, it must be played simply and straightforwardly), so that a soprano or tenor may sing along with the live voice <note>original: *viva voce*</note>, just as one does with the **Viola Bastarda**. Beyond this, however, it is also very useful and quite lovely to hear when it is used alongside other instruments in a full ensemble, or otherwise alongside the bass, or in place of the bass.

There are now two kinds of these: one with gut strings <note>original: *Gegensäitten*, likely a variant of *Saiten* made from animal gut</note>; the other with brass and steel strings. Some people now also string the standard common lutes with such metal strings; but the **fourth** and **fifth** strings <note>In the German numbering system of the time, these were the highest-pitched strings</note> are then tuned an octave lower than usual, just as on the theorbo. This is because the length of the body <note>original: *Corporis*</note> and the thickness of the brass strings cannot tolerate any other tuning and cannot reach the proper high pitch.

Those made in Rome, which are called the <term>Chitarrone</term> <note>A large, long-necked lute popular in Italy for vocal accompaniment</note>, have a very long neck, so that the total length including the body measures 6 1/2 feet and 2 inches; and the body is not so very large, wide, and awkward to hold and grasp as those made until now in Padua, which are only 5 feet long. The Roman ones (which are now also being made very neatly and diligently in Prague by a man named Martin Schott, and can be found in Plate V) have only 6 strings or courses on the fingerboard where the frets lie; the Paduan ones, however, have 8 strings. On the very long neck, however, both types have 8 strings in addition to those that lie on the fingerboard. Nevertheless, from year to year more changes in this regard occur and are devised; for that reason, nothing certain can be written about it.

# ON THE DESCRIPTION OF INSTRUMENTS.

<note>original: "DE ORGANOGRAPHIA." This is the title of the second volume of Praetorius’s work.</note>

The **Quinterna** or **Chiterna** is an instrument with four courses <note>A "course" refers to a pair of strings tuned to the same pitch or an octave apart.</note> which are tuned exactly like the very oldest first lutes (mentioned under Number 24). However, it does not have a rounded back, but is almost entirely flat like a **Bandora**, barely two or three fingers deep. Its illustration is to be found in the *Visual Index*, Plate XVI. <note>original: "Sciagraph. Col. XVI."</note>

Some have five courses of strings, and in Italy the *Ciarlatani* and *Saltimbanco* <note>Street performers and traveling acrobats; the name *Saltimbanco* literally means "jump on a bench."</note> (who among us are much like comedians and buffoons) use them only for strumming <note>original: "schrumpen"</note>, while they sing *Villanelles* and other foolish, ribald songs.

Nevertheless, other fine, graceful little songs <note>original: "Cantiunculæ"</note> and lovely tunes can be performed on it by a good singer and vocal musician.

---

### Chapter XXVII.
## PANDURINA: Little Mandore.
### (illustrated in the *Visual Index*, Plate XVI.)

This is called by some the **Mandürichen**, by others the **Mandore**, or **Mandurinichen** (perhaps because it can be easily held and handled by the hand <note>original: "forté quia manu facilè comprehendi & tractari potest"</note>). It is like a very small little lute with 4 strings tuned thus: g, d', g', c''. Some are also strung with five strings or courses, which can be easily carried under a cloak; these are said to be very common in France. Some players are so practiced on it that they can perform *Courantes*, *Voltas*, and other such French dances and songs—as well as *Passamezzos*, fugues, and fantasies—using a feather quill just as is done on the **Cittern**. Or they can play with a single finger so swiftly, accurately, and cleanly as if three or four fingers were being used. Though some do use two or more fingers, depending on how well-practiced they are.

---

## Chapter XXIX.
# PENORCON.
->(illustrated in the *Visual Index*, Plate XVII.)<-

The **Penorcon** is of almost the very same kind, except that it is somewhat broader in its body <note>original: "Corpore"</note> than a **Bandora**, and has a very wide neck or fingerboard, so that nine courses of strings can lie upon it side by side. In length, however, it is somewhat smaller than the Bandora, and larger than an **Orpheoreon**.

---

## Chapter XXX.
# ORPHEOREON.
->(illustrated in the *Visual Index*, Plate XVII.)<-

The **Orpheoreon** has the same proportions as a Bandora, yet is somewhat smaller, with brass and steel strings; it is tuned like a lute in Chamber Pitch <note>original: "Cammer Thon"; this was the standard pitch for secular and instrumental music in the early 17th century.</note> (namely with the fifth string-course at g).

### Chapter XXXII.
->Harp.<-

The **Harp**, by others called *Arpa* (from the Greek *harpazo*, meaning to seize or snatch, because the strings are snatched by the fingers) <note>original: "ab ἁρπάζω, rapio, quod Chordæ digitis qu; rapiantur"</note>, is called *kithara* in Greek; *un Harpe* in French; *Cetera* or *Arpa* in Italian; and *Harpa* in Spanish. To the Latins it is the *Cithara*, as it was also called by the name **Cithara** among the ancients. Concerning this, **Jerome** <note>Saint Jerome (c. 342–420 AD), the translator of the Vulgate Bible.</note> writes that the Cithara of the Hebrews had 24 strings or more (although Orpheus is said to have played the Cithara with only seven strings, as witnessed by **Virgil** in the 6th book of the *Aeneid*:
> The Thracian priest in his long robe 
> sings in response to the rhythms with the seven differences of voices) <note>original Latin: "Threicius longa cum veste sacerdos / Obloquitur numeris septem discrimina vocum." The "Thracian priest" refers to the mythical musician Orpheus.</note>
The strings are made from the dried, thinned, and twisted intestines of dead animals, which are called *fides* <note>A Latin term for gut strings or stringed instruments.</note>. These strings are struck in various modes with different, ringing strokes of the fingers. See **Pliny**, Book 7, Chapter 56, and **Turnebus**, Book 19, Chapter 30. And as Jerome writes in the *Epistle to Dardanus* <note>OCR reads "Cardanum," but this refers to the famous *Epistola ad Dardanum*, a medieval text often attributed to Jerome that describes musical instruments.</note>, it was made and formed in the shape of the Greek letter **Delta** (Δ), which is not very different from our current harps.

->At the present time, there are three types of Harps.<-

1. **The Common Simple Harp**; which has 24 or sometimes more strings, from F to f'' and a'', but contains no semitones <note>The "semitonia" refers to the sharps and flats; this was a diatonic instrument. See the **Sciagraphia** (the book's appendix of illustrations), Column XVIII.</note>.

2. **The Large Double-Harp**, or *Harpa doppia* (in **Sciagraphia**, Column XIX), which has a complete body and all the semitones. These extra strings are situated somewhat closer to the soundboard than the other strings, although they all lie level on the bridge.

3. **The Irish Harp**, or *Harpa Irlandica*, the structure and form of which can be found in **Sciagraphia**, Column XVIII. It has quite coarse, thick brass strings, 43 in number, and possesses an extraordinarily lovely resonance.

# ON THE DESCRIPTION OF INSTRUMENTS.

## Chapter XXXIII.
# Scheitholt.
<note>Also known as a "Log Zither," this is a simple folk instrument and a precursor to the modern Appalachian dulcimer.</note>
->(In the Illustrations, Vol. XXI.)<-

Although this instrument should rightly be counted among the **humble instruments** <note>original: "Lumpen Instrumenta," literally "ragged" or "pauper's" instruments</note>, I have nevertheless wished to describe it briefly here because it is known to so few people. It is a "Scheit" or a piece of wood, not very different from a small **monochord** <term>Monochord: a single-stringed scientific and musical instrument used for measuring intervals</term>, made quite simply from three or four thin boards joined together. At the top, it has a small neck containing three or four tuning pegs, and it is strung with three or four brass strings. Three of these are tuned in **unison** <note>original: "Unisono"</note>; however, one of these is held down in the middle by a small hook so that it must resonate a **fifth** <note>original: "Quint"</note> higher. If one desires, a fourth string can be added an **octave** <note>original: "Octav"</note> higher. All these strings are constantly thrummed near the bridge with the right thumb, while a small, smooth stick held in the left hand is moved back and forth on the foremost string. In this way, the melody of the song is produced over the **frets** <note>original: "Bünde"</note>, which are made of hammered brass wire.

---

## Chapter XXXIV.
# Trummscheit.
<note>Known in English as the Trumpet Marine, though it is a bowed string instrument rather than a trumpet.</note>
->(In the Illustrations, Vol. XXI.)<-

The **Trummscheit**, which was first derived and invented from the monochord, is called by **Glareanus** <note>Heinrich Glarean (1488–1563), a Swiss music theorist.</note> in the 17th chapter of the first book of his *Dodecachordon*, the *Magas according to Suidas* <note>original Latin: "Magas secundum Suidam." Suidas was a 10th-century Greek lexicographer; "Magas" refers to the bridge of a stringed instrument.</note>, or **Magadis**, and is described there in the following manner:

The Germans, French, and Netherlanders today use an instrument which they call a **Tympanischiza** <note>A Latinized term for "drum-shard" or "drum-stick," referring to its percussive, buzzing sound.</note>. It is made of three thin boards joined together quite simply like a **triangular pyramid** <note>original Latin: "Trigonia Pyramis"</note>, tapering to a point at the top. On the top board (otherwise called the **soundboard** <note>original: "Sangbodem"</note>), it is strung with a long gut string...
