# ON THE DESCRIPTION OF INSTRUMENTS.

...strung; it is played by drawing a bow made of horsehair and coated with pitch or *rosin* <note>original: "Colophonio"</note> over the string, causing it to sound.

Some also add another string, twice as short as the first, so that the former can produce a stronger tone and resonance together with the *octave* <note>original: "Octava"</note>.

In the writings of Athenaeus, in the passage where he recalls various instruments, a *Trigonon* <note>original: "Trigoni," an ancient triangular harp</note> is mentioned, which Plato includes among the *many-stringed instruments* <term>πολύχορδα (poly-chorda): instruments with many strings, often viewed with suspicion by ancient philosophers for their complexity</term> in the eighth book of his *Republic*.

I believe, however, and am of the opinion that the instrument of which I have just spoken is very ancient.

Street musicians carry it through the alleys, resting the tip—or as it is otherwise called, the neck, containing the *keys* or tuning pegs <note>original: "Clavis oder Wörbel"</note> used to tighten and tune the strings—against their chest. The other part, however, where the hollow body and the triangular base are located, they extend forward. They hold the instrument in the left hand and touch the strings very lightly at various points and *sections* (which on lutes and citterns are the frets) with the left thumb; with the right hand, they draw the bow back and forth across the strings.

The depth of the largest string begins at the bottom end and extends up to the tip placed against the chest. There, with the thumb of the left hand, the string is touched here and there to produce the different melodies. The right hand draws the bow across the string at the very top, between the left hand and the uppermost part, so that the shortest section of the string always yields the correct *tone* <note>original: "Tonum"</note>. From a distance, it sounds much more pleasant than when one is standing close to it.

On this instrument, players can easily produce the two *modes*, the *Ionian and Hypoionian* <note>These modes correspond roughly to the modern C-major scale; the Trumpet Marine naturally produces the harmonic series</note>, just as they can on trumpets, bagpipes, and other such instruments; however, they cannot manage the other *modes* <note>original: "Tonos"</note> as well.

And although those who are inexperienced in music must stick only to *thirds, fourths, fifths, and octaves*, being unable to find the whole *tones* and *semitones* <term>Semitones: the half-steps between notes</term>, someone who applies themselves with more diligence can indeed produce them. However, because the long string gives off a vibrating and buzzing *sound* <note>The Trumpet Marine uses a "trembling bridge" that rattles against the soundboard to mimic a trumpet’s blast</note>, the semitones cannot be easily observed.

# ON THE DESCRIPTION OF INSTRUMENTS.

This buzzing or snarling, however, is brought about by a small, curved piece of wood. Its widest and thickest foot is placed loosely under the string near the bottom end—much like the bridge on a violin—so that the other part or foot, which they reinforce with ivory or some other hard bone material, extends out like a tail or *Colurus* <note>original: "Colurus," likely referring to the curved geometry of the bridge foot</note>. This foot moves upon the resonance board or soundboard when the string is touched by the bow, and thus creates a trembling, snarling sound and resonance.

"I had to laugh," Glareanus <note>Heinrich Glareanus (1488–1563) was a famous Swiss music theorist often cited by the author</note> says further, "at the invention of this instrument. But the true reason why not all divisions and different points [on the string] produce such a *harsh sound* <note>original: "stridorem"</note> has been impossible for me to fathom or discover, no matter how diligently I have pondered it."

Sometimes they also insert a very fine little nail into the very bottom of this protruding part or foot, so that the trembling and snarling can be heard more strongly against the solid body.

And it is just like on a harp, where the strings also creak and snarl when they strike against the bottom wooden peg—with which the strings are mortised and fixed into the body of the harp—when they are plucked. This is called a "harping resonance" by common folk.

The length of this triangular *monochord* <term>monochord: traditionally a one-stringed scientific instrument used for measuring intervals; here used as a formal name for the trumpet marine</term> is nearly five *feet* <note>original: "Schuch," an old unit of measurement based on the length of a foot</note>. It is made of three small boards, each of which is 5 inches <note>original: "Zoll"</note> wide at the base and 2 inches wide at the top. (So much for the account from Glareanus.)

This *Trummscheit* <term>Trummscheit: German name for the Trumpet Marine, literally "drum-log," so-called because its buzzing sound was reminiscent of a drum</term>, as I have seen it—and I own one myself—is 7 feet and 3 inches long. In its triangular shape, each board is 7 inches wide at the bottom and barely 2 inches at the top. It is strung with four strings, such that the main and longest string is tuned to C, the second to c, the third to g, and the fourth to c'. The upper three always remain at one pitch and *tone* <note>original: "Tono"</note> as they are tuned to c, g, and c'. On the thickest string, however, the proper melody is produced by touching it with the thumb, just like a true *clarino* <note>original: "Clarien," referring to the high-register, melodic style of trumpet playing</note> on a trumpet. Thus, when heard from a distance, it sounds no different than if four trumpets were blowing together in lovely harmony. Otherwise, in all respects, it is constructed just as was translated and shown earlier from Glareanus.

### Chapter XXXV.
## The Monochord.
->(in the Illustrations, Column XXXV.)<-

The Monochord <term>Monochord: a single-stringed instrument used since antiquity to demonstrate the mathematical ratios of musical intervals</term> is described by the aforementioned **Sebastian** Virdung as follows: It is a rectangular box, like a chest or trunk, over which a single string is stretched. This string is divided using a compass <note>original: "Circkel"</note> to determine and prove all the musical harmonies <note>original: "Consonantien"</note> through their mathematical proportions. Therefore, based on those same measurements <note>original: "mensur"</note>, a "key" or bridge has been placed at each point to strike the string exactly at that mark, producing the correct pitch <note>original: "Stimm"</note> that nature has assigned to that specific measurement. and since this will be discussed more extensively in another place, and is also treated and described by several other authors, I have deemed it unnecessary to deal with it at greater length here.

---

### Chapter XXXVI.
## The Clavichord.
->(in the Illustrations, Column XV.)<-

The Clavichord <term>Clavichord: a portable keyboard instrument where strings are struck by small metal blades called tangents</term> was invented and laid out based on the Monochord, following the **Scale of Guido** <note>Guido d'Arezzo, the 11th-century monk who developed the system of solmization</note>, which originally had no more than 20 keys <note>original: "Claves"</note>. For instead of each bridge or fret on the Monochord, a key was made on the Clavichord. In the beginning, no more than 20 keys were made, in the **diatonic genus** <term>diatonic genus: the standard seven-note scale (white keys) without extra sharps or flats</term>. Among these were only two "black" keys: B-flat and B-natural <note>original: "b vnd ♮"; at the time, these were the only alterations to the basic scale</note>. For in an octave, they had no more than three types of **semitones** <term>semitones: the smallest interval in Western music, the distance between two adjacent keys</term>: A to B-flat, B-natural to C, and E to F—as can still be seen in very old organs. Later, however, people gave the matter more thought, and following **Boethius** <note>Annius Manlius Severinus Boethius (c. 477–524 AD), a Roman philosopher whose music theory was standard for centuries</note> and the **chromatic genus**, they added more semitones to it. Thus, it became a keyboard like this:

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;G#&nbsp;&nbsp;Bb&nbsp;&nbsp;c#&nbsp;&nbsp;d#&nbsp;&nbsp;f#&nbsp;&nbsp;g#’&nbsp;&nbsp;bb’&nbsp;&nbsp;c#’&nbsp;&nbsp;d#’&nbsp;&nbsp;f#’&nbsp;&nbsp;g#’’&nbsp;&nbsp;bb’’&nbsp;&nbsp;c#’’&nbsp;&nbsp;d#’’&nbsp;&nbsp;f#’’
F G A B c d e f g a’ b’ c’ d’ e’ f’ g’ a’’ b’’ c’’ d’’ e’’ f’’

[Sig: H 3]

That nearly everyone now knows and is aware that all symphonies <term>Symphonies: here referring to early keyboard instruments similar to virginals or small harpsichords</term> and clavichords now begin at the bottom from C, and mostly end at the top at <insert>high a or f</insert> (which is best), and occasionally end at <insert>high f</insert>.

Just as the lute is the foundation and starting point from which one can afterwards play all other similar stringed instruments—such as pandoras, theorboes, penorcons, mandores, citterns, harps, and even violins and violas—and can easily perform one's part, provided that something substantial has first been learned and understood on the lute.

Likewise, whoever learns and grasps the correct foundation on the flutes in the beginning can afterwards very easily make progress on all other wind instruments with finger-holes, such as cornetts, shawms, pommers, bassoons, dulcians, racketts, and the like.

In the same way, the clavichord is the foundation of all keyboard instruments <note>original: "Clavirten Instrumenten"</note>, such as organs, harpsichords, symphonies, spinets, virginals, etc. It is on the clavichord that organ students <note>original: "Discipuli Organici"</note> are first instructed and taught. Among other reasons, this is primarily because it does not require the great effort and displeasure of quilling <term>Quilling: the process of replacing the plectra (usually crow quills) that pluck the strings in a harpsichord or spinet</term>, nor the frequent tuning and maintenance. This is because the strings on the clavichord are and remain far more stable than on harpsichords or spinets. Indeed, clavichords are often found that do not need tuning for a year or more. This is a great advantage, especially for beginning students who are not yet able to tune or quill an instrument.

In the *Sciagraphia* <note>The "Sciagraphia" is the volume of woodcut illustrations accompanying Praetorius's text</note> Column 15, Number 2, a clavichord is depicted which was brought from Italy to Meissen some thirty years ago. In it, this feature is very skillfully and wisely observed: the string courses <note>original: "Chor-Saiten"</note> belonging to d and a are left "free" <note>This refers to an "unfretted" clavichord where these specific notes have their own strings</note> through all octaves and are struck by only a single key. The reason for this is so that when playing suspensions <note>original: "Syncopationibus"</note>, especially in cadences <note>original: "clausulis"</note> and elsewhere where seconds <note>The interval of a second</note> must be played simultaneously next to each other, two keys do not strike the same string at the same time and cause a discord <note>original: "κακοφωνίαν" (kakophonian)</note>.

Otherwise, for the other keys, it is handled as in other clavichords: two, three, or sometimes even four keys (which, due to their dissonance, must often not be struck at the same time) are used for one course of strings <note>This describes a "fretted" clavichord, where multiple keys share a single string to save space and tension</note>.

This year, I gave a design to a good master for a clavichord (in the same size and form as the second one in Column 15), in which not only are the semitones <note>Sharps and flats</note> <insert>♯ ♯</insert> and b doubled <note>Referring to "split keys" that allow for different tunings of enharmonic notes like G-sharp and A-flat</note>, but also the <insert>high g and d</insert>, as well as between the...

<summary>Praetorius argues that the clavichord is the essential foundational instrument for all keyboardists, much like the lute is for string players, due to its tuning stability and pedagogical simplicity. He also describes technical innovations in clavichord stringing, including "unfretted" strings for certain notes to avoid dissonance during cadences.</summary>

### Chapter XXXVII.
#### Symphonia.
->(in the Illustrations, Col. XIV.)<-

A Symphony <term>Symphony: in this context, a small rectangular keyboard instrument similar to a virginal</term> (as well as a harpsichord, virginal, or spinet) is commonly called an "Instrument" by most people without distinction (though quite incorrectly). For the name "Instrument" <note>original: "Instrumenti"</note> is far too general and applies to all musical instruments <note>original: "Instrumenta Musicalia"</note>; as was mentioned more extensively at the beginning of this work. Therefore, it cannot be applied or referred solely to this one type of instrument—namely the symphonies and harpsichords.

---

### Chapter XXXVIII.
#### Spinetta.
->(in the Illustrations, Col. XIV.)<-

The Spinetta (*in Italian*, Spinetto) is a small, rectangular instrument that is tuned an octave or a fifth higher than the standard pitch <note>original: "rechte Thon"</note>. These are usually placed on top of or inside the larger instruments. However, the large rectangular ones, as well as the small ones, are indiscriminately called spinets in Italy.

In England, all such instruments, whether large or small, are called Virginals.
In France, *E Spinette*.
In the Netherlands, *Clavicymbel*, and also *Virginall*.
In Germany, it is called an "Instrument" specifically <note>original: "Instrument in Specie, vel peculiariter sic dictum"</note>.

# ON THE DESCRIPTION OF INSTRUMENTS.

The Harpsichord <note>original: "Clavicymbalum"</note> or **Gravecymbalum** is a long instrument. It is called a **Wing** <note>original: "Flügel"</note> by some because it is shaped almost like one. Others call it—though incorrectly—a **Pig’s Snout** <note>original: "Schweinstopff"</note> because it is pointed at the front like the snout of a wild boar. It has a strong, bright, and almost lovely resonance and sound, more so than other instruments, because of its double, triple, or even quadruple strings. I once saw one that had two strings at unison pitch <note>original: "AEqual"</note>, one at a fifth, and one at the octave, all made of brass strings; they sounded together quite lovely and magnificent.

### Chapter XL.
## The Universal or Perfect Harpsichord.
<note>original: "Clavicymbalum Universale, seu perfectum"</note>

Because harpsichords, symphonies, and similar types (which are otherwise called "instruments," though as previously mentioned, less correctly) are somewhat **imperfect**—inasmuch as the **chromatic genus** <term>Chromatic genus: the use of semitones or "black keys" to play notes outside the standard seven-note scale</term> cannot be managed on them in the same way as on lutes and viola da gambas—some harpsichords and symphonies have been produced according to the designs of knowledgeable organists. In these, the **natural** key <note>specifically the B-natural key</note> has been divided and made double, so that in the **Aeolian mode** <term>Aeolian mode: a musical scale corresponding to the natural minor scale</term> (when it is transposed a fourth lower), one can have the third between B and F-sharp perfectly pure and just <note>Praetorius is referring to the "split keys" used in meantone temperament to avoid "wolf" intervals</note>.

In my humble opinion, it would be very useful and necessary—not only in chamber organs <note>original: "Positiffen"</note> and church organs, but also in harpsichords, etc. (where if needed one can easily retune the strings on the keys, loosening them slightly or tightening them correctly)—that not only the **natural** keys but also the **sharp** keys be divided and made double. Then, in the **Hypodorian mode** <term>Hypodorian mode: an ancient musical scale; here discussed in a transposed version</term>, if it is to be played starting on F (a second lower), one could have the minor third to F in the added adjacent G-sharp quite purely, and thus have many more such variations in the chromatic genus.

I have, however, seen in Prague with Mr. Carl Luyton <note>Carl Luyton (1557–1620) was a famous Flemish composer and the court organist to Emperor Rudolf II</note>, organist to his Roman Imperial Majesty...

However, this same harpsichord <term>Clavicymbel: a keyboard instrument where strings are plucked</term> or instrument can be shifted seven times—namely through C, C-sharp, D, D-sharp, E, F, F-sharp, G, G-sharp, A, B-flat, B-natural, and up to C—and thus be advanced by three full tones <term>Tonos: whole steps</term>, so that one can encounter almost no other instrument with which this one could not be tuned in unison. In this way, all three genera of modulation <term>genera Modulandi: the three ancient systems of tuning—diatonic, chromatic, and enharmonic</term>, namely the **Diatonic**, **Chromatic**, and **Enharmonic**, can be observed upon it. It would therefore be fair to call this a "perfect instrument, if not the most perfect" <note>original Latin: "Instrumentum perfectum, si non perfectißimum"</note>, because such variation through all the whole tones and semitones <term>Super- & Semitonia</term> is not to be found on other instruments.

For although a motet or madrigal can be played through all semitones—and thus in the chromatic genus—by a practiced and experienced master and lutenist upon the viols <term>Violen de Gamba: "leg viols," fretted string instruments played with a bow</term>, and especially upon the lute; yet it cannot be achieved as purely or accurately as on such a harpsichord. This is for the following reasons: because on the viols and the lutes...

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of musical temperament and the placement of frets on stringed instruments compared to the fixed pitches of keyboard instruments. It concludes the section on the specialized harpsichord and introduces the Clavicytherium.</meta>

# ON THE DESCRIPTION OF INSTRUMENTS.
66

the frets are all spaced equally far apart (though they get closer as they approach the bridge <note>the "Steig" or bridge is the wooden piece that supports the strings at the bottom of the instrument</note>, which is understood without saying so) from one another. Thus, the half-steps <term>Semitonia: the smallest interval in standard Western music</term> cannot and must not be called either "major" or "minor," but rather "intermediate" <note>original: "intermedia"</note>. For in my opinion, every fret or finger-position <note>original: "Bund / Band oder Griff"</note> contains 4 1/2 commas <term>Comma: a tiny musical interval, much smaller than a half-step, used to measure precise tuning</term>, whereas otherwise a major half-step <note>original: "Semitonium majus"</note> contains five commas, and a minor half-step <note>original: "Semit. minus"</note> contains only four.

And because there is only a difference of half a comma on either side, and such a small amount does not register much to the ear on the aforementioned instruments like viols and lutes (which are sweet and quiet in themselves), the major half-step sounds just as well as the minor on a single fret, as if it were perfectly in tune for both. This difference cannot be immediately observed or detected <note>original: "observiret vnd deprehendiret"</note>, especially since one can also "help" the strings by how one fingers them on the frets, naming and giving them the desired pitch. This is not possible at all on harpsichords <term>Clavicymbeln: keyboard instruments where strings are plucked by quills</term> (where the strings are fixed) or on organs (where nothing can be added to or taken from the pipes, but they must remain exactly as they were tuned and installed).

Therefore, on these keyboard instruments, the chromatic style <term>genus Chromaticum: a style of music using many successive half-steps</term> cannot be observed or achieved at all without a great number and variety of keys. If one wished to have this on the lute as well, one would have to cut off all the frets and play upon it fretless.

I have also been informed by a distinguished musician in Kassel, Christopher Cornet <note>A composer and Kapellmeister at the court of Moritz of Hessen-Kassel (c. 1575–1635)</note>, that he saw such an instrument or Spinet <note>original: "Spinett," a smaller type of harpsichord</note> in Italy belonging to an Italian named Julius Caesar <note>original: "Iulius Cæsar"</note>.

He also indicated that no nation could be found that could sing more purely or perfectly according to such "justified" <note>meaning mathematically corrected or tempered</note> instruments, harpsichords, or spinets than the Greek musicians <note>original: "Græci Musici"</note>, of whom four singers <note>original: "Vocales"</note> were present in that place at the time.

A few years ago, a magnificent positive organ <term>Positiff: a small, portable pipe organ used in chamber music</term> was also brought from Italy to the Archducal court in Graz; in this organ, all the half-steps are similarly found doubled and complete, and it is said to be an excellent piece of work.

### Chapter XLII.
## Claviorganum.

This is a harpsichord, or other symphony <note>here referring to a rectangular virginal or similar keyboard instrument</note>, in which several stops of pipes are mixed in alongside the strings, just as in a positive organ <term>Postiff: a small, portable pipe organ</term>. From the outside, however, it appears no different than a harpsichord or symphony, except that on some, the bellows are placed at the back, while on others they are built inside the body of the instrument.

### Chapter XLIII.
## Arpichordum.

This is an instrument like a symphony or virginal <note>a small, rectangular keyboard instrument</note> where, through special sliders <note>original: "Züge"</note> of small brass hooks under the strings, a harp-like resonance is created and produced.

### Chapter XLIV.
# Fiddle-work, Fiddle-Instrument, or Fiddle-Harpsichord.
### (in Drawing Plate III.)

This Fiddle-work <note>original: "Geigenwerck"</note> (which in shape and proportion from the outside is quite like any other common pointed harpsichord, and of the same size, so that it can be moved here and there on a table and easily carried from one place to another, and one person alone can produce upon it that which otherwise requires five or six fiddles <note>original: "Geigen," here referring to the viol family</note>) was first devised and constructed by a citizen of Nuremberg named Hans Hayden. The invention was perhaps initially inspired by the nature of the common hurdy-gurdy <note>original: "Lyren"; specifically the "Radleier" where a rosined wheel bows the strings</note> (where the strings are touched by a wheel and yield their resonance), and the matter was then thought out further.

Although some, such as Galilei <note>original: "Galilæus"; referring to Vincenzo Galilei, the music theorist and father of Galileo</note> and others, claim that such a type of Fiddle-work had already been invented and theorized <note>original: "außspeculiret"</note> before our time; be that as it may, in my opinion, such an invention was not perfectly put into practice or fully completed until the aforementioned Hans Hayden took it in hand and brought it to its proper state, as can now be seen clearly and in actual fact.

This fiddle-work, however, instead of tangents, has five or six steel wheels covered with very smooth parchment and coated on top with rosin <note>original: *Colophonio*</note>, or oil of spike or lavender <note>original: *oleo Spicæ vel lavendulæ*</note> (just like violin players use on their bows, or as it is commonly called, the fiddle-bow). These wheels are controlled and stepped upon with both feet by the organist himself on the floor below, using a large main wheel and various rollers located beneath the soundboard; or they may be pulled from above by the hands of a bellows-blower <term>Calcant: an assistant who usually pumped the bellows for an organ</term> using strings, so that the wheels must always remain in full motion.

Now, when a key <note>original: *Clavis*</note> is pressed down at the front, the corresponding string touches one of the revolving wheels and gives off a resonance, just as if a bow were being drawn and stroked across it.

The coarse strings are made of thick brass and steel, wound with pure parchment, so that the lowest ones are almost as thick as the heavy strings on the bass violas <note>original: *BassGeigen*</note>, since some in the bass register reach down to low F and D. Further up, they gradually decrease in size until, in the treble <note>original: *Discant*</note>, only bare, strong steel strings are found to be strung without parchment.

However, so that those who have not yet seen such an instrument and fiddle-work may know what unique benefit and use it has over other similar instruments regarding nuance <note>original: *Moderation*</note> and variety, I will set down here the own words and thoughts of the noble instrument maker and inventor himself, which he published in a small treatise in the year 1610, and leave it to everyone to judge for themselves.

> For some time now, composers have especially strived with all diligence toward how they might bring vocal music <note>original: *Musicam*</note> to its highest peak, such that it can hardly climb any higher. But regarding musical instruments, although great defects are found in some—namely, that they lack the most beautiful ornament, the nuance <note>original: *Moderation*</note> of the voices—no one among the many skillful instrumentalists who have ever lived has undertaken to remedy this defect and to bring the nuance of the voices to the keyboard <note>original: *Clavir*</note> as well.

> How much depends on the shaping <note>original: *formiren*</note> of the voice is known to those in the chapels <note>choir schools</note> who are accustomed to training the young boys and singers <note>original: *Cantores*</note>. Indeed, almost everyone otherwise understands what a poor state it is in for even a common orator <note>original: *Oratore*</note> when he speaks without the rising and falling of the voice,

<meta>This page continues the argument for the Geigenwerck’s superiority over other keyboard instruments. It specifically addresses the limitation of "modulation" (dynamic control and sustain) in organs and harpsichords, explaining why these traditional instruments cannot mimic the expressive qualities of the human voice or the violin.</meta>

-># ON THE DESCRIPTION OF INSTRUMENTS.<-
<note>original: "DE ORGANOGRAPHIA."</note>
<sig>I iij</sig>
<meta>catchword: voice,</meta>

[the] voice—as the text and *emotional affect* <note>original: *affectus*</note> require—maintains no *proper style* <note>original: *decorum*</note>; but rather speaks continuously in the same tone without pause. If this is true in speaking, it is much more tedious to hear in singing.

However, every keyboard instrument—including the organs, which otherwise hold the advantage over all other instruments regarding their *solemnity* <note>original: *gravitatem*</note>, as well as all other wind instruments—is afflicted with this defect: that they cannot be *modulated* <note>original: *moderiert*</note>, nor can the voices be forced into a loud or quiet sound and *tone* <note>original: *Sono*</note>. Instead, the pipe gives and keeps its sound in the same tone, however the instrumentalist strikes the *key* <note>original: *Clavem*</note>, and it is impossible to strengthen or soften the voice. Which, however, one can do with the bow on the violin, depending on whether one strokes and presses heavily or lightly upon it. And thus the instrumentalist on the keyboard is trapped, so that he cannot signal his *affects* <note>original: *affecten*</note>—as he could on the violin (even though he cannot express the text on it either)—whether sad, happy, serious, or playful thoughts are within him; which must happen solely through the *modulation* <note>original: *moderation*</note> of the voice. And although in the organs, by drawing or closing the registers, one can now make a quiet, soft, lovely sound, and soon again a loud din and clamor, this is still not called *modulation*—because it remains quiet or loud in the same tone—but is rather an unformed, unbroken voice, as was said before regarding an unpaused speech.

Likewise, one cannot make or produce the voices on stringed instruments <note>the author refers here to plucked keyboard instruments like the harpsichord</note> any quieter or stronger than what the *key* <note>original: *Clavis*</note> itself provides. And the *sound* <note>original: *Sonus*</note> cannot be sustained; but as soon as the string is struck and makes itself heard, the sound vanishes again, so that no full *beat* <note>original: *tempus*</note> can be perfectly *continued* <note>original: *continuirt*</note>.

This fading and vanishing of the voice is contrary to true *modulation* <note>original: *Moderation*</note>, for the voice should be able to swell from silence into strength.

Thus it is also necessary, if one otherwise wishes to sustain a whole beat perfectly, that it be *divided* <note>original: *diminuirt*; this refers to 'diminution,' the practice of breaking a long note into many fast, short notes to create the illusion of sustain</note> and struck twice; which, however, is against the nature of a magnificent, *solemn* <note>original: *gravitetischen*</note> song in *motets* <note>original: *Muteten*</note> and *concertos* <note>original: *Concerten*</note>, though it may *be acceptable* <note>original: *passiren*</note> in *passamezzos* <note>original: *Passamerzen*</note>, *galliards*, and dances.

On this Geigenwerck, however, one can have both: namely, the voice can be *sustained* <note>original: *continuiren*</note> and *modulated* <note>original: *moderiren*</note> as long as one wishes; and not only a *breve*, but even a *longa* and *maxima* <term>Breve, Longa, Maxima: terms for very long note durations in early music notation</term> can be *continued* <note>original: *continu-*</note> together without interruption...

<summary>This page discusses the expressive limitations of organs and harpsichords, focusing on their inability to vary volume or sustain notes. The author argues that the Geigenwerck is superior because it allows for "modulation" (dynamic control) and continuous sound, similar to a bowed violin.</summary>

And although the text cannot be expressed with words, the instrumentalist can nonetheless make his *sentiment* <note>original: *sensum*</note> known—whether sad or happy thoughts are within him—according to whether he strikes the *keyboard* <note>original: *Clavier*</note> boldly or gently. For one.

6. Sixth, one can also play it in the *manner* and style of other instruments, but especially like a lute.

9. 10. Ninth, it can also be played in a good hurdy-gurdy style. 11. Eleventh, it also has the quality of a *cittern* <note>original: *Cithern*; a wire-strung instrument</note>, in the way young fellows are accustomed to go *serenading* <note>original: *gassatum*</note> through the streets.

All of this, and even more, an organist can achieve because it is nothing other than a common *keyboard* <note>original: *Clavier*</note> and requires no special fingering or *application* <note>technical method of playing</note>, except that one should strike the keyboard with a light hand and not fall upon the *keys* <note>original: *Clavier*</note> with full force.

For in this matter, very diligent practice is highly necessary, so that the organist:
1. *exercises* <note>original: *exercire*</note> and accustoms himself to using his feet to step steadily and incessantly upon the two small wooden boards on the floor, which govern and turn the wheels above according to the *beat* <note>original: *Tact*</note> kept by him or the other musicians; in this way, he can keep time all the better and be less likely to be led astray.
2. That he takes very proper and careful heed not to strike the *keys* <note>original: *Claves*</note> with his fingers too hard or too softly, lest some strings buzz too loudly while others *respond* <note>original: *respondiren*</note> too little or not at all. This is something that cannot be mastered at first by anyone without particularly diligent and constant practice.

But he who is now a little accustomed to this, and understands the loveliness and *moderation* <note>control over volume and expression</note> that he can have on this instrument, will desire to use no other. It is also all the more agreeable because it does not require as much tuning as lutes and violins or other stringed *instruments* <note>original: *Instrumenta*</note>, because the strings are not made of gut <note>original: *schäffen*; literally "sheep-derived," referring to sheep gut strings</note> but are all of brass and steel, which through long use become better and better and do not soon go out of tune.

And because perhaps this work and instrument might be disparaged by some (who have never used it in practice or performance, and are either too lazy to *practice* and *exercise* themselves on it, or simply cannot make any progress with it) and might be regarded as a mere hurdy-gurdy <note>original: *Bawrenleyerwerck*; literally "peasant's lyre work"</note>, I therefore ask that they do not [judge it] as—

## Chapter XLV.
### The Regal.

-><margin>See *Theatrum Instrumentorum*, Plate IV.</margin><-
<note>original: *Sciagraph. Col. iv.*; refers to the volume of illustrations accompanying this text</note>

<image-desc>An ornate woodcut initial letter 'D' decorated with elaborate floral scrollwork and foliate motifs within a rectangular frame.</image-desc>By the word **Regal** <note>original: *Regall*</note>, one understands not only the **reed-work** <note>original: *Schnarrwerck*; a "buzzing" stop made of metal reeds</note> that is commonly and mostly found in the **breast-work** <note>original: *Brust*; the section of the organ located directly in front of the player</note> of large organs, but also those instruments found in Imperial, Royal, Electoral, and Princely chapels called a Regal. In these, one or more sets of **reeds** <note>original: *Schnarrwercke*</note> lie hidden in a long, narrow little chest with two bellows at the back. It is set upon a table and can be used in music much more conveniently and much better than a **harpsichord** <note>original: *Clavicymbel*</note> or **spinet** <note>original: *Symphony*</note>. For harpsichords are far too quiet in a full musical ensemble, and their strings cannot **sustain** <note>original: *Continuiren*</note> their sound and resonance for more than half a **beat** <note>original: *Tact*</note>.

In the Regals, however, the **sound** <note>original: *Sonus*</note> is not only sustained (in the same manner as in organs) as long as the **key** <note>original: *Clave*</note> is held down—which is highly necessary, especially in **concertos** <note>original: *concerten*</note>—but it can also be made quite soft through the deliberate closing of the lid, or quite loud when it is opened again. Thus, amidst a full, well-arranged ensemble of **singers** <note>original: *Vocalisten*</note> and **instrumentalists** <note>original: *Instrumentisten*</note>, it allows itself to be heard quite clearly. Therefore, it can be heard and used with pleasure not only in Princely chambers before the table and at other honorable **banquets** <note>original: *Conviviis*</note>, but also in small and large churches, sounding almost better than a **positive organ** <note>original: *Positiff*; a small, portable pipe organ</note>.

-># ON THE DESCRIPTION OF INSTRUMENTS.<-
<note>original: "DE ORGANOGRAPHIA."</note>

In my opinion, one could better distinguish one from the other by calling the stop in an organ a **Regal Pipe** <note>original: *Regall Pfeiffe*</note>, but calling this [the portable instrument] a **Regal Work** <note>original: *Regall Werck*</note>; so that one might better know how to refer to them correctly in conversation.

Sometimes in such a small case or **Regal Work** <note>a small, portable reed organ</note> there is only one type of Regal pipe or **reed-work** <note>original: *Schnarrwercklein*; a "buzzing" stop that produces sound via a vibrating metal tongue</note> at 8-foot pitch <note>the standard pitch where the keys match the expected musical notes</note>. Sometimes there are two reed stops, where one is set at 8-foot and the other at 4-foot pitch. Sometimes there are three reed stops, with three octaves one above the other, the lowest being at 16-foot pitch. In some, there is a fourth register with a small repeating **Cymbal** <note>a high-pitched, sparkling stop</note> included, which then sounds almost like a half-sized organ.

There are many and various different types both of the construction of such small cases and of the Regal pipes contained within them, which would be far too extensive to **specify** <note>original: *specificiren*</note> and describe here.

Among those made so far, however, those from **Vienna in Austria** are almost better than others; although many magnificent and good **Regal Works** made by other masters are also found, which can be used with great pleasure.

This is especially true when the lowest Regal pipe **C** at 8-foot pitch is about 5 or 5 1/2 inches long, four-cornered, entirely closed at the top but opened again at the bottom with 3, 4, 5, or more or less small holes, and crafted from tin; for these—as will also be discussed in Part IV—are not unlike a **Dulcian** <note>a Renaissance woodwind instrument, the ancestor of the bassoon</note> or **Bassoon** <note>original: *Fagotten*</note> and are very lovely.

Otherwise, they are also made in this style but somewhat shorter and entirely open at the top. Some are also made of brass in various ways, but these cannot have as lovely a **resonance** <note>original: *Resonanz*</note> as the **stopped** <note>original: *gedäckten*; pipes with a cap or cover on the end</note> ones.

Two years ago, in a prominent place not far from here, someone began making very fine and delicate small Regal works with wooden pipes, which not only have a good, quiet, soft, and lovely resonance, but are also very light and convenient to bring and carry from one place to another; these please me very much above others.

The tiny Regal works that can be folded into the bellows—first invented in **Nuremberg** and **Augsburg** <note>known as "Bible Regals" because they could be folded up to the size of a large book</note>—are indeed very nimble and convenient to carry and transport. However, the Regal pipes within them, because they cannot be made large due to the narrow space in the small **body** <note>original: *Corpore*</note> but are barely an inch high, are far too "buzzy" or raspy.

Near **Regensburg** in **Bavaria**, I saw a Regal Work devised and made by a monk, in which the mouthpieces were made of wood and the **tongue** <note>the vibrating part of the reed</note> or blade was made of cane—the same material usually used to make the reeds for wind instru—

<note>original: "DE ORGANOGRAPHIA."</note>

[reeds such as one] must make for instruments like **Dulcians**, **Krummhorns**, **Shawms**, and **Bagpipes**, etc. And this [type of Regal] had no special resonator bodies for the pipes; instead, the resonators were bored and channeled right through the entire body of the Regal, so that the resonance exited from the bottom. This certainly had a beautiful, lovely character and a very quiet resonance, but because the reeds <note>the vibrating "tongues" that produce the sound</note> were made of cane—from which they were constructed—they were very unstable, and one constantly had to tune them and adjust them.

And here I must not forget to add that some believe the **Regal** <note>a small, portable reed organ</note> got its name because the first one completed by the original inventor of this work was presented as a special gift **to a certain king** <note>original: *Regi cuidam*</note>, and was therefore called **Regal** <note>original: *Regale*</note>, as if it were **worthy of a king** <note>original: *quasi dignum Rege*</note>, or a **royal work** <note>original: *Regium vel Regale opus*</note>.

There is a distinguished organ and instrument maker now at an **Electoral Court** <note>the court of a high-ranking prince of the Holy Roman Empire</note> who claims he wants to and can build a Regal that would not go out of tune for a year and a day, even if it were moved from the cold into the heat **and vice versa** <note>original: *& contrà*</note>. If this could actually be achieved (about which I still have very great doubts), it would be worth any amount of money. For I have become more than well aware, with great burden, of the trouble and inconvenience it causes an organist and music director when one wishes to perform music **in choirs** <note>original: *per choros*; referring to the polychoral style where groups of musicians are placed in different areas of a church</note> in churches or before the dinner table with several Regal works—especially in winter, when the Regals must be brought from the cold of the church into the warm dining rooms.

In truth, it is found that the metal pipes in churches—though not so much in the large churches as in the smaller ones, where the winter cold and summer heat can penetrate more easily; whereas in large vaulted churches, just as in cellars, it is fine and cool in summer and not so sharply cold in winter—are forced so far down by the cold in winter, especially when a very great cold lasts so intensely and persistently, that the pitch sinks by a half **semitone** <note>the smallest interval in common use, such as the distance between C and C-sharp</note>, if I may call it that, if not further. This can be quite accurately observed and found in wind instruments like **Cornetts** <note>original: *Zincken*</note>, **Flutes**, **Trombones**, **Pommers** <note>powerful double-reed instruments, ancestors of the bassoon</note>, and **Bassoons**, but primarily on **Positives** <note>small, stationary pipe organs</note> which remain in warm rooms (although those actually rise in pitch even more because of the great heat from the warm stoves).

Furthermore, it is not a little surprising that all the voices in an organ—in which there are often several hundred, even several thousand pipes, as 3,742 pipes are found in the **Danzig Organ** <note>the famous Great Organ of St. Mary's Church in Gdańsk, one of the largest in the world at the time</note>—deviate from their proper pitch, to which they were initially tuned purely, all together: rising in the summer and sinking in the winter.

-># ON THE DESCRIPTION OF INSTRUMENTS.<-
<note>original: "DE ORGANOGRAPHIA."</note>

On the other hand, however, the **Regal** and all **reed-works** <note>original: "Schnarrwercke," referring to the buzzing, reed-based stops of an organ</note> become lower in pitch in the summer and in the heat, but in the winter and in the cold, they become higher and sharper. Regarding the cause of such a great mutation and change, it will be mentioned somewhat in the following Part IV. **To inquire into the cause of this,** says Master S. C., **I think it consists in the difference of the metal, because tin or lead is contracted by heat, but copper** <note>original: "aes Lypsium," likely referring to a specific brass or copper alloy</note> **is dilated. This could be learned from craftsmen who work with these metals. The cause cannot be attributed to the air by itself, unless when it affects the metals because of heat and cold; otherwise, if the air were dilated by heat, it would produce the same effect in lead and copper. But this does not happen. Therefore, the cause must be sought only in the metals.**
<note>original: "Causam sive huius inquirere, inquit Dominus S. C. eam in discrimine metalli consistere arbitror, quod stannum vel plumbum calore contrahatur, æs Lypsium verò dilatetur... Ergò tantum in metallis causa quærenda." This reflects early modern attempts to understand thermal expansion, though the theory here—that tin contracts with heat—is scientifically incorrect by modern standards.</note>

But because many different opinions and views tend to arise concerning this, I consider it completely unnecessary to discuss it further in detail here.

But that it is true, and is actually found to be so in practice, can be gathered among other things from the fact that a metal pipe, as soon as it is touched or held in the hand by the **organ maker** <note>original: "Orgelmacher"</note> while he is tuning, or at any other time, and thus feels the warmth of the hand, immediately changes its tone and rises slightly in pitch. But as soon as it remains untouched for a little while, it returns to its proper tone. This is also noticeably felt and found in wind instruments, especially in **flutes** and **cornetts**. <note>original: "Zincken," a wooden wind instrument with a trumpet-like mouthpiece</note> And although some are of the opinion that organs and **positive organs** <note>small, non-portable organs</note> in which all the ranks are made of wooden pipes do not experience such great mutation so severely, experience shows that in organs where some special wooden ranks are included alongside the metal pipes, everything—both the wooden and the metal pipes—deviate together, as no particular discordance is found when they are played together.

And since at this time no one can provide the actual cause and **probable reasons** <note>original: "rationes probabiles"</note> for such mutation and change, one must rightly consider it a special work of God, who planted such things into nature.

I previously never wanted to believe it, until I have now experienced and learned it myself in fact and truth.

### Chorus.
#### Num. I.

The **Chorus** <note>original: "Chorus"; in this historical context, it refers to a primitive woodwind or bagpipe-like instrument described in medieval texts, rather than a singing group</note> was an instrument that had a mouthpiece at the front for blowing, two pipes in the middle, and a large hole at the bottom where the sound and the wind exited again.

### Psaltery.
<note>original: "Psalterium"</note>
#### Num. II.
### Ten-Stringed Psaltery.
<note>original: "Psalterium dechachorum"</note>
#### Num. III. IV.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'D' within a square frame, embellished with intricate floral patterns and scrolling vines.</image-desc>
The **Psaltery** <note>a stringed instrument played by plucking, ancestor to the harpsichord</note> was formed in two ways: namely triangular, like a triangle (indicated as Nos. 2 and 3); and square (indicated as No. 4). As can be found in the *Theater* or *Sciagraphia* <note>original: "Teatro oder Sciagraphia," referring to the *Theatrum Instrumentorum*, the volume of illustrations accompanying this treatise</note>.

However, the author's words in the aforementioned book are these: "The **Psaltery**, which is still in use today, I have never seen in any form other than triangular. But I am of the opinion that the **Virginal** <note>a small, rectangular keyboard instrument where strings are plucked by quills</note>, which is struck and played with keys and **quill-plectrums** <note>original: "Fedder-kielen"</note>, was first conceived as being derived from the Psaltery. And although the Virginal, like a **Clavichord**, is contained within a long case, it nevertheless has many other characteristics that are more comparable to the Psaltery than to the Clavichord. For one must have a separate string for every key, and each string must be drawn longer and higher than the others. Consequently, from the shortening and tapering of the strings, something nearly like a triangle appears and can be seen upon the instrument or Virginal case."

## **Jerome's Drum.**
<note>original: "Tympanum Hieronymi." Jerome refers to Saint Jerome, to whom a famous medieval letter describing instruments was attributed.</note>

### **No. IX.**

The **Drum** <note>original: "Tympanum"; though we usually think of a drum, Praetorius describes a wind instrument based on a medieval misunderstanding of the term</note> (which was very much used for the praise of **GOD** the Almighty and is often mentioned in Holy Scripture) I find depicted as a long pipe which has a mouthpiece at the top into which one blows, and two holes at the bottom through which the voice and the wind exit. It was made in such a way that a woman could carry it in one hand.

In our current time, however, we call a **Tympanum** the large **Kettledrums** <note>original: "Heerpaucken"; literally "army drums"</note> **(Col. XXIII.)** made of copper kettles covered with calfskins, which one strikes with **Mallets**. These are played at the courts of princes and great lords for arrivals and departures, for dining and dancing, and are also used in wartime during field campaigns. These are quite monstrous **rumbling barrels**. We also have other **Drums** which are called **Soldier’s Drums**, which are used alongside **Cross-flutes** or **Swiss pipes** <note>original: "Zwerch- oder Schweizerpfeiffen"; these are transverse flutes or fifes</note>.

Otherwise, there is still a small **Hand-drum (Col. IX.)** <note>original: "Päucklin"; a tabor</note> that is very much used by the French and Netherlanders. One holds the **Hand-drum** with the left hand, and along with it a **Pipe** or **Stem-flute** <note>original: "Schwägel oder Stämmenpfeiff"; a tabor pipe</note> which has two holes at the top and one at the bottom, held with three fingers. One can whistle all kinds of dances and songs upon it while simultaneously striking the **Hand-drum** with a **Mallet** in the right hand.

But for what purpose and in what manner all these **instruments** were used by the **ancients**, I do not know, as I have neither heard nor seen any of them. The ***poets*** have also described many more ***instruments*** with strange names, of which I can know or learn nothing else except that they were ***musical instruments***. But how they were shaped, or whether their form was better or worse, prettier or uglier, more subtle or coarser than our own, I cannot yet find in any ***author*** who has written anything specific on the matter. I believe, however, that in the last hundred years all ***musical instruments*** have become so subtle, so beautiful, so good, and so well-made that neither ***Orpheus***, nor ***Linus***, nor ***Pan***, nor ***Apollo***, nor any of the ***poets*** has seen or heard them; and what is more, I do not believe they would have thought it possible to make or even imagine them.

# ON THE DESCRIPTION OF INSTRUMENTS.

As for the various other types of instruments found portrayed in the **Illustrated Appendix** <note>original: "Sciagraphia," the title of the volume of woodcut plates accompanying this book</note>—such as the **Dulcimer** <note>original: "Hackebret"</note> (Col. XVIII), **Hurdy-gurdy** <note>original: "Bawrenlyra," literally "peasant's lyre"</note>, **Keyed Fiddle** <note>original: "Schlüsselfidel," likely a Nyckelharpa</note>, **Xylophone** <note>original: "Strohfidel," literally "straw-fiddle"</note>, **Small Cymbals**, **Little Bells**, **Singing Globe**, and a **Basque Drum** <note>original: "Vntrambour de Biscaye," a tambourine</note> (Col. XXII); **Timpani** or **Kettle Drums**, **Soldier’s Drum**, and the **Anvil** (Col. XXIII); as well as other strange, foreign **Muscovite** <note>Russian</note> and **Turkish** instruments (Col. 29, 30, 31)—it is unnecessary to write much or remind the reader of them. Some of these might rightly be called "foolish" <note>original: "Dörliche"</note> (as Sebastian Virdung <note>author of a famous 1511 treatise on instruments</note> calls them) or "beggar's instruments." This is because they are known to everyone and do not strictly belong to the art of music. The only reason the **Anvil** was included in the **Illustrated Appendix** is because Pythagoras examined and discovered the differences in the sounds of hammers upon it. Through this, he found the mathematical proportions <note>original: "proportionibus"</note> that govern the musical harmonies <note>original: "Consonantien"</note> known at that time: namely, the **Octave, Fifth, and Fourth**. A longer and more detailed account of this can be found in Boethius, *Book 1 on Music, chapters 10 and 11* <note>original: "Boethio lib. 1. Musices, cap. 10. & 11."</note>, as well as in the *Second Exercise* of Sethus Calvisius.

<meta>This page continues the catalog of musical instruments, moving from the historical and symbolic instruments of antiquity mentioned on the previous page to highly specific, ingenious contemporary instruments and the introduction of performance styles for stringed instruments.</meta>

# ON THE DESCRIPTION OF INSTRUMENTS.
<note>original: "DE ORGANOGRAPHIA."</note>

At this point, I must also mention that a small, old **Positive organ** <note>original: "Positiff"; a small, portable pipe organ common in the Renaissance and Baroque</note>—crafted with such clean, pure, and delicate workmanship that it is said to have been made by a monk—has come into my hands. It was brought to the King of Denmark, **Christian IV**; its form and structure can be found in the **Theater of Instruments** <note>original: "Theatrum Instrumentorum," the appendix of woodcut illustrations for this book</note>, Plate [blank].

In this instrument, there is only one type of pipe: specifically, an open **Small Principal** <note>original: "Principälgen"</note> of 2-foot pitch. Although there are only 38 keys <note>original: "Clavir"</note> from F to a', there are additional pipes for an extra octave above these, which are arranged in a circular winding in the center of the instrument's body.

For these single pipes, there are three **stops** <note>original: "Register"</note>: the 1st for the fundamental pitch of the lowest pipes; the 2nd for the **fifth** <note>original: "Quint"</note>; and the 3rd for the **octave** above. Each stop can be drawn and used on its own, or two can be combined, or all three used together. Thus, from a single pipe for one key, two or even three distinct sounds <note>original: "discreti soni"</note> and different tones resonate and can be heard—namely, the fifth and the octave alongside the fundamental pitch. I leave it to a skillful organ builder to judge how such a thing is achieved, and I wish that some artist would undertake the task of replicating such a work.

Furthermore, there is another clever feature <note>original: "Kunststücke"</note> in this little instrument: when one half of the lead weights (which are divided and halved for this purpose) are removed from the bellows, it produces a very soft, quiet resonance <note>original: "Resonans"</note> like that of **transverse flutes** <note>original: "Querflöten"</note>. It sounds exactly as if a consort of transverse flutes were being played together in harmony.

# Chapter I.

## Concerning the dignity and excellence of Organs/ and how the same alone and especially directed toward Church and Divine Service/ is to be preferred above all other instruments.

What some consider to be the case / that next to **Theology** <note>original: "Theologia"</note>, the highest **place** <note>original: "locus"</note> should rightly be given and assigned to **Music** <note>original: "Musicæ"</note> (as a beautiful, glorious gift of God / and which is an image and likeness of heavenly *Music* / as the holy angels of God with the entire heavenly host constantly and without ceasing laud and praise their Creator / in a lovely **Harmony** <note>original: "Harmonia"</note> / and sing the **Holy, holy, holy Lord God of Sabaoth** <note>original: "Sanctus, sanctus, sanctus Dominus Deus Sabaoth"</note>) : is among many other of its utilities, powers, and effects perhaps not the least cause / that *Music* in itself is to be held more as a spiritual than an earthly essence / and therefore awakens in the hearts of men an inner devotion of the spirit / to praise God the Almighty with beautiful psalms and songs of praise all the more fervently. Therefore also both Kings / David and Solomon / when they wished to arrange the divine service in the Temple and Tabernacle at Jerusalem in the most glorious and decorative manner / appointed so many *musicians* / singers and *instrumentalists* / with great diligence and expense / to make the people all the more fervent and zealous. To which end David himself used his harp / and without doubt had several glorious organ works prepared and placed because of the size of the Temple.

Therefore Church *Music*, as a divine service / is still today rightly to be held in honor / and **celebrated** with all **reverence** <note>original: "reverentz celebrirt"</note> : To this belong skillful, famous *organists* / who rather encourage the listeners than make them weary / who also themselves with right devotion / present the texts or psalms which they **set to melody** <note>original: "melodiren"</note> in their hearts and thoughts to God. But if one does not take heed of this / but wishes to appoint anyone who can only make a **little jingle** <note>original: "Tänglein"; a derogatory term for trivial or unskilled playing</note> without distinction / then Church *Music* will easily fall into contempt / and because of such abuse will finally be discarded entirely / as experience testifies.

And generally, religion follows after it / as also happened in **Greece** <note>original: "Græcia"</note> / where in former times *Music* **flourished** <note>original: "floriret"</note> to the highest degree. ...more secretively; and through the rising and intake of the bellows, it is supplied with a constant and much stronger wind than other instruments, which must be guided and blown by human breath.

Indeed, this polyphonic, lovely work <note>The author uses the word "Werck" to refer to the organ as a mechanical and artistic masterpiece.</note> encompasses within itself everything that can be devised and composed in music, and produces such a true, natural sound, resonance, and tone, no different from an entire choir full of musicians, where various melodies are heard from the voices of young boys and grown men. If you wish to hear a **drum**, **trumpet**, **trombone**, **cornett**, **recorder**, **transverse flute**, **alto shawm**, **soprano shawm**, **dulcian** <note>An early bassoon-like instrument.</note>, **rackett** <note>A compact, deep-pitched reed instrument.</note>, **sordun** <note>A quiet, double-reed instrument.</note>, **crumhorn**, **violin**, **hurdy-gurdy**, etc., you can have all of these, and many other wondrous delights besides, in this artistic work. Thus, when you have and hear this instrument, you think no differently than that you have and hear all the other instruments together. I will not mention that on the organ, one who is often poorly experienced in this art can surpass excellent masters of other instruments, since one can reach directly into the mouth of this work <note>original German: "recht ins Maul zugreiffen," a metaphor for the direct physical control of the organ's mechanism</note>, using hands and feet simultaneously. And to confess the truth, no art has risen so high as the art of the organ: for human's subtle ingenuity and diligent reflection have brought it to the point that it can now stand perfectly well without any further addition, and it appears that nothing more is lacking for its perfection and completion, nor can anything be desired <note>original Latin: "desideriret"</note>, added, or increased.

For what an exceedingly excellent and, so to speak, almost divine work the organ is, is testified by Girolamo Diruta, an Italian <note>original Latin: "Hieronymus Diruta Italus," an influential organist and theorist (c. 1554–1610) whose work "Il Transilvano" defined organ technique.</note>, in a preface: whose own words, translated from Italian into German, read as follows:

> †† All arts and sciences (he says) which human reason and understanding can grasp, encompass, and understand through God's immeasurable grace and goodness, refer and draw themselves toward a primary intelligence <note>original Latin: "principale intelligens"</note>, as if toward their master, who because of his high excellence is understood, honored, and praised by all others. From this it follows that when one mentions and thinks of the "Philosopher" alone in philosophy, immediately **Aristotle** is understood as the prince of philosophers <note>original Latin: "Philosophorum princeps"</note>. In medicine, **Hippocrates**; in the art of poetry, among the Latins, **Virgil**, and among the Italians, **Petrarch**, are honored with the name of "The Poet" <note>original Latin: "Poëtæ"</note>.

# ON THE DESCRIPTION OF INSTRUMENTS.

Similarly, in Theology, the Prophet signifies King David; and by the name "Apostle," St. Paul is understood. Because these men surpassed all others in their art and skill, the general title of excellence was rightfully left and assigned to them. This custom was also held by the ancients in music and the art of singing, in that they gave and assigned the highest and most prominent title above all other musicians who ever flourished among them to Orpheus and Amphion.

In the same way, it continues to this day with the titles in instrumental music, where this previously mentioned instrument, because of its excellence, is called *Organum* (a Greek name that otherwise encompasses all instruments and tools <note>original Latin: *in genere alle Instrumenta, vnd Werckzeuge*</note> that exist in the world), or in German, an **organ**. This is because it contains, surrounds, and holds within itself all other instruments, whatever their names may be. Therefore, in this day and age, the said organ should rightly be regarded as a **King of all instruments**, with which the Divine Majesty is lauded, praised, and honored in the assembly of the faithful.

For similar reasons, the hand on the human body is called an *Organum* <note>original Latin: *Organum, ein Werckzeug aller Werckzeuge*</note>, a "tool of all tools," because in its work it presides over its office with all the dutiful services necessary for the performance of its tasks, and assists the other limbs.

There is no doubt, however, that the word *Organum* is not understood by everyone in its true, natural sense. For many are of the opinion that by this word *Organum*, only an organ is understood—one which is operated with bellows and used in churches and choirs for the glory of God. Of this, it is written in Psalm 150: "Praise the Lord with harps and organs." <note>Praetorius is referencing the Luther Bible translation of Psalm 150:4, which uses *Orgeln* where modern English translations often say "pipes" or "strings."</note> But just as the lute, harp, fiddle, and other stringed instruments, which get their sound through strings, are just as well called by the name *Organi* or *Instrumenti*, because the one who uses and plays such instruments does so to demonstrate and prove his art in fiddling and playing. Thus, the organ, in its already attained high status, encompasses all other instruments within its range. It rightfully bears the noble title and name of excellence, however, because it comes closest to the human voice (being governed by the wind and the hands of the master). For the pipes actually represent to the eyes the human throat or windpipe, through which it also carries its breath and forms the tone, sound, and voice. Indeed, one might well say that the organ is an artificially made animal, which through

### *Time.* <note>original: "Tempus"</note>
But as to when and at what time the organ was first invented and its use introduced into the Christian Church, the **chronicles** and **historians** do not agree at all.

One reads in **Volaterranus** <note>original: "Volat. lib. 22. an. 653."</note> that Pope **Vitalian** <note>original: "Vitellianus"</note>, under the reign of Emperor **Constantine III**, established singing and the organ in the churches. **Polydore Vergil** <note>original: "Polydorus lib. 6. Cap. 2. de invent."</note> and **Albert Krantz** <note>original: "Cranzius lib. 2. Metrop."</note> report: Pope **Vitalian I** made the church rules and arranged the singing, also using organs (as some claim) for greater fullness of voice and sweet sound. **Platina**, in his biography of Vitalian, writes—and **William Perkins**, an English theologian of Cambridge <note>original: "Guil. Perkinsus Anglic. Theol. Acad. Cantab."</note>, also recorded—that **instruments** <note>original: "Instrumenta"</note> driven by water or wind had their beginning around the year of Christ 660 or around the year 930. **Aimonius** places it in the year 820; **Genebrard** in 997. **Navarrus** <note>original: "Navarrus in lib. de Orat. & horis Canon. Cap. 16."</note> says that in the time of **Aquinas**, organs were not yet in use. However, **Thomas Aquinas** died around the year of Christ 1274, as **Chytræus** calculates it.

It is to be suspected, however, that organs are much older, and that **Vitalian**, around the year 660, only **approved** and **confirmed** <note>original: "approbiret vnd confirmiret"</note> them. For as the excellent contemporary chronologist **Sethus Calvisius** <note>original: "H. Sethus calvisius Chronologus nostro tempore præstantissimus"</note> maintains, as soon as the practice of much singing was established in the churches and divided into **choirs** <note>original: "Choros"</note>, undoubtedly—where two choirs could not be had—an organ was used as an aid. It would **modulate** <note>original: "moduliret"</note> the **chant** <note>original: "Choral"</note> simply and alone, also to the end that the singers might rest a little. Thus also, through the help and advancement of the organ, the **tetrachords of the ancients** <note>original: "tetrachorda antiquorum"; referring to the four-note groupings used in Ancient Greek music theory</note>—which were still in use in the time of **Boethius** (who flourished in the year of Christ 487, in which year he was Consul in Rome)—were abolished. The six **musical syllables** <note>original: "voces Musicales"; likely referring to the hexachord system of ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la</note> were invented, and the **musical scale** <note>original: "scala Musicalis"</note> was greatly improved, as can be seen in the work of **Guido** <note>original: "Guidone"; the monk Guido d'Arezzo, who is credited with inventing modern staff notation</note> (who flourished more than five hundred years after Boethius, around the year of Christ 1026). We still have him to thank that twenty **keys** <note>original: "Claves"</note> were organized, where previously there were first only four, then seven, soon fourteen, and finally fifteen.

Likewise, it was through the organ that our **polyphonic music** <term>figuralis Musica</term> <note>Complex music featuring multiple, independent melodic lines, which evolved alongside the organ's capabilities.</note> was invented; for the **harmonic music of the ancients** <note>original: "Musica harmonica apud veteres"</note> was altogether different from our

current <note>original: "iziger"</note>

And as for how the **chromatic keys** <note>original: "Claves chromaticæ"</note> or the **semitones** were invented, this comes from the **tetrachords of the ancients** <note>original: "ex tetrachordis veterum"</note>, who had the **conjunct tetrachord** <note>original: "tetrachordum Synnemmenon"; in Greek music theory, this was a specific four-note grouping—E, F, G, A-flat—that allowed for melodic flexibility.</note> (that is, of conjunct keys, as E, F, G, A, B-flat, C, D) in which the **B-flat** <note>original: "♭"</note> is inserted between A and **B-natural** <note>original: "♮"</note>. Since they now possessed this flat key and introduced it, the system was easily extended further to the others, if one wished to proceed further with the six musical syllables <note>The "hexachord" system (Ut, Re, Mi, Fa, Sol, La).</note>; and thus the **sharp** <note>original: "♯"</note> was undoubtedly invented next, as in G, A, B, C, D-sharp, etc.

As to the time when they first appeared in **Germany** and **France**, and when artistic organs existed in **Italy** and elsewhere, one can partly see and calculate this from the accounts of trustworthy historians.

**Aventinus**, in the third book of his *Annals of the Bavarians* <note>original: "annalibus Bojorum lib. 3."</note>, has recorded that **Constantine VI Copronymus**, son of Leo—who held the Constantinople Empire around the year of Christ 742—sent to **Pepin**, King of the Franks and father of Emperor **Charlemagne**, through special legates (the most prominent head of whom was **Stephen**, a Bishop of Rome), an excellently large instrument. This was a work that was then still entirely unknown to the French and Germans. He says that it was constructed with pipes of lead, and was simultaneously blown with bellows, and struck with hands and feet, and was called an **organ**, and was seen for the first time in France. **Lambert of Aschaffenburg** and **Marianus Scotus** write in their third books that this happened in the year 758. Although others write that the **pedal** <note>Foot-operated keys.</note> in organs was first invented in **Venice**. From this it is then obvious that this kind of instrumental music, which we today call an organ, is not so very old in the French and German churches.

However, so that credit may be given to both **Aventinus** (who says that the organ was still unknown to the Germans and French in the time of Pepin) and also to **Platina** (who maintains that the organ was placed in the church by **Vitalian** 300 years before Pepin): it must be understood that Platina undoubtedly refers to that crude instrument which had 15 pipes, into which the wind was let in by 12 bellows—the likes of one which stood in **Jerusalem** on the **Mount of Olives** and gave forth a sound as if it were thundering—or that he is looking to the very ancient **hydraulic instrument** <note>original: "Instrumentum Hydraulicum"; an organ that uses water to regulate wind pressure.</note>, which was commonly called an organ, as **Vitruvius** indicates in his tenth book on architecture, chapter 13.

# ON THE DESCRIPTION OF INSTRUMENTS.

The **body of the hydraulic organ** <note>original: "Hydravlici Corpus"; referring to the ancient water-powered organ</note>, along with its pipes, was cast and soldered together from bronze; it possessed only a single row or rank of pipes and produced various sounds through the pressure of poured-in water. However, the **body or case of our organ** <note>original: "Organi Corpus"</note>, which is skillfully joined together from wood, has many ranks full of pipes. It distributes and divides their clangor and tone through the pipes—at the front, at the back, in the "breast" <note>The "Brustwerk" or chest-level division of the organ.</note>, at the sides, and under the feet—by means of the air and wind supplied to it by the bellows.

*Leander* (as *Majolus* also relates) writes in his *23rd Colloquy* that he saw a very sweet-sounding organ in **Venice** made entirely of glass. Another organ has also been seen in which the windchests, pipes, keyboard, and bellows were made of **alabaster** <note>A soft, translucent, marble-like mineral.</note> (a stone that grows in the *Volaterran* fields in **Italy**). When the ingenious master from **Naples** had completed it and tuned it to sound exceedingly well, he brought it to the Duke of **Mantua**, *Federico*, and presented it to him. *Leander* testifies in his description of **Tuscany** that he himself saw this most wonderful work. Similar **positive organs** <note>Small, portable or semi-portable pipe organs.</note>, where not only the entire case and keyboard but also the pipes were made of nothing but glass and alabaster stone, were presented a few years ago to an **Electoral cabinet of curiosities** <note>original: "Churfürstliche Kunstkammer"; a collection of rare and marvelous objects kept by a Prince-Elector.</note> as "newly invented" works. However, that such **inventions** <note>original: "Invention"</note> were already old and existed before this time can be clearly seen from the aforementioned **historians**.

Among Christians, the most excellent and famous **musicians** and discoverers of new **inventions** in **music** were: **George the Priest** <note>original: "Georgius Sacerdos"</note>, a native of **Venice**. After he was **commended** to **Louis the Pious** <note>Son of Charlemagne and Emperor of the Romans (reigned 814–840).</note> by *Daldricus*, a Hungarian Count, he cast and completed this musical instrument, the **hydraulic organ** <note>original: "Hydravlicum"</note> (which they call an organ), at the **waters of Aachen** <note>original: "Graneischen Wasser"; referring to Aquisgranum, the imperial capital.</note>. (See *Aimonius, Book 4, Chapter 113, On the Franks*; and *Aventinus, Book 4 of the Annals*.)

*Gilbertus*, a prelate at **Reims**—who was later named Roman Pope **Sylvester II**—built an organ with the help of his **mathematics** which received its sound through the violent force of hot water in the **Year of our Lord 997**, as *Erfordiensis* and *Genebrandus* testify.

**Boëthius** <note>An influential 6th-century philosopher whose "De Institutione Musica" was the standard music theory textbook for a millennium.</note>, who was simultaneously a fine **mathematician, philosopher**, and an exceptional **poet**, is considered the inventor of the musical instrument called the **cittern** <note>original: "Chiterini"; a wire-strung fretted instrument.</note>. (*Bergomas* and *Genebrandus, Year of our Lord 515*.)

And so that we do not forget this, *Sabellicus* (Book 8, Ennead 10) reports that around the **Year of Christ 1470**, there was a man in **Venice** who was most excellent above all others in **music**.

<meta>This page continues the historical survey of the organ's development. # ON THE DESCRIPTION OF INSTRUMENTS.

Bernhard, surnamed "the German" <note>original: "Teutscher"; a nickname indicating his nationality</note> to identify the people from whom he descended, was the first to improve and enlarge the organ. He did this so that the feet, by pulling small cords—namely, in the **pedal** <note>The set of keys played with the feet.</note>—could assist in achieving greater harmony and a fuller sound. Otherwise, however, one cannot say for certain or truly know whether the very oldest organ was found in the Greek, Italian, Asian, or African churches.

It is indeed much to be lamented that we can have nothing definite or entirely certain regarding the beginning and first **invention** <note>original: "Invention"; referring here to the creative design</note> of the organ, nor how long ago the oldest organ works might have been built. It would be most desirable and necessary to know this, for through it we would not only see the gifts God has bestowed upon men to create musical instruments in such a way, but we would also see before our eyes the diligent and laborious reflection of our dear ancestors who died several hundred years ago. They have, as it were, set up the ladder for their descendants to climb higher in the future and shown the way to wander further and further. This might also drive us to similar diligence: to use this present magnificent time (in which one believes almost all things have climbed to the highest peak) in the **liberal arts** <note>The traditional academic subjects, including music.</note> so much more tirelessly and usefully for the honor of God.

However, this incomplete knowledge must rightly be blamed solely on the professional organists, organ builders, and masters. Even a hundred years ago, or more or less, they tore away such old works without any reflection or looking back. Despite how diligently one might search and study, they left behind nothing in writing concerning the types and inventions found at that time.

Nevertheless (so that we may report something in this work regarding those organs of which the **remains** <note>original: "rudera"; ruins or fragments</note> are still present now or were a few years ago), one can have certain experience and information that organ works were built six hundred years ago. Evidence and date inscriptions of this are still present and can be found here and there, among other places in **Halberstadt** and **Erfurt** in the **Pauline Churches** <note>Churches belonging to the Order of Saint Paul the First Hermit.</note>.
