In St. James’s Church, one such organ once stood; others were placed high up near the choir like swallows' nests <note>Small organs attached to the upper walls of a church, resembling the nests of swallows.</note> and were built within a narrow space and frame. Initially, such small instruments had no more than a single sound, without any variation or stops. To speak in our modern terms, this was nothing other than a <term>Mixture</term> <note>An organ stop where multiple pipes of different pitches—usually octaves and fifths—sound simultaneously for every single key played.</note>, which was composed of 10, 15, and even 20 pipes for every <term>key</term> <note>original: "Clave"</note>. Within this arranged mixture, the largest pipe of each key was placed at the front in order—much like we arrange our **Principal** <note>The main set of pipes that forms the visual front of the organ and provides its foundational sound.</note> today—though it was also for appearance. These instruments sounded sharp and strong, almost screaming. Their keyboards, however, lacked <term>semitones</term> <note>The "black keys" (sharps and flats) on a modern piano; early organs often only had the "white" natural keys.</note>, as follows:

->♮ c d e f g a ♮ c d e f<-
->But some were like this:<-
->c d e f g a b c d e f g a.<-

From this, it can be seen that for the earliest organs, they used no more than these eleven keys, in which the ancients included the three *tetrachords* <note>In ancient Greek music theory, a scale of four notes spanning a perfect fourth.</note>:

1. The *Tetrachord of the Low* <note>original: "ὑπάτων" (hypaton)</note>, from B-natural to E. (B-natural, however, was the largest and eleventh string, which Timotheus of Miletus devised in the time of Philip, the father of Alexander).

->2. The *Tetrachord of the Middle* <note>original: "μέσων" (meson)</note>, from E to a.<-
->3. The *Tetrachord of the Disjunct* <note>original: "διεζευγμένων" (diezeugmenon)</note>, from B-natural to e.<-

->♮ C D E F G A ♮ c d e<-
<image-desc>Three horizontal curly brackets are placed beneath a sequence of notes to group them into musical tetrachords. The first bracket groups ♮ C D E; the second groups E F G A; the third groups ♮ c d e.</image-desc>

But shortly after the time of Timotheus of Miletus, the 4th *Tetrachord of the Extreme* <note>original: "ὑπερβολαίων" (hyperbolaion)</note>, e f g a, was invented in the higher register. Thus there were 14 strings, and finally the lowest key, A, was added outside these tetrachords to serve as a foundation, so that nothing would be lacking from the music of the ancients in this regard. And so, in 15 keys, the "Hard Song" <note>original: "Cantus durus"; music based on the hexachord containing B-natural.</note> was played. However, when they wanted to bring it into "Soft Song" <note>original: "Cantum mollem"; music using B-flat.</note> or transpose it, they took and joined the *Tetrachord of the Conjunct* <note>original: "συνημμένων" (synemmenon)</note> to it. Regarding these, see Sethus Calvisius, *Exercises*, page 105.

All of this happened, as mentioned, in the time of Alexander the Great, before the birth of Christ. As for the organs—whose structures until a few years ago...

...to be found, they were first made long after the birth of Christ and indeed with no more than 11 or 12 **keys** <note>original: "Clavibus"</note>—similar to the time of the aforementioned Timotheus of Miletus <note>An ancient Greek musician known for adding strings to the lyre; Praetorius is drawing a parallel between ancient Greek string counts and early organ keys.</note>, following the first three **tetrachords** <note>In ancient music theory, a scale of four notes spanning a perfect fourth.</note>.

This is quite surprising, and perhaps happened because back then builders had no experience or practice with keyboards. They started with just a few keys, or as the saying goes, they had to "learn to walk by holding onto the benches" <note>An idiom suggesting they were like toddlers taking their first steps in a new craft.</note> until they progressed day by day and increased the number of keys. However, Lord Calvisius <note>Sethus Calvisius (1556–1615), a famous German music theorist and astronomer.</note> believes it was because the **mixture** <note>An organ stop where multiple pipes of different pitches sound for every single key.</note> already contained so many octaves above the base note that they felt it was unnecessary to add more octaves to the keyboard itself. Furthermore, the **natural range of the human voice** <note>original: "Natürliche Ambitus in humana voce"</note> does not require much more than eleven keys; if the music went higher, they simply played it an octave lower—at least until they invented more keys, as will be mentioned further in Chapter 7.

## Chapter IV.

### How the first type of small organs was enlarged by one octave and developed into the "Medium-sized Work."

<image-desc>Decorative initial B featuring leaf and vine motifs within a square border.</image-desc>

Without doubt, the organ remained in this form and state for many years—since it had only just emerged as a new **invention** <note>original: "Invention"</note> and the craft was passed from one person to another over a long period—before this wonder, new at that time, became known throughout the world and was built in various distant places.

But when, from that time onward for a hundred years or more, the art of organ building came into common use and flourished into a point of pride (of which many were no doubt quite envious), builders began to think more deeply on the matter. They started making larger "works" [instruments], twice as large as the first ones. Evidence of this is found not only in various reliable historical reports but can still be seen today with one's own eyes in prominent cities, foundations, and monasteries.

Thus, one innovation grew out of another, and among the masters, one **talent** <note>original: "Ingenium"</note> sought to outshine the others.

It also appears logical from the two types of keyboards mentioned (one being "soft B" or **B-flat** <note>original: "b mol"</note> and the other "hard B" or **B-natural** <note>original: "♮ dur"</note>) that people back then—perhaps about a hundred years after the first invention—were already puzzling over the introduction of **semitones** <note>The "black keys" on a modern keyboard, providing sharps and flats.</note>. Indeed, 400 years ago, several semitones were already found in keyboards: specifically the B-flat in the B-natural keyboard, and the E-flat in the B-flat keyboard.

## Chapter V.

### How the Pedal was invented / and why the first and Upper Keyboard, which previously had no Name / was called the Manual.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'O' with floral and scrollwork patterns.</image-desc>
Even though organ works increased in size and the number of pipes / and the keyboards multiplied / it still remained / according to the first **invention**, that there was nothing more than the **Principal** <note>The main, foundational set of pipes in an organ that gives it its characteristic sound.</note> and **Mixture** (which at that time was not yet divided / but was a single **arranged** <term>disposition: the specific selection and arrangement of stops in an organ</term> voice sounding together); except that more **keys** <note>original: "Claves"</note> were made higher up / and the pedals were also already invented about 400 years ago. This is shown by the appearance of very old **structures**, even if no other records could be found: Because the two outermost **side-towers** <note>The large, protruding vertical sections of an organ case that hold the longest pipes.</note> were **arranged** for the pedal, and the middle section was for the manual.

And here the diligent **speculation** <note>In this context, 'speculation' refers to deep theoretical study and creative engineering.</note> and deep reflection of our dear old ancestors is rightly mentioned with all praise / that they invented a way to assist the musical sound with foot-treads.

And as **Sabellicus** <note>Marcantonio Sabellico (c. 1436–1506), a Venetian historian who recorded the history of the city and its innovations.</note> writes / and as is also mentioned in **Part 1, Volume 1, Chapter 10, Section 4** / a German by the name of **Bernhardus** brought the pedal from Germany to **Venice** in **Italy** around the year of our Lord 1470.

Although the pedal is used very little and quite rarely in **Italy, England**, and other places / where organ art currently **flourishes** and **excels**. Indeed, some **writers** <note>original: "Scribenten"</note> claim that **music** in **Italy** had formerly completely perished / and had to be brought back to them by the Germans.

From this first **invention** of the pedal / (which initially had only 8 **keys**, namely ♮ C D E F G A B <note>Praetorius uses the old German notation where 'h' represents B-natural; the range described is a single octave from B-natural up to the next B-natural.</note>) / after a long time another **manual keyboard** was invented; which was used for the bass in place of the pedal / though it was operated with the left hand / just as it is entirely equal in form and size to the **manual keyboards**. Just as another followed from the first established **manual keyboard** / which will be discussed later / and its **arrangement** described.

After this invention of the pedal / the very first keyboard / which we now call the **Manual** <note>From the Latin 'manus', meaning hand.</note> / was not called **Manual**, but **Discant** <note>The 'Discant' usually referred to the highest part or voice in a composition.</note>; and the pedal by its name

<term>Mixture Pipes: sets of multiple pipes that sound simultaneously for a single key, often at high pitches</term> must have produced an exceptionally strong sound and volume, and a powerful "shouting" (to which the heavy wind pressure of the time surely contributed).

And this was all the more the case because, in such low registers, nothing more could be played between an Octave than just a Fifth and a Major Third—especially since every <term>Manual Key: a key on the hand-operated keyboard</term> required a whole hand or a full fist to be pressed down. Therefore, to speak for our modern ears, listening to such a thing must not have been particularly pleasant (unless the <term>Mixture</term> pipes or the back-position pipes broke through with their high-pitched "shouting" and made a recognizable melody of the <term>Plainchant: the traditional unison singing of the church</term> audible to the listener).

However, the twelve large bass pipes or <term>Pedals</term> were arranged in the two side towers, and the <term>Treble</term> was placed between these high towers according to its scale.

The opinion of **Mr. Sethus Calvisius** <note>Sethus Calvisius (1556–1615) was a famous composer and music theorist of the late Renaissance.</note> regarding the sound and nature of ancient organs and ancient harmony is as follows, as he wrote to me in a certain letter <note>original: "in quadam Epistola"</note>:

> "Now the question is: Can one still find traces <note>original: "vestigia"</note> of the ancient harmony? It has undoubtedly been preserved in the churches. We still have two instruments from ancient music in constant use: the Bagpipe and the Hurdy-gurdy <note>original: "Leyre"</note>. In these, a particular harmony <note>original: "Consonantia"</note> sounds continuously; on the bagpipe, it is only a Fifth; on the hurdy-gurdy, however, three or four strings sound, namely a Fifth and an Octave simultaneously through three strings. Afterward, other keys are struck that touch the fourth string to modulate a fitting plainchant melody."

> "This has without a doubt always remained in the church, and on the organs, they must have had another special rank of pipes for the harmonies, in which they always pulled the harmonies that fit and matched the plainchant key—just as happens on the hurdy-gurdy—such as <term>c g c</term> or <term>d a d</term> or <term>e b e</term> etc. <note>These are "drone" notes that provide a constant harmonic background.</note> They kept these keys sounding continuously and then played a plainchant melody based on C, D, or E over them, much like one plays a shepherd's dance on an instrument. And this has been the nature of music on all instruments from the beginning of the world, as the ancient writers indicate. From this, it is easily understood that at that time, such music did not require nearly as many keys as were indicated at the end of the second chapter."

Afterward, however, when some ingenious musicians <note>original: "Ingeniosi Musici"</note> arrived, they experimented further in private and at their own discretion <note>original: "sine arbitrio"</note>, and to the plainchant, which they played in the higher <note>original: "acutiori-"</note>...

...carried by these sounds, they tested consonances below, striking two keys together in the right manual. They finally discovered how the <term>Plainchant: the traditional melodic singing of the church</term> could be properly ended and brought together to rest in a <term>Cadence: a melodic or harmonic configuration that creates a sense of resolution</term> <note>original: "Clausula"</note>, for this was the most important objective. But as soon as they learned to make these cadences (which no doubt cost much effort, as they are of many kinds), they were also able to find the other consonances and set two voices in simple counterpoint <note>original: "Contrapuncto simplici"</note>, thus first inventing a <term>Bicinium: a musical composition for two voices</term>. Afterward, they gradually progressed further and achieved a <term>Tricinium: a musical composition for three voices</term>, until they also discovered <term>florid counterpoint: a complex style of polyphony where voices move in varied rhythms</term>.

However, this proceeded slowly, for in the beginning, the consonances required much effort because the tones and semitones could not be tuned purely. Therefore, the instruments or organs were not tuned as purely as they are now. Nor did they dare to trust that Thirds and Sixths were consonances, since the ancient musicians all agreed that they should not be consonances. Therefore, no one wanted to be so presumptuous or think himself so clever as to claim he knew better than **Ptolemy**, **Boethius**, **Euclid**, and other excellent musicians.

I am of the opinion that if one wished to hear that ancient harmony today and how ancient music sounded, one would need only to take the entire full chorus <note>original: "volle Werck"</note>—namely the Principals, Octaves, Super-octaves, Fifths, Cymbals, Mixtures, and Sub-basses, and whatever else is available that is customarily drawn for the full chorus and is a true example <note>original: "specimen"</note> of the ancient mixture. And then, in the **Pedal**, hold a Fifth with both feet, such as C-G, D-A, F-c, etc., and lead the melody of a Plainchant (like a Responsory, Introit, or German hymn) in the **Manual**, using only the lowercase letter-keys:

c d e f g a b<gloss>natural</gloss> c<gloss>—</gloss> <note>German "h" is English "B-natural."</note>

(For in the ancient organs, smaller pipes were not available.) In this way, one would come quite close to the ancient style and harmony, although in the beginning, they would not have had it quite so good.

### Chapter IX.

## Concerning the Nature of Bellows of that Time.

One must, however, realize that at the aforementioned time, two hundred and fifty or three hundred years ago (when such great instruments as the one at **Halberstadt**, of which we are now treating, were built), there was still little invention and reflection regarding **bellows** <note>original: "Blaßbälgen"</note>. For at this Cathedral organ in Halberstadt, 20 bellows—and at the one in **Magdeburg**, 24 very small bellows (according to the order and shape found in the *Sciographia* <note>The *Sciographia* was the volume of woodcut illustrations published by Praetorius to accompany this text.</note>, Plate XXVI)—were provided. These were not very different in size and proportion from our current blacksmith's bellows. They were not regulated by lead or stone weights, but were operated by such a means that one person was always needed for every two bellows; when one bellows was trodden down by the weight of the bellows-treader <term>Calcant: from the Latin "calcare" (to tread); the laborer who pumped the bellows by stepping on them.</term> with one foot, the other was pulled back up with the other foot. Thus, for 20 bellows, ten people—and for 24, twelve of them—must necessarily have been present.

And one must rightly wonder why our dear ancestors, who reached such heights of invention in other matters concerning the organ, did not also reflect and speculate better upon another and more convenient manner regarding the wind (by forming bellows that could give better and more steady wind, and also regarding the treading, since people of equal strength and weight are not always available to tread and regulate such bellows, nor can they be weighed out like physical weights).

->ON ORGANOGRAPHY.<-

In such a way, one might not without reason fall into strange reflections on how the tuning and according must have behaved with such uneven, forced wind; since nothing else is to be found in its arrangement <note>original: "disposition." In this context, it refers to the list of pipes and stops available in the organ.</note> than a **Mixture** <note>original: "Mixturwerck." In these early medieval organs, this was often a "Blockwerk," meaning all the pipes for a single key sounded at once, as the ability to select individual stops had not yet been invented.</note> consisting of octaves, fifths, fourths, and many unisons <note>original: "æqualen"</note>, arranged from the largest to the smallest.

Since this is difficult for modern organ builders—as I myself have heard and seen—to tune cleanly and accord even with good, steady, and correct wind, how laborious and difficult must it have been for our dear ancestors? Not to mention the hardship the **bellows treaders** <note>original: "Calcanten." These were the laborers who operated the bellows by stepping on them to provide air to the instrument.</note> had to endure in such constant treading and movement. In my opinion, however, their greatest advantage was that they did not need to tune such instruments for testing against specific chords <note>original: "Concordanten"</note>; for no polyphonic compositions <note>original: "Composition mit vielen Stimmen"</note> were played on them, but only the simple, plain **chorale** <note>original: "Choral." Here referring to the liturgical plainchant or simple unison hymn melodies.</note> was performed upon them.

Therefore, they primarily had to tune each **key** <note>original: "Clavem"</note> purely in itself according to the nature of a Mixture—doing so, however, according to their previously tuned **Principal pipes** <note>original: "Præstanten." These were the primary pipes, often located in the front of the organ case, which served as the reference for the rest of the instrument.</note>, which were the only ones they could draw individually at that time. It would be desirable for such an instrument to be made playable and sounding again today, so that one might hear and observe the difference between that style and our current one.

one must out of necessity consider them a **Whole Work**; the medium type, however, a **Half**; and thus the small ones, which were the very first and oldest, one must consider and call a **Quarter Work**. And so, one name arose from the other, just as they followed one another in unequal sizes.

And indeed, in those times, the Large Works were rightly called "Whole" according to their nature; because they were arranged as a completely perfect **mixture arrangement** <note>original: "Mixtur disposition." In medieval organs, this refers to a "Blockwerk" where many pipes of different pitches sounded together for every single key played, as individual stops had not yet been developed.</note> from such large pipes down to the smallest. From this, such a number of pipes stood one after another upon a single **key** <note>original: "Clave."</note>; and from such a great mass of pipes, a powerful sound inevitably had to follow, which could not happen in the medium-sized works. Likewise, the first Small Works could not match the medium ones in their nature. Therefore, as just mentioned, at that time such questions and answers were quite necessary to distinguish between the works. Even in our own time, such questions still arise from common honest folk and old organists.

And some were of the opinion that such names as **Whole**, **Half**, etc., had their origin in the number of **bellows** <note>original: "Bälge."</note>. This, however, cannot be the case. For if one looks only at the two mentioned cathedral organs (to say nothing of others of their kind) at **Magdeburg** and **Halberstadt**; the Magdeburg organ had 24, while the Halberstadt organ had only 20 bellows, though they were of the same size in both. Since they were otherwise entirely equal in size and arrangement, they cannot be distinguished by name because of the bellows. Therefore, in those times, they were simply called **Whole**, **Half**, and **Quarter** according to the size of the structures and the **facade pipes** <note>original: "förder Pfeiffen." These are the pipes displayed in the front of the organ case, which determine the instrument's visual and acoustic scale.</note>.

Just as now, in the same manner, the works are named after their **Principals** <note>The main, most characteristic set of pipes in an organ that provides its foundational sound.</note> and also have only three types of names. For example, if an organ has a **Principal** of 16-foot tone and an **Octave** of 8-foot tone in the **manual** <note>The keyboard played with the hands.</note>, it is called a **Large Principal Work**. Among the ancients, however, it was called a **Whole Work**, in which the F in the **pedal** <note>The keyboard played with the feet.</note> was usually calculated at 24 feet according to **choir pitch** <note>original: "Chormaß." A historical pitch standard used to align instruments with church choirs, which often differed from modern concert pitch.</note>, and a mixture was included—even if no other voices were present.

Referring to the 8-foot pitch which sounds at the same octave as the human voice.</note> **Principal Work**, but was called a **Half Work** by the ancients.

### Chapter XI.
### On the Difference Between the Old and Our Present Organs.

If we pause here a little and wish to compare <note>original: "Conferiren."</note> and behold the beginnings and inventions <note>original: "invention."</note> of the dear ancients with our own present time, one will find that, regarding the main invention of the organ along with everything belonging to it, the difference is not so exceedingly great. And it is truly a cause for wonder how it reached such a stage so quickly in the beginning, so that up until now no one has been able to theorize <note>original: "speculiret."</note> much higher or further, nor devise anything more through other means: except that we are now able, through long practice and observation, to bring to light all those same things the ancients discovered in a somewhat more natural, convenient, more elegant, and lovelier manner.

And in the oldest works, it is likewise to be found that they were governed and brought to sound by wind and bellows <note>original: "Blaßbälge."</note>, just like our own. Likewise <note>original: "Item."</note>, that the bellows had those same means—namely, the wind-valves or vents <note>original: "Ventiel."</note> through which the wind is led out from the bellows—and were covered and fitted with leather.

Furthermore, that they used channels or wind-pipes <note>original: "Windtröhren."</note> so that the wind was guided from the bellows to the work; likewise, that structures of various forms were arranged, in which the windchests <note>original: "Windtladen." These were constructed with rollerboards <note>original: "Wellbretern." A mechanism used to transmit the movement of a key to a pipe that is not directly above it.</note>, linkages <note>original: "Angehengen."</note>, and **Pedal** and **Manual** keyboards <note>original: "Claviren."</note>. ("Mounted on the base" means that these pipes are set directly upon the bare foundation—namely, onto the windchests—because at that time neither stops <note>original: "Register."</note> nor sliders were present.) Therefore, this type or invention of **spring chests** <note>original: *Springladen*. A complex wind chest where each pipe has its own secondary valve held by a spring, allowing for very stable wind pressure.</note> is not a new thing, as some might think, but flowed from the oldest invention and has already been in use for nearly two hundred years.

As it happened in the Diocese of Würzburg in a monastery just a few years ago: such a spring chest—made by an organ builder named Timotheus—was taken out of a very old organ built by a monk, and in its place, a new chest with **sliders** <note>original: *Schleiffen*. The "slider chest" uses a sliding strip of wood with holes to turn stops on and off; it was simpler but more prone to jamming than the spring chest.</note> was installed.

In these spring chests, every **voice** <note>original: *Stimme* (rank of pipes or stop).</note> has its own individual valve and requires much labor to build; however, they are very good because the air cannot "run together" <note>This refers to "bleeding" or "ciphering," where air leaks from one pipe channel to another.</note> or leak through. These valves are pulled up all at once by a single **stop** <note>original: *Register*.</note>, and yet alongside them in the chest, there are separate valves for each **key** <note>original: *Clave*.</note> which are pulled down by the keyboard.

The Low Germans and the Dutch held these spring chests in higher regard than slider chests, because the wind could be kept purer beneath the pipes without *vices* <note>original: *vitia* (Latin: faults or defects).</note> or particular flaws. Also, during changes in the **weather** <note>original: *Gewitters*. Changes in humidity cause wood to swell or shrink; slider chests often jammed or leaked as a result, while spring chests were more mechanically resilient.</note>, they remained stable, whereas slider-work often suffers from significant defects.

However, when people in these lands applied themselves with great effort to making slider chests accurately and perfectly, and the Low Germans and Dutch came to Saxony and saw that by the same advantage it was also possible to produce perfect slider chests, they followed suit and began to adopt them. Thus, Master Fabian Peters of Sneek (in Rostock, Stralsund, and other places) is said to have made such things.

It is certainly no small task to make spring chests accurately (as I have heard from knowledgeable organ builders and can judge myself by reason), although more wondrous variations in the pipework—such as separated **Basses**, wooden conduits <note>original: *holz verleitungen*. Tubing used to "convey" wind to pipes that are not positioned directly over their assigned wind-hole.</note>, and other features—can be achieved and managed on slider chests, which cannot be done in the same way on spring chests.

Nevertheless, both inventions—just like both types of **bellows** <note>original: *Blaßbälgen*.</note> covered with wood-chips and leather—are good and durable, if only every master would rightly observe the clear gifts brought to light with the greatest diligence. Unfortunately, in current times, there is a lack [of such skill], to the great detriment of the poor people who, in cities and villages, [wish to build] a small organ to the honor of the Lord of Hosts, according to their...

### Chapter XIII.

### The Modification and Multiplication of Keyboards.

Just as people were diligent about changing and dividing the stops two hundred and fifty years ago—achieving this through divine inspiration—and just as the invention of **semitones** <note>original: *Semitonien*. These are the "half-steps" or the black keys on a modern keyboard that allow for more complex harmonies.</note> (the nature of which was indicated above in Chapter 6) emerged from the first invented keyboards and pedals—which remained in use in nearly the same form for three hundred and fifty years—so too have keyboard designs been constantly improved from that time to the present. They have been variously altered, reduced in size, and increased in number, until finally the old style of <term>keys</term> <note>Latin: *Claves*. The physical levers pressed by the organist.</note> fell out of use and our current style began to emerge. However, this happened in such a way that a single key was once 3 1/2 inches wide (that is, three good fingers wide), making it twice as large as one of our current keys. I myself have measured and sketched such keys on an old, small organ still located in the Cathedral of Minden. It is only a pity that no date was found on it.

Shortly thereafter, the keys were reduced even further, so that a **fifth** <note>A musical interval covering five scale degrees.</note> was as wide to reach as an **octave** <note>A musical interval covering eight scale degrees; today, this is the standard reach for an average hand.</note> is today. This can still be seen in the old organ at St. Giles in Braunschweig; the drawing and dimensions of which can be found in the *Sciographia* <note>A volume of technical illustrations accompanying this work.</note>, Columns XXVII and XXVIII.

I have also included here the **verses** <note>original: *Carmina*.</note> which are still found written beneath that same organ:

And in these aforementioned organs, the **manual keyboards** <term>ManualClavir: The keyboards played with the hands, as opposed to the pedals</term> were almost identical to our current ones in every respect; for the **semitones** <note>The "black keys" or sharps and flats</note> were also situated between the keys just as they are now, and were black or otherwise distinct in color. The only difference was that they were slightly larger—nearly the width of one key wider in the **octave**—than our current ones. Consequently, they were difficult to reach, had a deep "drop" <note>The distance the key travels when pressed</note>, and were heavy to strike.

The reason I have set down here several **keyboard arrangements** <term>Clavierdispositiones: The specific layout and range of keys on an instrument</term> along with their superscript markings and double letters, as well as the names of several masters, is so that the style and custom of our ancestors—and how inventions have increased and advanced from year to year over time—might be better known and more interesting to many.

Regarding the distinction of the letters from octave to octave: the first octave remained on its own <note>i.e., written as simple capital letters</note>; the second was marked with a small tilde (~) above it; and the third octave was indicated with double letters. This was done so that, as the number of keys <note>original: *Clavium*</note> continued to increase, a clear distinction could be observed. However, they always began these octave divisions from **B-natural** <note>represented by the natural sign ♮</note> to **B-natural**. Why they did this, or what their thoughts and intentions were in the matter, cannot be known for certain.

->Chapter XIV.<-

# On the Variation and Multiplication of Pipes and Stops.

CONCERNING the variation in pitch (specifically the various depths and heights) of the very first kind of stops and pipes—namely, the open Principals <note>The "Principal" is the core, foundational sound of the organ</note>—our ancestors arranged them all together. Since even 150 years ago they knew of nothing else but this one kind, they placed them in their single great **Hindersatz** <term>Hindersatz: A "back-set" or large mixture of pipes located behind the facade, which all sounded at once</term> or **Mixture** <term>Mixtur: A stop composed of multiple pipes of different pitches that sound together for a brilliant effect</term> arrangement. These were often as many as 56 pipes strong for a single key, grouped together with the **Præstanten** <term>Præstanten: From the Latin "praestare" (to stand before), these are the pipes visible in the front of the organ case</term>, as was somewhat reported above in Chapter 7.

For our great 32-foot **Subprincipal** (calculated according to our current pitch) and the great 16-foot **Principal**; likewise our **AEqual-Principal** <note>8-foot pitch, which matches the human voice</note>, or the great **Octave** 8-foot; the 4-foot **Octave**; the 3-foot **Fifth**; the 2-foot **Superoctave**, etc., as well as our **Mixtures**—all of these stood together in their *Hindersatz* and were arranged as one (though the *Præstanten* or Principals could sometimes be separated). Today, we can pull out each of these as individual stops using the invented means of **Spring-chests** <term>Springladen: A type of windchest where each pipe is controlled by a secondary valve or "spring"</term> and **Slider-chests** <term>Schleiffladen: A mechanism using a sliding piece of wood to open or close the wind supply to a specific rank of pipes</term> to create a "Full Work." But in those days, they had to make them all sound at once through a general **Channel** <term>Canel: A wind groove or duct</term> or wind-lead, which every key possessed for its assigned pipes, and they had to be taken together as a single voice.

It certainly sounds impressive when one says there were 56 pipes on a single key. However, when one looks at it correctly—and considering that in our current time we might use only 5 keys (or 5 composed voices), such as roughly c, g, c', e', g' on the **manual keyboard** <term>ManualClavir: The keyboard played with the hands</term>, and in the...

### ON ORGANOGRAPHY.

A single pedal key C, which always presses down its own specific bass voices and others at the same time when the "full organ" is drawn, can be calculated—to speak in the common way—as having 4 pipes for each key: namely, the **Principal**, **Octave**, **Quint**, and **Superoctave** (which are commonly drawn for the full organ in both large and small instruments). Additionally, there is the **Mixture** <term>Mixtur: A stop where multiple high-pitched pipes sound for every single key to add brilliance</term>, consisting perhaps of 6 pipes. (For our mixtures are merely a supplement to the whole work or to other voices. Therefore, they are often designed to "repeat" like the **Zimbel** <term>Zimbel: A high-pitched, piercing stop that "repeats," meaning the pitch jumps back down an octave as the player goes up the keyboard to keep the sound from becoming too shrill</term>, because even in the very lowest large keys, the pipes are not very large but small; indeed, larger pipes are unnecessary there because they are already present in the **Octaves**, **Principals**, **Gedackts** <term>Gedackt: From the German "gedeckt," meaning "covered" or "stopped" pipes, which sound an octave lower than open pipes of the same length</term>, and **Quintadenas**, etc.). This results in 10 pipes for every key. Thus, those six keys mentioned previously would account for 60 or even 62 pipes in number, which all respond at once, just as if everything stood on a single key without the use of sliders or registers.

However, if I use both feet on the pedal to play C and c; and in the manual use the left hand for e, g, c̄, ē; and the right hand for ḡ, c̿, e̿, g̿—that makes 10 keys—and I calculate four pipes for each key in the four aforementioned stops, plus at least 6 pipes in the Mixture (although frequently there are 10, 12, or 14 pipes present in a Mixture), then there are 100 pipes sounding all at once.

It was roughly a hundred years ago—at almost the same time that the Lord **Luther**, through God's providence, brought the Christian Evangelical teaching and the pure Word of God to light—that through the special inspiration of GOD, this musical invention also truly distinguished itself. It began to come to light so perfectly for the praise and glory of GOD that men learned to recognize the different types of sound, how to derive one from another, and how they might be varied through a certain means invented for that purpose: the **spring chests** and **slider chests** <term>Spring- und Schleiffladen: Mechanical systems in the windchest that allow the organist to "turn on" or "turn off" specific sets of pipes (stops)</term>. And just as the Holy Scripture remained hidden for so long under the Papacy and resembled a mere common mask, so too did Music and its instruments and works remain in a poor and almost negligible state; until, as just mentioned, they were raised up by God's gracious, fatherly will and emerged again, illuminated, from a black, darkened cloud. In our time, Music has risen and improved from day to day to such an extent that it can now hardly go any higher.

And the first modification of the pipes was that one [covered] the open pipes at the top...

...covered and tested what kind of tone and sound they might give off; from this, the style of **Stopped Pipes** <term>Gedackten Pfeiffen: From the German *gedeckt*, these are pipes capped at the top. This causes them to sound an octave lower and have a softer, hum-like quality compared to open pipes.</term> originated.

From this, they proceeded immediately to divide the great multitude of pipes in the previously mentioned **Hindersatz** <term>Hindersatz: The "rear-set," referring to the large block of pipes in early organs that all sounded at once before the invention of sliders allowed for separate stops.</term>. For instance, the pipes that were an octave higher than the **Prestant** <term>Prestant: From the Latin *praestare* (to stand before), these are the large, decorative pipes that stand in the front of the organ case.</term> or front pipes were taken out of the **Mixture** and placed on a separate register and slider, and named the **Octave**. Likewise, the pipes that stood at a pitch a fifth higher than this **Octave** were also separated and called the **Fifth** <note>original: "Quinta"</note>.

In the same way, they created the **Rauschpfeife** <term>Rauschpfeife: A "rustling pipe" stop. In this context, it is a compound stop where two pipes sound for every key.</term>, which at the beginning of this new invention was considered very good. It was composed of two pipes: namely, the **Fifth** just mentioned and a small **Octave** of 4-foot pitch. Thus, these two pipes—which always sound a fourth apart, such as C to F, D to G, or E to A <note>original: "ut-fa, re sol, mi la"</note>—stood on a single key. When a coarse variety of open and stopped voices is drawn with it, it truly "rustles" <note>Praetorius is using a play on words: the name "Rauschpfeife" suggests the German "rauschen," meaning to rustle, whistle, or murmur.</note> accordingly.

Nevertheless, their **Mixture** remained strong enough because of the large number of pipes mentioned before. At that time, they placed the Mixture all by itself on a separate windchest and let the wind in and out through a **ventil** <term>Ventil: A valve used to control the flow of air to specific parts of the organ.</term>. To this Mixture, they only drew the **Principal** <term>Principal: The core, foundational sound of the organ, providing the basic pitch.</term> alone, which was then called the **Full Work** <note>original: "volle Werck"</note>, and indeed it was. The reason was that since the Mixture already contained an Octave, Fifth, Superoctave, and other even smaller voices, one needed nothing more than the Principal as the foundation. However, when the Mixture was separated again by its corresponding valve or wind-gate, one then had the various changes of sound on the front slider-chests, such as the **Octaves**, **Fifths**, **Small Octaves**, **Stopped pipes**, **Zimbels**, and **Rauschpfeifes**.

In the same way, proper **bellows** with correct wind pressure and weight were also invented for use approximately one hundred and nineteen years ago <note>Praetorius was writing around 1619, so he dates this improvement to around 1500.</note>. These, however, were still covered with tanned horse and ox hides, just as they had been for several hundred years before, and had to be greased every five years.

Ninety years ago <note>Approximately 1530.</note>, they came even closer to the current state of things. The Mixtures remained on their separate chests and valves, but more voices were added, namely the pointed pipes, which they called **Spitzflutes**...

...called flutes, and something of **reed-works** <term>Schnarrwerck: "Snarling" or "rattling" works; these are reed stops, where the sound is produced by a vibrating metal tongue rather than a column of air.</term> was invented: and **span-bellows** <term>Spänbälge: A type of wedge bellows constructed with multiple folds or "spans" of wood and leather to provide a more steady wind supply.</term> were also manufactured.

At that time, many **works** of this kind, both small and large, were built; just as in **St. John’s** in **Göttingen**, a small **work** is found suspended on high, and is still used today, which has its lovely **voiced stops** and also good **Trumpets**.

Likewise in **Nordhausen** in **Saint Blaise’s Church**, one stood with three **manual keyboards** and was recently dismantled. One **keyboard** had the large **Principal** and **Mixture** alone: the **Mixture** could be drawn off, but the **Principal** (although it could be used by itself when the Mixture was drawn off) could not be drawn off at all, and thus always remained in the sound <note>In early organ building, the main stop was often "permanently on," as the slider technology for silencing it had not yet been fully implemented for the largest pipes.</note>. The other **keyboard** also had its own **chest**, upon which the other **voices**, such as the **Stopped Flutes, Octave, Fifth, Superoctave, Cymbals**, etc., were placed. The third **keyboard** was used for the **Rückpositive**.

And so they immediately attempted **strange ideas** at first with the **invention** of the **stops** and the changing of the **voices**; however, this **idea** was found to be very good for maintaining a long, pure, and enduring sound. This **work**, however, had a **Principal** of 16-foot, and its **keyboards** started at **F**, and—like almost most organs of that time—it stood about a tone higher than our current **Chamber Pitch** <term>Cammerthon: "Chamber pitch," the standard pitch used for instrumental music in the 17th century, which was often lower than the "Choir pitch" (Chorton) used for organs.</term>; for indeed, regarding the pitch, nothing certain was ever observed by them.

Just as the *Tremulant* <note>A mechanical device that causes the air supply to fluctuate, creating a vibrato effect.</note> also emerged along with these aforementioned new voices.

## The 1st Chapter.
# Concerning the proper names of Organ Works according to their size.

Since foot-pitch <note>The "foot" (f.) is a measurement of the length of the pipe. An 8-foot pipe is the standard length required to produce a pitch that matches a human voice.</note> will be mentioned frequently in what follows: singers <term>Cantoribus</term> especially should take note that 8-foot pitch is the proper choir-standard <term>Chormasse</term> <note>The reference pitch for vocal music, where the written note corresponds exactly to the sounding pitch.</note>, which has the natural height and depth of the human voice. And according to this standard, the others must be regarded either as doublings or halvings.

For as often as this number is doubled, the pipe sounds an octave lower; when it is halved, it sounds an octave higher.

For example, 16-foot pitch sounds one octave lower, and 32-foot pitch sounds two octaves lower than 8-foot pitch or the choir-standard.

Conversely, 4-foot pitch sounds one octave higher; 2-foot, two octaves higher; and 1-foot, three octaves higher than the choir-standard, as can be seen in the following illustrations.

<image-desc>Musical notation on multiple staves showing the pitch relationships between different pipe lengths. Labels below the staves indicate: 16-foot pitch, 8-foot pitch, 4-foot pitch, 2-foot pitch, and 1-foot pitch. The notes ascend by octaves from a very low C (CC) to a very high C as the pipe length decreases.</image-desc>

Furthermore, it is to be noted that organ works <term>Orgelwercke</term> <note>Refers to the different divisions or the overall size classification of an organ.</note> are named according to feet: Small, 4-foot pitch: its Principal's <note>The "Principal" is the foundational rank of pipes that gives the organ its characteristic sound.</note> lowest key <note>original: "Clavis"</note> in the manual and pedal [sounds as follows]:

Medium or choir-standard <term>Chormässig</term> of 8-foot pitch: its Principal’s lowest key in the manual and pedal.

The 32-foot pitch, however, is an octave lower than the 16-foot; yet it is of a quite unnatural and indiscernible tone and sound <note>original: "Soni vnd Klanges"</note>.

In what manner our ancestors titled and named their organs has been sufficiently reported in the preceding Part III concerning old organs.

At our present time, however, there are primarily three kinds of organ works <term>Orgelwercke</term> <note>Refers to the different divisions or size categories of the instrument.</note> whose names are to be properly called and remembered. And this is because one has three types of Principal styles and sizes, which are placed at the front of the work as an ornament, and the structures or cases are proportioned accordingly: For as the saying goes, *the naming is done according to the more prominent part* <note>original: "à potiori parte fit denominatio"</note>.

<margin>1.</margin>
The name of the first kind is the Great Principal <term>groß Principal</term>; which is called 16-foot pitch by organ builders because of the length of its body <term>Corporis</term> and its deep sound. In an organ where such a Principal stands at the front for use in the manual, its proper name is a "Great Principal Work." In such an instrument, the "Great Octave" is of 8-foot pitch, and the "Octave" is of 4-foot pitch. And sometimes in such works, Sub-principal or Sub-stopped <term>Subgedacte</term> <note>A "Gedackt" or "stopped" pipe is capped at the top, sounding an octave lower than an open pipe of the same length.</note> Basses of 32-foot pitch are found in the pedal.

<margin>2.</margin>
The name of the second kind, however, is "Equal" <note>original: "A Equal", from the Latin "aequalis"</note>, or as others call it, the Middle- or Choir-Principal <term>ChorPrincipal</term>. It is rightly so called because it corresponds in depth and height with the human voice; and these Principals...

is reckoned at 8-foot pitch because of its body length and sound. Now, where such a Principal is found standing in the <term>Manual</term> <note>The keyboard played with the hands.</note> and is used there—even though a Great Principal Bass of 16-foot pitch might occasionally be present in the <term>Pedal</term> <note>The keyboard played with the feet.</note> or in the side towers—it is called an **Equal-Principal-work** <note>original: "AequalPrincipalwerck"; referring to the standard unison pitch where the lowest C pipe is roughly 8 feet long.</note>; in such an instrument, the Octave is of 4-foot pitch and the Small Octave is of 2-foot pitch.

The third type is an **Octave- or Small Principal**, which has a body length and sound of 4-foot pitch. In works where a Principal of this size is found, they are rightly called, according to their measure and order, a **Small Principal Work**. In these, the Small Octave is of 2-foot pitch, and the Super-octave is of 1-foot pitch, which is otherwise called a <term>Sifflöte</term> <note>A high-pitched flute stop.</note>.

And although an organ builder must often adapt to the location and space available, and must either add to or reduce the size of his structures; and therefore the largest pipes of the Principal are often not placed in the front view because the size of the housing cannot accommodate the length of the pipe bodies; and sometimes it also happens that the Principals are replaced with even larger pipes merely for appearance's sake <note>original: "pro forma"</note> to fill out the size of the case; nevertheless, it must remain and rest upon the three described types: namely 16, 8, and 4-foot pitch Principals.

However, these described names, as just mentioned, are reckoned solely according to the manual keyboards. Otherwise, Great Principal Works are to be found where the **Pedal Principal Bass** is set at 32-foot pitch because the Principal in the Manual is of 16-foot pitch. This occurs when the arrangement <note>original: "disposition"</note> of the structures is such that the special Basses are ordered to be placed on the sides next to the manual work. And since these large **Sub-Principals** cannot naturally or possibly be used in the manual, but belong solely to the Pedal for the bass, and are crafted by few organ builders, an organ cannot take its proper name from such a Bass in the Pedal, but rather from the Manual.

Even if some very small little works are found whose Principal is only of 2-foot pitch, these do not belong among the number of names for organ works, but only under the arrangement of the <term>Positive</term> <note>A small, often movable organ without a pedalboard.</note>. This is because they commonly have other coarser stops as their foundations <note>original: "Fundamentis"</note>, such as a <term>Gedackt</term> <note>A "stopped" pipe which sounds an octave lower than its physical length.</note> or <term>Quintadena</term> <note>A stopped pipe that sounds the fifth (twelfth) prominently.</note> of 4-foot or even 8-foot pitch, and are therefore called Great- or Church Positives, or Small Octave Principal little works. Indeed, every organ builder should rightly see to it that his arrangements are orderly disposed <note>original: "ordine disponiret"</note> regarding size and tone, so that—just as with other instruments—one may judge them according to their names, sounds, and the arrangement of their stops.

### Chapter II.

# On all sorts and various names of the stops in organs, how they are correctly named according to their sound or tone and their particular properties: Also how such stops are calculated differently based on the length of their bodies, generally according to the feet or number of feet in their various lower and higher pitches. With a more detailed report on what is necessary to know about each stop in particular <note>original: "in specie"</note>.

Something should probably be said here regarding the <term>scaling</term> <note>original: "Mensur"; the ratio of an organ pipe's diameter to its length, which determines its tonal character.</note> of the pipes according to the length of their bodies: But because this concerns organ builders alone, it is unnecessary to mention it here.

Nevertheless, this can be indicated here <term>in passing</term> <note>original: "obiter"</note>: That a <term>Principal</term> <note>The standard open metal pipes that form the backbone of organ sound.</note> and all open pipework—reckoning from the body and the scaling length (which does not begin from the lower foot, which is only a conduit for the wind, but from the <term>labium</term> <note>original: "Labio"; the "lip" or mouth of the pipe where the air vibrates to create sound.</note> or mouth-hole, from which the upper body is made to sound)—almost always has as many feet in length as is said of its sound or pitch. Although their lengths are also unequal, and one must be shortened somewhat compared to another because of unequal widths (though only very slightly, so that it is hardly noticeable in the small pipes): Since reason dictates that when width is added to an object, something must conversely be taken away from its length; likewise, if width is reduced, length must be added.

With the <term>Stopped</term> <note>original: "Gedact"; pipes that are capped or plugged at the top, producing a sound an octave lower than an open pipe of the same length.</note> stops, however, there is a different meaning and understanding regarding the name or number of feet. For although such a Stopped pipe is equal to the width or thickness in circumference of every Principal, and is sometimes even slightly wider; it is still not even half as long. As an example: The Principal pipe is of 8-foot pitch and also has 8 feet in body length: The Stopped pipe is indeed also of 8-foot pitch and in body width—<term>if I may speak with the craftsman here</term> <note>original: "liceat hic loqui cum artifice"</note>—is almost uniform with the Principal: But it is and has only 4 feet in length, and almost a bit less; the reason being because it is stopped: For every open pipe, as soon as it is covered, becomes deeper by an octave, or a fifth, or a sixth. It is also the same with the <term>Quintadehn</term> <note>A stopped stop that sounds both the fundamental tone and the fifth above the octave (the twelfth).</note> type, only that it is much longer than a Stopp-

...stopped; <note>The text continues from the previous page, completing the word "Gedackt."</note> because they are slightly wider than a 4-foot Principal, whereas the <term>Gedact</term> <note>From the German "Gedeckt," meaning "covered" or "stopped." These pipes are capped at the top, which makes them sound an octave lower than an open pipe of the same length.</note> is as wide as a medium-sized 8-foot Principal.

The reason these two types of stopped pipework have such unequal widths and yet both produce an 8-foot tone is this: because of the narrowness of the <term>Quintadehn</term> <note>A stopped pipe voiced to emphasize its first overtone, the fifth (quint), hence the name.</note>, the "Quint" or fifth sounding within it can be brought out. This is further assisted and promoted by the <term>beard</term> <note>original: "Bart"; small metal plates or rods soldered near the mouth of the pipe to stabilize the airflow.</note> that goes around the <term>labium</term> <note>The "lip" or mouth-hole of the pipe.</note> or mouth-hole, and especially the very narrow "cut-up" (the height of the mouth opening). Without these two aids—namely, that the Quintadehn is narrower than the Gedact and that it has the "beard" to steady the wind—no fifth would be heard in its sound, but only a plain stopped character.

However, so that the distinction may also be understood in how we speak: for those stops where the pitch matches the physical <term>scaling</term> <note>original: "Mensur"; the ratio of a pipe's diameter to its length.</note>, as in open pipework, we say "it is an 8-foot Principal" or a "4-foot Octave." But for the others, such as the various stopped types where the scaling does not <term>correspond</term> <note>original: "respondirer"</note> to the pitch, we say it is a Gedact or Quintadehn "at 8-foot tone," a Nachthorn "at 4-foot tone," a Block-flute "at 2-foot tone," and so on.

->But enough of this for now.<-

In the beginning, it is important to observe well and with diligence that there are only two types—namely, open and stopped pipes—from which all other types and variations of sound follow. And although some might not wish to include the <term>reed stops</term> <note>original: "SchnarrWercke"; literally "growling-work," these pipes use a vibrating metal tongue to produce sound.</note> here as a third type, it is nonetheless indisputable that the change of sound in them results from the variation of their <term>bodies</term> <note>original: "Corporum"</note> (just as happens with other open and stopped pipes). Therefore, they should rightly be included, especially since many more wonderful variations can be proven and found in them than in other pipework.

And so, (1.) the pipes in organs are divided into flue-work and reed-work.

## Concerning open stops that are equally proportioned and are of the <term>Principal scaling</term> <note>original: "Principal Mensur"; refers to the standard ratio of diameter to length used for the main foundation stops of the organ.</note> in their width. ### Principal.

This name PRINCIPAL (which the ancients, our dear ancestors, called <term>Præstanten</term> <note>From the Latin "praestare," meaning to stand before or excel; these pipes often stand prominently in the front of the organ case.</note>) was not assigned to such pipework by chance or mere whim. <meta>This page continues the technical classification of organ stops, moving from the general table of voices on the previous page to a detailed description of the "Principal" family, which forms the core tonal foundation of the organ.</meta>

[...can] perform, they are rightly, well, and justly titled with the name **Principals**. Although by some it is called by the name *Doeff* <note>original: "Doeff"; a Low German or Dutch term for the Diapason or Principal stop.</note>.

->But there are four kinds of these:<-

### 1. Large Sub-Principal Bass of 32 Feet.

This voice cannot be used on the <term>Manual</term> <note>The keyboard played by the hands.</note> keyboard, as previously mentioned, but must be used for the <term>Pedal</term> <note>The keyboard played by the feet.</note> alone. This is because its tone is so unnaturally deep that if even a single key were to respond as a bass note, one hears more of a "wind-sucking and snorting" than a proper, discernible, pure tone. What kind of horrible, indistinct, and abominable harmony would result if it were played in chords <note>original: "Concordantenweise"</note> on the manual? Organists and listeners alike would soon grow weary of it and listen with annoyance. Therefore, such a stop should and must only be used on the pedal alongside an added voice of 16 feet.

### 2. Large Principal of 16 Feet.

This voice is now in common use. If it is carefully and precisely made and voiced <note>original: "Intonirt"</note> according to proper foundational proportions of the body and the <term>labia</term> <note>The "lips" of the organ pipe where the sound is produced.</note>, a truly noble sound and resonance can be heard. It can also be played well on its own on the manual (provided that in the low register one does not play chords that are too thick with thirds and fifths) and used lovely at a slow tempo. However, it is even better if it has another higher voice alongside it to help project the sound, as will follow.

### 3. Equal Principal of 8-Foot Tone.

This body size or 8-foot tone is the most lovely of all. It is the "equal tone" <note>original: "Aequal Thon"; referring to the pitch that matches the human voice, now called "unison" or "at pitch."</note> most similar to the human voice and all the most noble instruments. Indeed, all voices that are of 8-foot tone are quite suitable for <term>Motets</term> and choral harmonies, and may be used without hesitation or auditory faults according to properly set composition and rules. Within this, a strange mystery is hidden: such an 8-foot tone takes upon itself all the secret impurities inherent in the other smaller voices, bringing them into its own purity and honor, and making them partakers of the same. Of this, God willing, more can be written in detail at another time.

### 4. Small Principal or Octave Principal, 4 Feet.

This is also a lovely voice to use alone. However, because it lacks any particular sweetness or loveliness on its own—especially in the high register—it is common practice in such "Octave" or "Small Principal" divisions, as mentioned at the start, to arrange and build a foundation voice such as a **Quintadehn** or **Gedact** of 8-foot tone to go with it.

<summary>This page defines the four primary sizes of Principal pipes, ranging from the massive 32-foot pedal pipes to the 4-foot Octave Principal. Praetorius highlights the 8-foot Principal as the most "noble" and "mysterious" because of its ability to blend and purify the sound of higher-pitched stops.</summary>

ON ORGAN-MAKING.

In some 8-foot organs <note>original: "Equal Wercken"; instruments where the foundation stop is 8-foot pitch, corresponding to the human voice.</note>, a small Principal Treble of 4 feet is also sometimes crafted, which begins at the "unlined" f <note>The f below middle C.</note> at a pitch of 1 ½ feet and ascends as far as the keyboard goes. Usually, however, these are only started at middle C or a.

## Swiss Flute.

<image-desc>Large ornamental initial 'E' featuring scrolling foliage and a face within the design.</image-desc>

There is yet another type of voice, similar to the Principals but with a very narrow <term>scale</term> <note>The ratio of a pipe's diameter to its length, which determines its tonal character.</note>, which has been called "Swiss Flutes" <note>original: "Schweitzerpfeiffen"</note> by the Dutch and Netherlanders. This name is perhaps used because the pipes are so long and appear to have the proportions of a Swiss fife in relation to the narrowness of the pipe body. They possess a very distinctive, sweet, sharp sound, almost like the resonance of a <term>viol</term> <note>A stringed instrument; here referring to the "string-like" quality of the organ stop's tone.</note>, which arises from their narrowness. They are made with small "beards" <note>original: "Bärttlein"; small metal plates or wooden blocks attached to the sides of the pipe mouth to help the pipe "speak" more quickly.</note> (as the organ builders call them); otherwise, they would hardly achieve good <term>intonation</term> <note>The process of "voicing" or adjusting the pipe to produce the desired tone.</note> due to the excessively narrow scale. For this reason, one must also make the treble and smaller pipes somewhat wider.

->There are, however, only two types of these:<-

1. **Large Swiss Flute of 8-foot pitch.**
2. **Small Swiss Flute of 4-foot pitch.**

From this Small Swiss Flute, some only build the treble part, calling it a Swiss Flute Treble (*Discant*). Likewise, in the <term>Pedal</term> <note>The keyboard played with the feet.</note> it is found alone at 1-foot pitch and is called (3.) the Swiss Flute Bass or Swiss Bass.

These voices are not common, nor are they easily constructed; because of their difficult intonation, they require a truly honorable and experienced master.

The Large Swiss Flute in the pedal also provides a beautiful, sweet bass, much like a bass viol, when used with quieter stops. It should be noted, however, that on the <term>Manual</term> <note>The keyboard played with the hands.</note> this voice requires a slow tempo and clean fingering without special <term>coloratura</term> <note>original: "Colloraturen"; rapid, ornamental melodic runs or divisions.</note>, because of its slow "speech" <note>original: "anfallens"; the time it takes for the pipe to begin sounding after the key is pressed.</note>. Otherwise, it cannot achieve its characteristic sweetness and purity.

There is also another type of <term>Swiss Flute</term> <note>original: "Schweitzerpfeiffen"</note> which is voiced according to the <term>Prestant</term> <note>original: "præstanten"; pipes that "stand before" the others in the front of the organ case.</note> or <term>Principal scale</term>, but these are stopped <note>original: "gedäckt"; covered at the top with a cap.</note> at the top. Even though they would normally be expected to overblow <note>Changing pitch due to air pressure and the pipe being stopped.</note>, they actually sound at the correct pitch, just as if they were open and not stopped at all.

# Octave.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut drop cap 'G' begins the next paragraph.</image-desc>

Just as four types of Principals have now been established; so too do four types of *Octaves* follow from that same *Principal scale*: namely the *Great Octave*, the *Octave*, the *Small Octave*, and the *Little Super-Octave*.

### 1. The *Great Octave* is of 8-foot pitch.

This *Octave* belongs solely to the large <term>Great Organ</term> <note>original: "PrincipalWerck"; the main division of the organ.</note> and is no different in scale and sound than a <term>Unison Principal</term> <note>original: "AEqualPrincipal"; an 8-foot stop that sounds at the same pitch as the written note.</note>. Indeed, some call it the "Small Principal" when compared to the 16-foot Great Principal. However, because a "Small Principal" of 4-foot pitch stands in the <term>Rugpositiv</term> <note>original: "RückPositiff"; the organ division located behind the organist's back.</note> to distinguish it from the 8-foot pitch, and furthermore, since Principals are mostly made of tin while Octaves are made of lead or <term>half-work</term> <note>original: "halbwerck"; an alloy consisting of half tin and half lead.</note>—which are placed inside the organ case while the Principals are placed at the front—this voice is rightly called the *Great Octave*.

### 2. The *Octave* is of 4-foot pitch.

This belongs to the <term>Unison divisions</term> <note>original: "AEqualWercke"; divisions based on the 8-foot pitch standard.</note> and is so named because its pitch stands exactly an *Octave* higher than the *Unison Principal* and similar 8-foot stops. It can also be used on its own and allows itself to be drawn with both higher and lower-pitched stops.

### 3. The *Small Octave* is of 2-foot pitch.

This is otherwise called the *Super-octave*. However, because even smaller *Octaves* exist (as follows), this voice cannot properly be called the "Super-" or "Highest Octave." Following the order established above—where the *Great Octave* is 8-foot and the *Octave* is 4-foot—it is only right that this be called the *Small Octave* of 2-foot pitch, and the following be called the *Little Super-Octave* of 1-foot pitch.

### 4. The *Little Super-Octave* is of 1-foot pitch.

It is otherwise called the *Sedecima* <note>original: "Sedeze"; from the Latin 'decimus sextus', meaning sixteenth, because it is the sixteenth note above the fundamental.</note> because it stands two *octaves* above the 4-foot *Octave*. But because the 4-foot *Octave* is not a foundation or <term>unison voice</term>...

is [present], this cannot well be reckoned among them or called a <term>Sedecima</term> <note>original: "Sedez"; a stop sounding two octaves and a fifth above the fundamental, or a 1-foot stop.</note>; rather, it rightly retains the name **Superoctave**, and belongs primarily in large <term>Positives</term> <note>Small, often portable organs, or a specific division of a larger organ.</note> where the **Principal** is disposed at 2-foot pitch.

5. To this category also belong the <term>Quints</term> <note>Stops tuned a perfect fifth above the fundamental, providing harmonic richness.</note> of 6, 3, and 1 1/2-foot pitch; the latter type is called a <term>Quindecima</term> <note>original: "Quindetz"; properly a 2-foot "fifteenth," but here used incorrectly by some for the 1 1/2-foot stop.</note> by some, but incorrectly.

6. Likewise, the **Rauschpfeife** <note>literally "rustling pipes"</note>, which is an old name devised by the ancients. Back then, some combined these two voices and registers—namely the Quint 3-foot and Superoctave 2-foot—into one; while others placed them together on a single register and made a special voice from them, which they titled with the name *Rauschpfeife*, just as the Mixture and Cymbals have one name and register but more than one pipe [per key]. Some have also called it <term>Rauschquinte</term>, because the Quint is coarser than the Superoctave. They also had a *Rauschpfeife Bass*, which is still found in use today.

## Mixture / Cymbals.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'V' with intricate floral and scrollwork patterns.</image-desc>

From or according to this same <term>scale</term> <note>original: "Mensur"; the ratio of a pipe's diameter to its length, which determines the "fatness" or "thinness" of the sound.</note>, the Mixtures and Cymbals are now designed and crafted in large and small dispositions. These rightly belong to the **Principal** and **Octave** families of stops, as they are of the very same scale, and the Octaves and Quints are anyway drawn for the Mixture and Cymbals to achieve the "full organ" sound. And because their dispositions and variations are made in many ways by organ builders, according to the nature and circumstances of the instruments and churches, it is not possible to write about them *specifically* <note>original: "in specie"</note>. Only this: though they always ascend by a single octave and then immediately <term>repeat</term> <note>original: "repetiret"; referring to "breaks," where the high-pitched ranks jump back down an octave to avoid becoming too shrill as they go up the keyboard.</note>, this distinction exists: one type is called a "Great Mixture," which the ancients placed in their works (because at that time they did not yet know of many different types of stops as we do now). And as previously indicated, these were often 30, 40, or more pipes strong [per key], among which the largest was 8 feet. In current times, however, the Great Mixtures are only 10, 12, or occasionally (though very rarely) 20 pipes strong per rank, and the largest pipe at the lowest **key** <note>original: "Clave"</note> is of 4-foot pitch.

2. The second type is called a Mixture, because it is populated with pipes in the middle range—neither too large nor too small. This is precisely the one now made for **Unison Principals** <note>original: "AequalPrincipal"; an 8-foot stop sounding at pitch.</note> and also for the large Principal divisions, consisting of 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, and 9 pipes or <term>ranks</term> <note>original: "Choren"</note>; in these, the largest pipe is commonly of 2-foot or 1-foot pitch.

<meta>catchword: 3. The</meta>

It contrasts the massive 40-rank Mixtures of older organs with the more moderate 10-20 rank designs of the early 17th century.</summary>

->ON ORGAN-MAKING.<-

3. The third kind is called the small **Mixture**, or as the Netherlanders named it years ago, **Scharp** <note>original: "Scharp"; cognate with the English "Sharp," referring to its bright, piercing tonal quality.</note>: and not without reason, for it is a truly sharp-sounding stop, and yet consists of only three pipes, disposed as f c f̅ <note>f, middle c, and the f above middle c</note>, etc. It is disposed to repeat often. It is frequently placed in the <term>Brustwerk</term> <note>The "breast-work," a small organ division located directly in front of the player at chest level.</note> in large organs, or substituted for the main Mixture in small ones. Some builders use very small, subtle, and "young" <note>Praetorius uses "jung" (young) here to imply small, high-pitched pipes.</note> pipes for this, the largest being only 3 inches long, such as f f̅ c̅ f̅̅ : or three or four pipes in unison and one small Octave, but no <term>Quint</term> <note>A pipe sounding a fifth above the fundamental.</note>, and they progress from one octave to the next: this they call a **Scharp**. (**To repeat** means to restart the pitch sequence several times across a keyboard through the octaves—for example, moving from one c or f to the next—and it remains the same pitch level; because of this, Mixtures and Cymbals cannot be used alone for playing [polyphony]. <note>The "breaking" or repetition of these high stops prevents the pipes from becoming physically too small to produce sound as the player moves up the keyboard.</note>)

# Cymbals.

1. **Coarse Cymbal** is composed of 3 pipes.
2. **Ringing Cymbal**, 3 pipes strong, repeating throughout the entire keyboard in f and in c; it is arranged as f a c, which is said to be the most artistic arrangement.
3. **Cymbal** consists of 2 pipes and repeats several times, mostly by octaves.
4. **Small Cymbal** consists of one pipe and repeats often.
5. **Repeating Cymbal** is composed of 2 and 1 pipes, repeating continually.
6. **Cymbal-Basses** are of two or at most three kinds: the largest are about a half-foot pitch and repeat once. The others are somewhat smaller and repeat twice, yet all are arranged through <term>fourths</term> and <term>fifths</term>.

## II.

# Hollow Flute.

This is an open stop <note>original: "offenes Stimmwerck"; pipes that are not capped at the top, allowing for a brighter, clearer sound.</note> which has a much wider but somewhat shorter <term>scale</term> <note>original: "Mensur"; the ratio of a pipe's diameter to its length.</note> than the **Principals**, and has wide <term>bodies</term> <note>original: "Corpora"; the main vertical section of the organ pipe.</note> throughout. In their width, they are nearly the scale of a **Stopped Pipe** <note>original: "Gedacter Mensur"; referring to the Gedackt or Stopped Diapason family, which has a rounder, softer tone.</note>, except that they have narrower <term>lips</term> <note>original: "Labia"; the mouth of the pipe where the air vibrates to create sound.</note>. And because they are open and so wide, they sound very hollow; therefore, the name **Hollow Flute** <note>original: "Holflöit"; known in modern organs as the Hohlflöte.</note> has been given to them.

->ON ORGAN-MAKING.<-

## 1. Large Hollow Flute, 8-foot pitch.

Ancient organ builders, sixty or more years ago, placed such a stop in the Pedal of choral or cathedral organ divisions. They made it as large in pitch as the **Principal**; since at that time they knew nothing of the various distinct Basses or <term>Untersätze</term> <note>Literally "Lower-sets"; these are large-scale, deep-sounding pipes that provide the foundation of the organ's bass.</note>. They called such a bass the Sub-bass, the <term>Thunbass</term> <note>Literally "Thunder-bass," named for its resonant, booming quality.</note>, or even the **Coupler** <note>original: "Coppel"; usually referring to a stop that joins two keyboards, but here used to describe a foundational rank that "joins" the sound together.</note>. This was because it sounded wide and resonant, and because these organs were pitched a fifth lower than standard <term>Choir Pitch</term> <note>The standard pitch used for church music; Praetorius notes that older organs often deviated from this standard.</note>, it gave the instruments a special surging quality in those depths. These are still found in many old cathedral organs; an unknowledgeable person might think, because of its resonance and how it fills the space, that it is an **Untersatz**, as it was used in place of one in those completed instruments.

## 2. Hollow Flute, 4-foot pitch.
## 3. Hollow Quint, 3-foot pitch.

These are used in both the Manual and the Pedal as one desires. The old masters liked to use the **Hollow Quint Bass** in choral organs to lead the <term>Cantor</term> <note>The "SangMeister" or singing master responsible for leading the liturgy.</note> and the choir members astray—sometimes out of sheer mischief—from the correct pitch and the start of the chant.

## 4. Small Hollow Flute, 2-foot pitch.

This is also called the **Night-horn** <note>original: "Nachthorn."</note> by some, because it is hollow and its resonance is shaped almost like the sound of a horn. However, it is not quite rightly named according to its sound, since the character of the <term>Quintadehn</term> <note>A flute stop designed to emphasize the fifth as a prominent overtone, creating a thin, "nasal" sound.</note> is much better suited to that name.

## 5. Small Flute Bass, 2-foot pitch; this is also very good for use in choral music.

## 6. Quint Flute, 1 1/2-foot pitch.

## 7. Siff-flute, 1-foot pitch. Some count the <term>Suiflöit</term> or <term>Siefflitt</term> <note>The Sifflet is a very high-pitched, wide-scaled flute stop.</note> among the Principal stops.

## 8. Little Forest Flute, 1 1/2-foot pitch.

This stop is still common today in the coastal cities <note>Likely referring to the Hanseatic port cities like Hamburg or Lübeck, which were centers of innovative organ building.</note>; because it is so small, it **repeats** <note>See the previous page for an explanation of "repetition" in high-pitched stops.</note> two or three times across the keyboard.

## 9. Small Flute Bass, 1-foot pitch.

This is arranged in place of, and in the same manner as, the <term>Bawrflöitlin</term> <note>Literally "Little Peasant Flute," a rustic, high-pitched stop.</note>, but it is somewhat brighter and

...clearer in sound. And these small voices—when drawn with 8-foot stops <note>original: "Aequal-StimmWercken"; refers to stops at unison pitch, the standard pitch of the keys.</note> both with and without the tremulant—are quite good and unusual to hear in their tone.

## Schwegel.
<note>The Schwegel (or Schwiegel) was historically a simple three-holed flute, but here refers to a specific rank of organ pipes.</note>

Here is another special type of sound and name, which does not have quite as wide a <term>scale</term> <note>original: "Mensur"; the ratio of a pipe's diameter to its length, which determines its tonal character.</note> as these Hollow Flutes. These were named *Schwegel* by the Netherlanders nearly a hundred years ago (as can be seen in Sebastian Virdung’s *Musica* <note>Referring to *Musica getutscht* (1511), the earliest printed treatise on musical instruments in the West.</note>), because compared to other narrow-scaled pipework, they sound hollow, yet soft, and their resonance is very similar to that of transverse flutes. They are sometimes shaped like Gemshorns, though somewhat wider at the bottom and top, while still tapering at the very top. The <term>lip</term> <note>original: "Labium"; the metal edge of the pipe's mouth where the air is cut to create sound.</note> is narrow, and they are quieter than the <term>Spill-flutes</term> <note>original: "Spilflöitten"; a flute stop with a characteristic "spinning" or bright tone.</note>. There are, however, only two types:

1. **Large Schwegel, 8-foot pitch**
2. **Small Schwegel, 4-foot pitch.**

As for where such a soft sound originates, I shall let others who are knowledgeable in the matter provide the report. Let this be enough said regarding this scale, from the largest to the smallest.

---

## III. Open pipe stops which do not have uniform body widths.

This is the second type of open pipe, which—because they are quite wide at the bottom and pointed at the top, and are thus more than half-closed—possess a very different resonance than the previously described <term>Principal-scale</term> <note>The standard width used for the main foundation pipes of an organ; "Principal" refers to the core sound of the instrument.</note> types. Because their proportions and resonance sound like a horn, they are appropriately called **Gemshorns** <note>original: "Gemßhorn"; literally "Chamois horn," named after the mountain goat whose horns the tapered pipes resemble.</note>. There are several varieties of this type, such as the Gemshorn, Block Flute, Spitz Flute, Flach Flute, Dulcian, and the like.

## Gemshorn.
