->ON ORGAN-MAKING.<-

## 1. Large Gemshorn is of 16-foot pitch.
This is a lovely voice, but it is better used in the Pedal than in the <term>Manual keyboard</term> <note>original: "ManualClavir"; the keyboard played with the hands rather than the feet.</note>, unless another voice of 8-foot or 4-foot pitch is drawn with it.

## 2. Unison Gemshorn is of 8-foot pitch.
<note>original: "AequalGemshorn"; 'Aequal' refers to the unison pitch where the pipe length matches the standard pitch of the key pressed.</note>
And it is a particularly lovely and sweet voice to hear when it is made and <term>voiced</term> <note>original: "Intoniret"; the process of adjusting a pipe's mouth and wind to achieve a specific tone.</note> according to all its requirements from a proper fundamental division <note>Referring to the mathematical calculation of the pipe's diameter and length.</note>. It produces wonderful variations when combined with other voices. It could also well be titled *Viola da Gamba* <note>A stringed instrument of the Renaissance and Baroque, known for a reedy, expressive tone.</note> because, when made correctly, its resonance very closely mimics that instrument. The Netherlanders also call it the <term>Koppel-flute</term> <note>original: "Coppelflöiten"; literally 'coupling flutes', often a wide-scaled flute stop meant to blend well.</note>; they are longer than a <term>Gedeckt</term> <note>original: "Gedact"; a stopped pipe, literally 'covered', which sounds an octave lower than an open pipe of the same length.</note> but shorter than a <term>Principal</term> <note>The core, standard-toned pipes of the organ.</note>.

## 3. Octave Gemshorn is of 4-foot pitch.
This voice is used not unlike the 8-foot voice described above for many lovely variations. Both can be placed and used in both large and small Principal divisions.

## 4. Small Octave Gemshorn is of 2-foot pitch.
This belongs more in the <term>Ruckpositiv</term> <note>original: "Rückpositiff"; a smaller organ case located behind the organist's back, usually featuring bright, delicate stops.</note> and small Octave-Principal divisions than in the Great organ. However, it should not be excluded from other large <term>dispositions</term> <note>original: "dispositionen"; the specific list of stops chosen for an organ.</note>, for it provides a lovely character in the Manual, and also a beautiful bass in the Pedal for the <term>Chorale</term> <note>The traditional hymn melody, often played on the pedals for clarity.</note>, and lets itself be heard quite distinctly and properly.

<term>Quint</term> <note>Stops tuned to the interval of a fifth above the foundation pitch.</note> stops are also designed from this Gemshorn type, such as:

## 5. The Large Gemshorn Quint, 6-foot pitch.
## 6. The Gemshorn Quint, 3-foot pitch: And then
## 7. The Small Gemshorn Quint, one-and-a-half foot pitch:

This pipe is half as wide at the top as it is at the bottom. The <term>lip</term> <note>original: "labium"; the metal edge of the pipe's mouth.</note> is divided into five parts: one part is the width of the mouth, and then the height is cut up to half that width.

And this last voice is otherwise not incorrectly called *NASARD* <note>original: "NASATH"; a flute-toned quint stop known for its "nasal" quality.</note> because, due to its small size, it "snuffles" as it were when combined with other voices, especially when it is voiced correctly and not too sharply. It also provides a beautiful <term>treble</term> <note>original: "Discant"; the highest part or range of a composition.</note> in the right hand when used with other drawn stops. Some craft the Nasard according to a wide <term>pipe scale</term> <note>original: "Pfeiffwerck Mensur"; the physical proportions of the pipe's diameter relative to its length.</note> and with narrow lips.

->ON THE DESCRIPTION OF INSTRUMENTS.<-

Some call the <term>Gemshorn</term> <note>literally "chamois horn"; an organ stop with tapered pipes that produce a light, slightly nasal, horn-like tone.</note> a "Pointed Flute" [Spitzflöit] as well, and this is solely due to its shape and proportions, as such pipes look very similar to hand-spindles.

Some still call Gemshorns "Block-pipes" [Plockpfeiffen] even now, but this is an incorrect naming. Block-pipes have a different shape and sound; the 4-foot Pointed Flutes (of which we shall speak immediately) could more rightly be called Block-pipes or <term>Block-flutes</term> <note>the recorder family of instruments</note> if they were made with a wider opening at the top than the Gemshorns. This is because they would then yield a resonance naturally like the other wind instruments called Block-pipes. However, skilled masters do not craft voices of this kind smaller than 2-foot pitch.

Some craft the Block-flutes almost in the manner of <term>transverse flutes</term> <note>original: "Querflöiten"; flutes held horizontally.</note>, such that the <term>body</term> <note>original: "Corpus"</note> is made twice as long as the standard <term>scale</term> <note>original: "Mensur"; the ratio of a pipe's width to its length.</note> usually requires, and it is covered at the top; therefore, it must <term>overblow</term> <note>forcing the air to make the pipe sound a higher harmonic</note> at the <term>octave</term> <note>original: "Octav"</note>.

# Pointed Flute.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial E featuring floral and foliage patterns.</image-desc>
There are other voices of nearly this same kind which are also tapered and are called Pointed Flutes [Spitzflöit]. This particular scale has not been in common use for very long.

There is, however, a significant difference between the Gemshorns and these Pointed Flutes; the latter is wider at the <term>mouth</term> <note>original: "labio"; the lip or opening where the sound is formed.</note> and more pointed at the top than the aforementioned Gemshorns—which is why it is rightly called a "Pointed Flute." There are only two varieties of size and pitch:

1. Pointed Flute of 4-foot pitch.
2. Small Pointed Flute of 2-foot pitch.

I have also found a variety of Pointed Flute that is only slightly open at the top and has a very narrow mouth; these produce an exceptionally lovely resonance, but they are very difficult to bring to a pure and correct <term>voicing</term> <note>original: "Intonation"; the delicate adjustment of a pipe's parts to ensure it speaks clearly and at the right volume.</note>.

# Flat Flute. <note>original: "Flachflöit"</note>

Now there is another kind of voice of almost this same <term>scale</term> <note>original: "Mensur"; the ratio of a pipe's width to its length</note>, and they are called Flat Flutes. These are not very wide at the <term>mouth</term> <note>original: "labio"</note>, having a narrow, low <term>cut-up</term> <note>original: "vfschnidt"; the height of the opening in the pipe's mouth</note>, yet they are given a very wide lip; therefore, the sound is "flat" and not "plump" <note>original: "pempich"; a term describing a full, round, or bulbous tone</note>. They are only slightly tapered at the top, but because of their difficult <term>voicing</term> <note>original: "Intonation"</note>, they require an experienced master organ builder. Otherwise, they sound very well, and somewhat "flatter" than the <term>Gemshorns</term> <note>organ stops with tapered pipes and a light, horn-like tone</note>; for this reason, they are rightly christened with the name Flat Flute. There are three types of this stop, distinguished by their tone and pipe length:

->As<-

1. **Large Flat Flute, 8-foot pitch.**
2. **Flat Flute, 4-foot pitch.**
3. **Small Flat Flute, 2-foot pitch.**

All three are very good and useful to employ for lovely variations when many voices are arranged in an organ. They also provide beautiful <term>basses</term> in the Pedal division for prominent use, for they are somewhat louder, yet more "foreign" in sound, than the Gemshorns.

The small Flat Flute in particular—when it is tuned as a <term>Quint</term> <note>a stop sounding a fifth above the foundation tone</note>—may be used in the <term>Rückpositiv</term> <note>the division of the organ located behind the organist’s back</note> along with a <term>Zimbel</term> <note>a high-pitched mixture stop</note> and a <term>Quintadena</term> <note>a stopped pipe that strongly sounds its fifth harmonic</note> to create a "fiddling" treble sound; for it allows itself to be heard as something very similar to that. This concludes the report on this kind of stop.

---

# Dulzain.

There remains one more voice that is of unequal width: wide at the top, but considerably narrower at the <term>mouth</term> <note>original: "labio"</note>. Such a voice is called a Dulzain. It is found in the new organ at Stralsund <note>likely referring to the Stellwagen organ in St. Mary's Church</note> and is of 8-foot pitch. Because of its very difficult voicing, it cannot be made any smaller. It sounds somewhat similar to the instrument called the <term>Dulcian</term> <note>a Renaissance woodwind, the predecessor to the bassoon</note> because the body [corpus] widens at the top, just like the Dulcian instrument, while being narrower at the mouth. However, since the Dulcian itself must remain a <term>reed</term> <note>original: "Rohr"; an instrument that produces sound via a vibrating tongue</note> or "snarling" instrument, and the voice described here belongs to the flute or flue pipework <note>original: "Pfeifferwerck"</note>, the same can [be compared to] the—

## IV. On Stopped Pipes <note>original: "Gedacten Pfeiffen"</note> / And first of the Quintadena, Night Horn, and Transverse Flute.

### Quintadena <note>original: "Quintadehna"</note>

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'E' decorated with elaborate foliate scrollwork and floral patterns.</image-desc> This stop has not been in use for long, perhaps only 40 or 50 years, as it is not found in old organs. It is a lovely stop (called the "Wooden Bell" <note>original: "Holschelle"</note> by some) in which two distinct sounds—namely the **Fifth** <note>the interval of five notes, like C to G</note>, "do" and "sol"—can be heard in the ear. For this reason, it was originally called *Quinta ad una* <note>Latin: "a fifth with the one"</note>. The **proportions** of its **body** <note>original: "Corporis"</note> are nearly the same, though a fair bit wider, as the **scale** <note>original: "Mensur"; the ratio of width to length</note> of the **Principal** <note>the fundamental, open pipes of an organ</note>. Because it is **stopped** <note>the pipe is capped at the top, which lowers the pitch</note>, it sounds an octave lower than an open pipe of the same length. There are only three types of these, which are crafted from the same scale but vary according to their pitch or length:

->As<-

#### 1. Large Quintadena, 16-foot pitch.

This stop is quite lovely to use and hear both on the **manuals** <note>original: "Manualiter"; the keyboards played by hand</note> and the **pedals** <note>original: "Pedaliter"; the keyboard played by the feet</note> when another 8-foot stop is combined with it.

#### 2. Quintadena, 8-foot pitch.

This is used as a foundation both in the **Rückpositiv** <note>the small organ case located behind the organist's back</note> or in the small Octave Principal division. It is also very convenient to use in the Pedal for the **Chant Bass** <note>original: "ChoralBaß"; the melodic line of a hymn or plainsong</note>.

#### 3. Quintadena, 4-foot pitch.

This is a lovely stop, especially when heard alongside larger stops to provide variation; however, it is not found in a smaller size, as it cannot be effectively crafted any smaller.

<header>ON THE DESCRIPTION OF INSTRUMENTS <note>original: "DE ORGANOGRAPHIA"</note></header>

# Night Horn <note>original: "Nachthorn"</note>

This small **Quintadena** <note>a stopped pipe that sounds both its fundamental tone and its fifth</note> is widened in its **scale** <note>original: "Mensur"; the ratio of a pipe's width to its length</note> by some organ builders, though only to a specific degree. Because it gains a horn-like sound from this widening, and the **Fifth** <note>the secondary, higher interval heard within the tone</note> becomes somewhat quieter, it is called the **Night Horn**. This name is quite fitting. This variety can be combined with many other stops for a very lovely and diverse range of sounds.

From this same scale or style comes the **Night Horn Bass**, in both 4-foot and 2-foot pitch. It is an elegant stop, especially pleasant to hear in the bass.

The builders in the Low Countries <note>original: "Niederländer"</note> make the Night Horn **open** <note>without a cap on top</note>, like a **Hollow Flute** <note>original: "Holflöite"</note>, though somewhat narrower, and they gradually taper the top. The **lip** <note>original: "Labio"; the edge of the pipe mouth where the air vibrates</note> is not cut as high as that of the Hollow Flute. This gives it a unique sound, almost like a joyful shout <note>original: "juchete"</note> or a rhythmic sobbing <note>original: "schlüggete"</note>.

---

# Transverse Flute <note>original: "Querflöit"</note>

Furthermore, from the invention of the **Quintadena**, a new variety has been discovered which very closely matches the sound of the **transverse flute** <note>a flute held horizontally</note>, which is why it is so named.

However, this sound does not arise from natural **voicing** <note>original: "Intonation"</note>, but rather from **overblowing** <note>original: "vberſetzen oder vbergallen"; forcing the air so the pipe sounds a higher harmonic rather than its fundamental</note>. This overblowing occurs because the **body** <note>original: "Corpus"</note> of the pipe is more than twice, and nearly one and a half times, as long as its narrowness would usually dictate.

To explain: when the 'c' of a 4-foot pitch sounds, the pipe body is actually so long that, based on its length, it could and should sound at a 12-foot pitch. Yet, it only sounds the **Fifth** due to the overblowing. Because of this unnatural length relative to its narrowness, the pipe can produce no other sound but this Fifth.

This type of Transverse Flute is indeed very good and is also a new invention. However, there is another type of **open scale** where the pipe body is twice as long; this kind is found in the new wooden organ belonging to the Prince <note>referring to the Duke of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel</note>, which the Most Reverend...

In their resonance, they are even more similar to the natural sound of a transverse flute than the **stopped pipes** <term>Gedacten: pipes with a cap on top that sound an octave lower than an open pipe of the same length</term>. Pipes of this kind are also present in His Princely Grace’s aforementioned magnificent great organ at Gröningen, in 8-foot and 4-foot pitch in both the Manual and Pedal.

->V.<-
->### Stopped Pipes of All Kinds.<-

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap D containing floral and architectural motifs</image-desc> In former times, this stop was simply called "Flutes" by the ancients in their works. The Netherlanders and some others call them **Bourdon**, especially when they have a narrow **scale** <term>scale: the ratio of a pipe's width to its length</term>. Some also call them **Barem** when they are voiced very quietly and gently. However, there are six types of **Gedackts** <note>stopped pipes</note> or entirely covered stops, categorized by their pitch and length.

->#### 1. Large Stopped Pipe at 16-foot pitch.<-

This stop is mostly placed in the Pedal and called the **Large Stopped Untersatz** <note>a deep bass stop sounding an octave below the standard 8-foot pitch</note>. It is also sometimes extended into the Manual. However, because of its thumping, quiet sound and its extreme depth, it is not particularly pleasant or clear to the ear, as experience and nature testify. And although this stopped scale is also occasionally built at 32-foot pitch in the Pedal and called a **Large Stopped Sub-Bass**, one can hear a proper, clear tone from it much less than from open pipes—as was previously reported regarding the **Large Sub-Principal**. In my opinion, for a 32-foot pitch, no better stop could be installed than the **Flachflöte** <note>literally "Flat Flute"; a stop with a wide, clear tone</note>; however, I leave such things to be tested by a skillful organ builder.

->#### 2. Stopped Pipe at 8-foot pitch.<-

This is now a common stop in general use. It is often placed as the foundation in small "Octave Principal" divisions, and it is also included and specified for large **Rückpositiv** <note>the division of the organ located behind the organist's back</note> sections.

->#### 3. Small Stopped Pipe at 4-foot pitch.<-

<sig>S ij</sig>
<meta>image quality: clear; catchword: Wird (translated as: Will be / Is)</meta>

<summary>Praetorius describes the construction of wood transverse flute stops, citing the famous Compenius organ, and begins a classification of 'Gedackt' or stopped pipes from 16-foot to 4-foot pitches.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the catalog of "Stopped Pipes" (Gedacten), following the description of the Barem or Bourdon. It focuses on smaller-scale flutes, experimental designs by Esaias Compenius, and the regional differences in organ registration between Germany and Italy.</meta>

<header>ON THE DESCRIPTION OF INSTRUMENTS <note>original: "DE ORGANOGRAPHIA"</note></header>

It <note>the stopped flute stop</note> is also commonly placed in all sorts of arrangements of organ works and positives <note>small portable organs</note>. However, it is especially good and provides fine and diverse variations, particularly when combined with **Quintadenas** <term>Quintadehn: a stopped pipe that sounds its third harmonic (the twelfth) prominently</term> and **Gemshorns** <term>Gemshorn: "Goat horn," a pipe with a tapered, conical body</term>.

Approximately 28 years ago, a strange type was invented by a then-young master, E. C. <note>Esaias Compenius, the famous organ builder mentioned on the previous page</note>. He made a stopped pipe of 4-foot pitch with two **mouths** <note>original: "labiis" / lips</note> that correspond exactly to one another, so that one can look right through the pipes; he named this the **Double Flute** <term>Duiflöit: from the Latin 'duo' for double</term>. This stop changes its sound quite significantly compared to other types of stopped pipes. However, it has not yet become common at this time.

### 4. Small Super-Stopped-Flute is 2-foot in pitch. <note>original: "Supergedäcktlein"</note>

Even though this is small, it still provides lovely variations when paired with larger stops, as was mentioned regarding the **Sifflet** <term>Suiflöit: a high-pitched, wide-scaled flute stop</term> and others; this is especially true where a good **tremulant** <note>a device that causes the air to fluctuate, creating a vibrato effect</note> is available. Indeed, provided it is of the correct **scale** <term>menſur: the ratio of a pipe's width to its length</term> and voiced with pure, consistent tone, it can be used for an excellent **treble** <note>original: "Discant"</note> part in the right hand, sounding exactly like a small recorder <note>original: "Plockflöitlein"</note>. Likewise, when combined with the large 16-foot **Rackett** <term>Rancket: a low-pitched, buzzy reed instrument with a compact body</term> or **Sordun** <term>Sorduen: a quiet, muffled reed stop</term>, it creates a strange and unique sound that is a pleasure to hear.

### 5. Stopped Fifth, 3-foot pitch. <note>original: "Gedacte Quinta"</note>

This stop has been called by some—such as Gregorio Vogel—the **Piper’s Flute** <note>original: "Pfeifferflöit"</note>, which stood a **fifth** <note>an interval of five notes</note> above the standard choir pitch.

### 6. Peasant Flute Bass, or "Little Peasant," 1-foot pitch. <note>original: "Bawerflöit Baß/oder Päurlin"</note>

This stop is very highly regarded among us in Germany, especially when one wishes to play the **Chorale** <note>the main hymn melody</note> in the **Pedal** <note>the keyboard played with the feet</note>. The Italians, however, despise all such tiny bass stops of 2-foot or 1-foot pitch, because they sound like mere octaves and bring no resonance <note>fundamental depth</note> with them.

From this design and scale of the **Stopped Pipe** <note>original: "Gedacten"</note>, another has now been invented which is reopened to some extent by means of certain small, measured tubes; for this reason, it is correctly called the **Chimney Flute** <term>Rohrflöit: a pipe with a cap and a small protruding tube or "chimney" that alters its harmonic profile</term>.

Stops of this type, however, are constructed in various ways. Some makers let the tubes extend half-out and half-in; others place them entirely inside so that nothing is visible except the hole at the top. These latter ones are the most durable, as the tubes cannot then be bent or damaged; however, these must then be tuned with **tuning caps** <term>Deckhütten: movable sleeves used to adjust the pitch of stopped pipes</term>.

### 1. Large Chimney Flute, 16-foot pitch.

If one of these large, stopped stops were to be used throughout the entire **manual** <note>the keyboard played by the hands</note>, this **Large Chimney Flute** would be far superior because it sounds louder and purer than the fully stopped variety; this is because it allows a fine, well-sounding **fifth** <term>Quintam: the third harmonic, which sounds a perfect fifth interval above the octave</term> to be heard alongside the fundamental tone.

### 2. Chimney Flute is 8-foot pitch.
### 3. Small Chimney Flute is 4-foot pitch.
### 4. Small Super-Chimney-Flute is 2-foot pitch.

These are all very suitable and lovely for all kinds of registrations, but they are especially useful when paired with **Quintadenas** <term>Quintadehn: a stopped pipe that highlights the interval of a twelfth</term>.

5. There is also no type of stop that provides a better **Peasant Flute Bass** <term>Bawrflöit: a high-pitched, rustic-sounding flute stop</term> of 1-foot pitch than this one. It possesses a sound exactly as if someone were whistling with their mouth at a high pitch, and it gains this quality from the attached chimney. This small stop is called the **Chimney Bell** <term>Rohrschell</term> by some because it contains and lets a bright fifth be heard; however, if its true characteristics are considered, it has not been named correctly.

Mention should also be made here of **wooden pipework** <term>Pfeiffwerck: the collective pipes of an organ</term>. However, because of various ways of dividing the foundations—as I have personally observed with great diligence—and because its sound requires a completely different explanation and can hardly be compared to other organs in terms of volume and workmanship, I must address it separately. This is proven by the aforementioned musical organ located at **Hesse Castle** <note>Schloß Hessen: a ducal residence famous for its elaborate organ built by Esaias Compenius around 1610</note>.

Its strange, soft, subtle sound and loveliness cannot be adequately described in writing. To avoid being overly long-winded, I have chosen to only provide a few more reminders and indications about such pipework for the time being.

->VII.<-

# Concerning Open Reed Stops.

Because **reed stops** <term>Schnarrwercke: literally "rattling works," these are organ stops where sound is produced by a vibrating metal tongue</term> are quite common and known to everyone, it is unnecessary to provide many reminders here, except to say that every master has a different method for arranging the length and structure of these open **resonators** <term>Corporum: the body of the organ pipe sitting above the reed assembly</term>. While some build the **Posaunes** <term>Posaunen: a powerful, low-pitched reed stop, named after the trombone</term> 16 feet long in the body, just as they hold a 16-foot pitch in resonance, this is quite rare. Others, however, build them 12 feet long, so that the resonator deviates from the true pitch by a **fifth** <note>an interval of five scale degrees; in this context, the pipe body is physically shorter than the wavelength it produces</note>, and this is the best method. The most common method uses an 8-foot **scale** <note>original: "Mensur"</note>. Some craft the Posaunes at only 6 feet long. Others at 5 feet, covered slightly at the top with a hole cut into it like a square **bung** <note>original: "Spund"</note>, etc. However, because these resonators are so small, they have a very thin and flat-falling sound and resonance. But if the stop is intended to boast, show off, and sound **stately** <note>original: "gravitætisch"</note>, it must be 12 feet long. And such variation is also maintained in the other succeeding open reed stops: Thus,

| If the scale of the Posaunes is | Then the Trumpets are | Shawms are | |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| 16 Foot | 8 Foot | 4 | |
| 12 | 6 | 3 | Foot. |
| 8 | 4 | 2 | |
| 6 | 3 | 1 1/2 | |

However, since so much depends on the scale and length of the resonators in reed stops—

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of reed stop construction, specifically focusing on how the "scale" (width) and the "mouthpiece" (shallot) affect the sweetness of the tone, and how temperature affects tuning.</meta>

# ON THE DESCRIPTION OF INSTRUMENTS <note>original: "DE ORGANOGRAPHIA"</note>

...does not lie in the bodies; rather, the low or high pitch of the resonance stems not from the body or structure (though it must still have its proper regularity and measurement), but from the **mouthpieces** <term>Mundstücken: also known as shallots in reed pipes, these are the components the metal tongue vibrates against</term>. Furthermore, if the mouthpieces are elongated and narrow, they produce a far sweeter resonance than if they are short and wide. This is also found to be the case in other pipe and flute work: a wider **scale** <term>Mensur: the ratio of a pipe's diameter to its length, which dictates its tonal character</term> is never as sweet in its resonance as a narrow one.

Therefore, every organ builder should rightly strive for very narrow scales; for the narrower they are, the sweeter and more pleasant they become. However, because bringing such narrow scales to the correct **intonation** <term>intonation: the process of adjusting a pipe to ensure its speech and tone are correct</term> is not within every organ builder's capability—requiring as it does good understanding, great diligence, and excellent effort—most builders, being lazy masters <note>original: "faule Patres," literally "lazy fathers"</note> who are reluctant to learn anything more, commonly stick to the usual wide scales. In this way, they do not have to rack their brains too much, finish the work more quickly, and fill their purses better.

In the land of Hesse, a special kind of **Trombone stop** <term>Posaunen: a powerful reed stop intended to imitate the brass instrument</term> was found in a monastery. On its mouthpiece, a small brass plate was soldered, having a fairly longish hole in the center; only then was the proper **tongue** <term>zünglein or blätlein: the vibrating metal reed</term> placed over it and bound with annealed brass or steel strings <note>likely wire</note>, so that it cannot rattle or blare so harshly. Because it is dampened somewhat more than usual in this manner, it gives—when properly intoned and blown by a good master—a majestic, muffled resonance that does not rattle, much like a real trombone.

Nonetheless, they must still be tuned by sliding the uppermost body up and down, and they remain **mobile Regals** <note>original: "Regalia mobilia"</note>. For the loss of tuning does not arise (as some believe) from the upward or downward shifting of the **tuning wires** <term>kröckel or dröstlin: the wires used to adjust the vibrating length of the reed tongue</term>, by which the Regals must otherwise be tuned. It is, after all, impossible for the wires to move up and down on their own. Rather, it happens because of the delicate brass tongues, which curve outwards in warm weather due to the heat (as can also be tested with paper or thin wood). Because the opening at the mouthpiece is thereby widened, the resonance sinks somewhat lower. In cold weather, however, the tongue turns inward and closer to the mouthpiece, making the hole smaller and causing the resonance to rise higher. Every person who handles organs and **Regals** <term>Regaln: small, portable reed organs consisting mostly of reed stops</term> experiences this change daily: as soon as the cold winter weather changes and turns to a thaw, the Regals sink in pitch and become deeper. But as soon as it begins to freeze again, they thus

# ON THE DESCRIPTION OF INSTRUMENTS <note>original: "DE ORGANOGRAPHIA"</note>

<meta>catchword: because</meta>

they soon become higher: Therefore, even adjusting the tuning wires <note>original: "vff binden der Kröckel"; the wires that press against the reed tongue to change its vibrating length</note> cannot help much.

And this same phenomenon is found not only in **harpsichords** <term>Clavicymbeln: early keyboard instruments where strings are plucked by quills</term> and **virginals** <term>Symphonien: a term often used in this period for stringed keyboard instruments like the virginal or clavichord</term> with their steel and brass strings, but also in the strings of lutes and violins, which are made of sheep gut. From heat, they slacken, expand, and widen, and therefore the **pitch** <term>Resonanz: here referring to the frequency or pitch of the sound</term> descends; from cold, however, they contract and pull closer together, which causes the pitch to ascend. Consequently, in winter, if the **instruments** <note>original: "Instrumenta"</note> have stood continuously for several weeks in the cold, they may have ascended and risen by almost half a tone or more. For this reason, if an intelligent master has not calculated the **scaling** <term>Mensur: the specific length and tension of a string relative to its pitch</term> on harpsichords and virginals so that every string can safely be pulled higher by a half-tone if necessary, almost all the strings will snap. I have often experienced this myself, not without damage and great frustration.

And from this fundamental principle—that the variation in the **Regal** <term>Regall: a small pipe organ consisting entirely of reed stops</term> and other **reed stops** <term>Schnarrwercken: literally "buzzing work," the general category for all reed-based organ stops</term> arises from the small brass tongues—comes a **test** <note>original: "Proba"</note> by which one can learn whether a Regal has been accurately and diligently voiced through its reeds or tongues. For when a reed stop is diligently crafted by a good master, it shifts with the changing weather uniformly across the entire **keyboard** <term>Clavier</term>. Either they all drift further away together in the warmth and heat, or they all move closer to the mouthpiece in the cold and frost. In such a case, one can use that stop on an organ (or otherwise) quite well even without drawing the **flue pipes** <term>Flöitwerck: the "flute-like" pipes of an organ that produce sound by air vibrating against a lip, rather than a reed</term> and other pipes, just as if it had remained perfectly in tune.

But when a flue stop is drawn with it, the defect is revealed: either the reed stop as a whole has shifted below or above the flue stop. In that case, the reed stop was prepared diligently and accurately. However, if it is found that the reed stop has not shifted uniformly across the entire keyboard—where one **key** <term>Clavis: a single key or note</term> is too low compared to the flue pipes, the second is too high, and the third is in tune—it is a certain sign that the mouthpieces were not fitted with uniform tongues. Instead, one tongue is thick and another thin, for a thick, heavy tongue does not allow itself to be forced by heat or cold as quickly as a thin and weak one.

Now, although a detailed report should also be made here regarding all other kinds of reed stops, it is impossible to describe them all due to the many variations and various inventions, especially...

...because more and many foreign ones are being invented daily; and to accurately imitate another instrument blown by mouth through such a **reed stop** <term>Schnarrwerck: a category of organ stops that use a vibrating metal tongue to produce a buzzing, "snaring" sound similar to a reed instrument</term>, and to correctly match its character and resonance, is very difficult; so I will only mention some of the most prominent types here for information.

### Shawms <note>original: "Schalmeyen"</note> are 8-foot tone:

But they are no better imitated than with actual shawm **pipe bodies** <term>Corpora: the resonant tubes of the organ pipes</term>, though made slightly wider; they then combine that same character very nicely with the true sound of the shawm.

### Crumhorn <note>original: "Krumbhorn"</note> is only 8-foot tone:

And although it is possible to bring this stop to 16-foot tone—though it is very rarely found there—because it sounds somewhat strong and goes so deep, it is not very pleasant **for the hands** <term>Manualiter: music played on the keyboards (manuals) with the fingers</term>, but better to be used **for the feet** <term>Pedaliter: music played on the pedalboard with the feet</term> alone at such a depth.

However, there are various inventions for these: For although some wish to achieve such a sound in a true Regal body (which is closed at the top with a lid, and two, three, or more small holes are drilled either in the lid itself or at the bottom next to the **shallot** <term>Mundstücke: the "mouthpiece" or block holding the vibrating reed tongue</term>); or otherwise by other means; therefore they could well be categorized among the **stopped** <term>Gedacte: pipes that are capped at the top, which lowers their pitch by an octave compared to open pipes of the same length</term> reed stops. Yet, this invention—where the pipe bodies are equally wide, open at the top, and 4 feet in length—is the best and most consistent type of Crumhorn.

But, like other such lovely reed stops, they require certain and proper understanding and are not easily made or finished by just anyone.

### Coarse Regal <note>original: "Grob Regal"</note> are 8-foot tone:

In organs, these are mostly made of brass and worked to a **scale** <term>Mensur: the specific dimensions and proportions of a pipe that determine its tone color</term> of 5 or 6 inches in height. Although sometimes, especially in the **Regals** <note>small, portable organs containing only reed stops</note> made in Augsburg and Nuremberg until now, one finds very small bodies for the Regal pipes that are barely an inch high and yet have an 8-foot pitch: as was mentioned more extensively in the preceding Part II, No. 43.

**Maiden Regal** <note>original: "JungfrawenRegal"</note> or **Bass** is 4-foot tone; in itself it is a small open Regal with a small, slight body, about one or at most two inches high; it is named so because, when used with other stops and flute-works in the pedal, it sounds like a maiden's voice trying to sing a bass part.

This small **Regal** <term>Regal: a reed stop with very short resonators, producing a characteristic buzzing or "snarling" sound</term> at 4-foot pitch is also called a **Violin-** or **Fiddle-Regal** <term>Geigen- or GiegenRegal</term> by some. However, since every stop should sound as it is intended and be named for its own character without the help of others, one cannot more fairly name this stop anything other than a "small Regal."

### Cornetts <note>original: "Zincken"</note> at 8-foot pitch:

These are used only through half the **keyboard** <term>Clavir: here referring to the manual or keyboard of the organ</term> in the **treble** <term>Discant</term>. They have **pipe bodies** <term>Corpora: the main resonators of the organ pipes</term> of equal width throughout, somewhat pointed at the bottom and open at the top. Because of this, they have a somewhat hollow sound, like a **flute stop** <term>Flöitwerck</term>, and are not so "snaring" or buzzy; for, due to their thick tongues and strong wind pressure, the buzzing is somewhat lost and suppressed.

The **Cornett** <note>In this context, a reed stop imitating the woodwind instrument, not the flute mixture common in later organs</note> is mostly used in the bass alone. It is indeed of **Regal-scale** <term>RegalMensur: the specific proportions or measurements used for Regal pipes</term>, but narrower and longer. For even if it is only of 4-foot or 2-foot pitch, the **pipe body** <term>Corpus</term> is 9 inches high—and thus higher than an 8-foot Regal body. Therefore, it compares quite well to a human voice. However, some organ builders make the bodies in the Cornett barely 4 or 5 inches high; for builders vary greatly in this matter, and thus nothing certain can be written about it.

## VIII. Stopped Reed Stops <note>original: "Gedäcte Schnarrwerck"</note>

### Sorduns <note>original: "Sordunen," from the Italian 'sordo' meaning muted or muffled</note> are of 16-foot pitch:

Because of their design—being "stopped" <note>the top of the pipe is capped or plugged</note> and containing a hidden internal **pipe body** <term>Corpus</term> with fairly long tubes—they cannot be easily voiced much higher if they are to retain their true character. Their outer body is indeed about two feet high, and its width is like that of a 4-foot **Night-horn** <term>Nachthorn: a wide-scaled flute stop with a soft, horn-like quality</term> body. It is, however, very lovely and quiet when it has been made by a true master, and is thus very useful to combine with string or flute stops. One must take great care, however—just as with other large **pipework** <term>Pfeiffwerck</term> of 16-foot pitch—to avoid playing **chords** <term>Concordantiis: harmonizing intervals, specifically thirds and fifths</term> in the left hand, so that such deep tones do not ruin the sound and make it unpleasant to hear. It is, above all, elegant to use in the **pedal** <term>Pedal: the keyboard played with the feet</term> for many different registrations.

# ON THE DESCRIPTION OF INSTRUMENTS <note>original: "DE ORGANOGRAPHIA"</note>

->**Great Racketts** <term>Groß Rancket: a reed stop with a very short exterior body but long internal tubing</term> are also of 16-foot pitch:<-
->**Racketts** are of 8-foot pitch:<-

These are an exceptionally lovely, stopped <note>referring to "gedackt" or capped pipes</note> species of **reed stops** <term>Schnarrwercken: literally "snarling works," the general term for reed pipes</term>; they are to be intonated very quietly and are quite suitable for many **variations** <term>variationibus: musical variations or different registration combinations</term> and changes.

Both of these stops have equally small **pipe bodies** <term>Corpora: the resonators of the pipes</term>; their largest is approximately one good span <note>roughly 9 inches</note> long. They contain a hidden **inner body** <term>Corpus</term> within them, similar to the **Sorduns** <term>Sordunen: quiet reed stops with folded internal tubes</term> mentioned previously.

**Bear-pipes** <term>Baerpipen or Baerpfeiffen: a reed stop with a distinctive growling or muffled tone</term> are also of 16- and 8-foot pitch and should not be made smaller, or they lose their proper name and sound. They perhaps take their name from the quiet growling of a bear, as they sound deep within themselves and **respond** <term>respondiren</term> with a humming **intonation**. Though they do not have tall **pipe bodies** <term>Corpora</term>, they are quite wide, shaped like two funnels placed together, yet with a uniform width in the middle and almost entirely stopped. When made of wood, however, they are constructed somewhat differently, as can be seen in the **Book of Illustrations** <term>Sciagraphia: the volume of technical drawings accompanying this treatise</term>. One can shape them in many ways, but it is their **characteristic property** <term>proprium</term> that they must be narrow at the bottom and then immediately expand greatly in width.

In Prague, in the Jesuit church, I saw a **reed stop** <term>Schnarrwerck</term> invented by Father Andreas. it had a very lovely resonance, where the **pipe body** <term>Corpus</term> was square and led back and forth alongside itself <note>referring to a folded or "boustrophedon" internal structure</note>, always increasing in width, as can be seen in the **Book of Illustrations** <term>Sciagraphia</term>.

**Bombard** <term>Pombarda: a powerful reed stop, often the precursor to the Trombone or Tuba stops</term>: This is almost in accordance with the **invention** <term>Invention</term> of the **Sordun**, except that the emission of the resonance through the small holes is altered, and it requires larger mouthpieces and tongues. Consequently, it allows itself to be heard more clearly and strongly. It is to be built at 16- and 8-foot pitch. However, **Bombards** are more appropriate and better suited for the Pedal than for the Manual, as they provide a strong sound to a pleasant and moderate tone.

**Bassoon** <term>Fagott</term> is of 8-foot pitch: It has **pipe bodies** <term>Corpora</term> that are of uniform width and narrowness, the largest being 4 feet in length, and it is played **on the keyboard** <term>Manualiter: played with the hands on the manual keyboard rather than the feet</term>.

**Dulcian** <term>Dulcian: a reed stop intended to mimic the soft-toned predecessor of the bassoon</term> is only of 8-foot pitch: By some, it is stopped at the top, and its resonance is let out through several small holes at the bottom on one side; these are to be found in the **Regal-organs** <term>Regalwercken</term> made in Vienna, Austria. Others, however, leave it entirely open at the top, which is why they are not quite so quiet and resemble the wind instrument of the same name. It more rightfully belongs in the Pedal than in the Manual. And because their **design** <term>Invention</term> is altered in various ways, it is unnecessary to write more about them here.

### Apple or Knob Regal, 8-foot pitch:

It is so named because of its proportions, as it stands like an apple on a stem; the largest **pipe body** <term>Corpus: the resonator or main structure of the pipe</term> is approximately 4 inches high and has a small tube, about the size of its mouthpiece. Upon this tube is a round, hollow knob full of small holes, drilled like a pomander <note>original: "Biesemknopff," a decorative perforated metal ball used to hold aromatic musk or ambergris</note>, through which the sound must exit. In the manner of all **Regals** <term>Regal: a small organ or an organ stop consisting of short-resonator reed pipes</term>, it is lovelier and much quieter to listen to than other varieties; it serves well in **positive organs** <term>Positiffen: small, movable organs without pedals, often used in homes</term> used in private chambers.

**Little-Head Regals** <note>original: "Köpfflin Regal"</note> are of 4-foot pitch; these also have a small round knob at the top, like a button, which is split apart in the middle like an open helmet. This causes the resonance to reflect back into the lower pipe body; it is a good and lovely sound.

## Chapter III.

### Instruction on how one may correctly and purely tune the reed stops in organs, as well as the Regal stops specifically and other instruments such as harpsichords, spinets, and the like, by oneself; likewise, in what manner the other pipes should be tuned or assisted during the tuning process.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'E' featuring floral scrollwork and leaf patterns.</image-desc>
It is indeed a good thing, and no extraordinary effort, to engage and purely tune the **reed stops** <term>Schnarrwercke: literally "snarling works," the general term for all reed-based stops</term> in an organ, provided that the foundation of the other **flue pipes** <term>Flöitwerck: "flute-work," the standard non-reed pipes that produce sound via a whistle-like mechanism</term> is already in tune. Nevertheless, there is an advantage to this method: when one wishes to tune a 16-foot reed stop, another stop from the flue pipes—such as an 8-foot **Principal** <term>the primary foundation stop of the organ</term> or Great Octave—should be drawn with it. Likewise, if an 8-foot reed stop is to be tuned, a 4-foot stop like the Octave should be used. For a 4-foot reed stop, however, a Principal or Great Octave, or a Quintadehn <meta>catchword: -tadehn</meta>...

stops of 8-foot pitch, with the Octave of 4-foot pitch drawn and tuned accordingly. This is done for the following reasons: because the voices of the **flue pipes** <term>Pfeiffwerck: refers here specifically to the "flute-work" or flue pipes, as opposed to reed pipes</term>, when they are at an **equal pitch** <note>original Latin: "AEqual"</note> with the **reed stops** <term>Schnarrwerck: literally "buzzing-work," the family of reed stops like Trumpets or Regals</term>, tend to deceive the ear and waver.

And if the flute-work—such as the **Principals** <term>Principalen: the core, foundational stops of the organ</term>, **Octaves**, or **Quintadenas** <term>Quintadeenen: flute stops that sound a prominent fifth (the "twelfth") above the fundamental</term>—according to which the reed stops are to be tuned, is not entirely accurate and pure, and an organist cannot tune the Regal by itself (in the same manner that a keyboard instrument is tuned purely through its own intervals rather than by comparing it to other voices); then there is yet another advantage. One may play a **concordant chord** <term>Concordant: a harmonious set of notes, like a major chord</term> for every out-of-tune Regal pipe (provided that the flute-work and the reed-work are not standing together on the same manual), and thereby adjust the reed voice until it is pure within or between those notes. 

For example: If one wishes to tune the low **C** or **c** in the **Pedal reed stop** <term>Pedalschnarrwerck: reed stops played with the feet</term>—whether it be in the **Trombone** <term>Posaun</term>, **Trumpet** <term>Trummet</term>, etc., or whatever else is counted among the reed stops—one should play a chord on the **Manual** <term>Manual: the keyboard played with the hands</term> like this: **c – e – g – c̅**. Then the out-of-tune Pedal **C** or **c** in the reed stop must be brought to its purest resonance against that same chord (because it contains a **perfect** <note>original Latin: "perfect"</note> third and sixth, as well as a fourth, fifth, and an octave). This works even if the other previously mentioned flute pipes are not entirely pure themselves.

Likewise, if a reed stop in the **Chair Organ** <term>Rückpositiff: the division of the organ located behind the organist's back</term> cannot be accurately set against a flute stop that is out of tune, it is better to use a flute stop from the **Great Organ** <term>Oberwerck: the main, upper division of the organ</term> to play the concordant chords. One may then test and tune the Regal pipes in the Chair Organ one after another against the aforementioned chords in the Great Organ.

Conversely, one can also tune a Regal in the Great Organ against a flute stop in the Chair Organ in this manner. However, one must pay attention to this: because some reed stops sound very quiet, they cannot be tuned or set against voices that sound far too loud.

Just as a Regal or reed stop is tuned higher or lower by the wire or **tuning crook** <term>krucken: the sliding wire used to adjust the vibrating length of the reed tongue</term> that passes through the pipes—where the more the wire is pulled out or struck with a **tuning tool** <note>original: "Plectro"</note> (which widens the vibrating part of its **tongue** <term>Labium: the "lip" or reed tongue</term>), the deeper the pipe sounds; and the deeper the wire is struck in, the narrower and higher its resonance becomes—so too are the other pipes in organs and **positives** <term>Positiffen: small, movable organs</term> tuned higher or lower, though in a different manner. Specifically: an open flute pipe becomes higher if the top of the pipe is widened, or if some material is removed from it [shortening it]; it becomes lower, however, if the top is made narrower with a **tuning horn** <term>Stimmhorn: a cone-shaped tool used to flare or close the tops of metal pipes</term> or pressed inward. But one must take great care not to easily remove material from the pipes, for it is much easier to make a pipe higher than **lower**...

must be tuned to match; and it is a certain sign that a lazy and negligent organ builder—one who has not paid proper attention to the **scale** <term>Mensur: the ratio of a pipe's width to its length, which determines its tonal character</term>—has been at work when the tops of the pipes in **organs** <term>OrgelWercken: the various divisions or the whole mechanism of the organ</term> are found to be heavily pressed together, looking like a heap of crumpled **Three Kings' hats** <note>A reference to the pointed, mitered style of hats associated with the Magi; here used to describe pipes mangled by crude tuning</note>.

The **stopped pipes** <term>Gedacten: from the German 'gedackt,' meaning 'covered' or 'capped'; these pipes are closed at the top, sounding an octave lower than an open pipe of the same length</term>, however, are tuned by the caps or "sleeves" which they possess. For the lower these are pressed, or tapped with a small wooden block, the higher the **pitch** <note>original Latin: "Sonus"</note> becomes; the higher they are moved up, the deeper the pitch becomes.

One also finds stopped pipes that are soldered shut at the top; these are tuned by the **tuning ears** <note>original: "Bärten" (beards/ears). These are metal tabs near the mouth of the pipe</note> attached to them. The further these are moved away from the **lip** <note>original Latin: "Labio"</note>, the higher the resonance; the closer they are moved, the lower it becomes.

Sometimes it also happens that a **flute pipe** <term>Flöitpfeiffe: a flue pipe</term> or **reed pipe** <term>Schnarrwerkspfeiffe: literally a 'buzzing-work' pipe</term> falls completely silent. This can easily occur if a speck of dust or a fly settles in the **mouth** <term>Labial: the 'lips' or opening of a flue pipe where the air vibrates</term>, or between the **tongue** <note>original: "Blat"</note> and the **shallot** <note>original: "Röhre"</note> in the reed-work. If one carefully removes the obstruction, the pipe will easily sound again.

In the same way, saltpeter, rust, or other filth often settles in the pipes, especially on the **brass tongues** <term>Messingsblätlein: the vibrating metal reeds that produce sound in a reed pipe</term> and shallots of the reed-work; this can likewise be removed before one attempts to **voice** <note>original: "streichen," literally 'to stroke' or 'curve' the metal tongue</note> the reeds. One must take care, however, not to curve the reeds too much or too little. For if they are too stiff, the wind cannot overcome them to produce a resonance; but if they are too soft, the wind overcomes them too easily and presses the tongues firmly against the shallots, which likewise causes them to fall silent.

And although mention should primarily be made here of the manner in which a **Symphonia** <note>In this context, likely a hurdy-gurdy or a specific keyed instrument</note>, **Harpsichord** <term>Clavicymbel: a keyboard instrument where strings are plucked</term>, or similar instruments should be strung and quilled: nevertheless, because this is properly the concern of the instrument makers, and can be learned better and more thoroughly through practice than through written instruction—especially since the gauges of wire strings are now very inconsistent, with the same gauge number being sometimes thick and sometimes thin—and because defects occasionally occur in the **tangents** <term>Tangenten: the metal uprights that strike or pluck the strings</term>, it is unnecessary to write at length about this here.

## How one can accord and purely tune a Regal, Harpsichord, Symphonia, and similar instruments for oneself.

Here, the following must primarily be observed with diligence:

1. That one chooses a certain **key** <note>original Latin: "Clavem"</note> from which to begin the tuning, and according to which the others are to be drawn in, one after another.
2. That all **Octaves** and **perfect or major Thirds** <note>original Latin: "Octaven vnd Tertiæ perfectæ seu majores"</note> be tuned entirely purely, both the lowest **key** <note>original Latin: "Clavis"</note> against the highest, and the highest against the lowest.
3. That all **Fifths** <term>Quinten</term> are not tuned straight and pure, but are left slightly "narrowing" against each other (to a certain degree). This means the highest key must be...

# ON THE DESCRIPTION OF INSTRUMENTS <note>original Latin: DE ORGANOGRAPHIA</note>

...should be slightly relaxed or stand a bit lower. However, if one wishes to tune the **fifths** <term>Quinten: an interval of five scale degrees</term> from below—that is, the lowest **key** <term>Clavem: here referring to the pitch or the key on the manual</term> against the upper—it must stand too high and "waver," and thus be slightly more than perfectly pure.

If these three things are correctly observed, one cannot easily go wrong in tuning. Yet the last point—correctly drawing in the **fifths** (according to the manner described above)—is the most difficult, or rather the most important to heed. For an entire **instrument** can be tuned by **octaves** and **fifths**, provided only that the **major thirds** <term>Tertiae majores</term> are used as judges <note>referring to using thirds as a check to see if the temperament is balanced</note>, of which more will be said at greater length elsewhere.

Some experienced tuners can also tune purely by **octaves** and **fourths** <term>Quarten: an interval of four scale degrees</term>; these are tuned similarly to the fifths in their wavering, but **on the contrary** <note>original Latin: contrariè</note>, or **vice versa**. For the upper key should waver slightly too high against the lower, while the lower should waver too low against the upper. The word **Beating** <note>original German: Schweben, literally "soaring" or "hovering"</note> is an organ builder's **term** <note>original Latin: Terminus</note>, used by them when a **concordance** <note>original: Concordantz; a harmonious interval</note> does not stand purely. It is so common among them, and thus among many **organists**, that it is difficult to do away with. Therefore, I must also use it in the future (though quite reluctantly), while keeping in mind whether it is high or low. For "beating" is meant to signify as much as "impure"—that is, tuned either too high or too low. They derive the term from this: when one wishes to draw in and tune the **octaves**, **fifths**, and **fourths** in organs, the **resonance** and sound in the pipes wavers and strikes several beats, just like a **tremulant** <term>Tremulant: a mechanical device that causes the air in the organ to pulsate, creating a vibrato effect</term>. The closer one brings the tuning to purity and agreement <note>original: accort</note>, the more the beating gradually disappears and the beats become fewer, until the **octave** or other concordant intervals finally lock in correctly. Thus, from such beating, **dissonances** <note>original: Dissonantiẽ</note> can be observed and recognized much more easily and sooner in organs than in **regals**, **harpsichords** <term>Clavicymbel</term>, and similar **instruments**.

Accordingly, since the **octave**, which encompasses within itself a **fifth** and a **fourth**, must be and remain perfectly pure, while something is taken away from the **fifth** (as the first part), it follows necessarily that just as much must be given back to the **fourth** (as the other part) as was taken from the fifth, so that the **octave** remains pure.

The **fifth**, which contains a **major third** and a **minor third**, must (as previously mentioned) not stand perfectly pure. However, since the **major third** is pure, it follows that the **minor third** must be impure by as much as the fifth is affected.

**From the major third** <note>original Latin: Ex Tertia majore</note> arises the **minor sixth** <term>sexta minor</term> **by transposition** <note>original Latin: per Transpositionem; in this context, inversion</note>. Just as when the lowest key is placed an octave higher, or the highest key is taken an octave lower: exactly as the **major third** is pure, so must the **minor sixth** become pure.

Likewise, where one key stands pure against another, all other keys (bearing the same name) must be pure against it. For example: if the key **C** is pure against the **C** above it, it follows that all keys named **C**, whether they be small or large, however they may be, must be pure against...

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of musical temperament. # ON THE DESCRIPTION OF INSTRUMENTS <note>original Latin: DE ORGANOGRAPHIA</note>

...or must be another part. Furthermore, if one **D** is pure against another, it follows that all **Ds** must be pure against each other.

From the **minor third** <term>Tertia minore: a musical interval spanning three semitones</term>, the **major sixth** <term>Sexta major: a musical interval spanning nine semitones</term> is produced by **transposition** <note>here meaning inversion, where the notes of an interval are flipped</note>, as previously mentioned. Just as the minor third is impure and wavering, so too must the major sixth waver or be impure; yet in this manner: if the minor third has too little <note>is tuned "narrower" than its pure mathematical ratio</note>, then the major sixth must have too much <note>be tuned "wider"</note> so that the **octave** <term>Octava</term> remains exactly just. And so by **inversion** <note>original Latin: per inversionem</note>: if the major sixth wavers too much, the minor third must waver too little, for when these two are joined together, they must produce a pure octave. Since one does not give each part its due <note>meaning they aren't tuned to their natural, perfect ratios</note>, it follows that one part must have more than the other.

Likewise, where one **key** <term>Clavis: referring to the specific pitch or the physical key on the keyboard</term> wavers against another, it is certain that all other keys (of that same name) waver against each other. This is exactly the same as just mentioned regarding pure-standing keys, with only this difference: that one part becomes as much too high as the other becomes too low.

In what manner one key must stand too low against another can be seen more clearly and understandably in the following table. Namely:

| In | the | key against the | must be tuned |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Fifths** and **Minor Thirds** | **upper** | **lower** | †† somewhat and as much too low as the |
| **Fourths** and **Major Sixths** | **lower** | **upper** | **lower** (or **upper**) against the **upper** (or **lower**) wavers too high. |

<note>This table describes the mechanical process of "tempering" an instrument. In the tuning systems of this era, certain intervals were deliberately tuned slightly out of tune (wavering) to allow the instrument to play in multiple keys while keeping the octaves pure.</note>

The **octaves**, **major thirds** <term>Tertiae majores</term>, and **minor sixths** <term>Sextae minores</term> (as often mentioned) remain pure. Now, if an **interval** <term>Intervallum</term>, or rather a **concordance** <term>Concordant: a harmonious blending of sounds</term>, is to remain exactly just, then both **intermediate parts** <note>the smaller intervals that make up the larger one</note> must be equal: either both pure, or both wavering (one too high, the other too low).

But if one intermediate part is false and the other is pure, then the entire interval must be false and cannot remain pure. And this is from a **geometric principle** <note>original Latin: ex principio Geometrico</note>. *For if an uncertain number is added to a certain number, then the whole becomes uncertain. Or, if an uncertain quantity is added to a defined quantity, that whole quantity becomes uncertain; and given one inconsistency, many more follow.* <note>original Latin: "Si enim ad certum numerum incertus addatur, tum totus ille fiet incertus: Vel si ad quantitatem definitam incerta addatur quantitas, tota illa quantitas fiet incerta, & dato uno inconvenienti, sequuntur plura."</note>

...as many of those as are still to be used in the deep bass are far too impure and spoil even the best and clearest hearing if full chords are used.

When this <term>descending: tuning downward from a reference pitch</term> <note>original Latin: descendendo</note> has been completed in this way, one then proceeds <term>ascending: tuning upward</term> <note>original Latin: ascendendo</note> and tunes the high f̅ to the already tuned f quite purely; then the g̅ to the g, and so on, through the entire range in which the <term>keyboard: the compass or layout of the instrument's keys</term> <note>original: Clavir</note> is arranged.

But here in the upper **keys** <note>original Latin: Clavibus</note>, one must pay even closer attention with a more diligent and sharper ear than before in the lowest ones. One must ensure the **octaves** are tuned equally and quite purely, so that both **keys** in the octave interval sound so much alike as if they were but a single pipe or string. Furthermore, one should always keep the **pure major thirds** <note>original: Tertien perfecten</note> as a **judge** <note>original Latin: Iudice</note> and guide. For example, once the high f̅ is justified against the lower f, then test that f̅ against the d, and hear whether this **major third** <note>original Latin: Tertia perfecta</note> is quite pure. **Likewise**, when the g̅ is tuned after the g, then test the g̅ with the b; when the a̅ **accords** with the a, test it with the f. When all of this is completed in this manner, it yields a pure **harmony** <note>original Latin: Harmoniam</note> without any deception. But this must be learned through practice and much use.

When these aforementioned **keys** are set—for the octaves as well as the **pure thirds** must be tuned quite **perfectly** and purely, and the **fourths** <note>original: Quarten</note> even more than purely; while the **fifths**, as indicated above, should be somewhat **beating** <term>schwebend: the acoustic "shimmer" or interference that occurs when an interval is slightly out of tune, essential for temperament</term>—then after that, only the octaves are tuned purely against one another, upward and downward across the whole keyboard, excluding the **semitones** <term>Semitonia: the sharps and flats (black keys)</term>.

->## ON THE DESCRIPTION OF INSTRUMENTS.<-

**Octaves** $b$ <note>original: $b$; in this system, $b$ refers to B-flat</note>, $h$ <note>original: $h$; in this system, $h$ refers to B-natural</note>, and $B$ $b$: And the **fifth** $a$ to $b$-flat; yet it should be <term>beating: a rhythmic "throbbing" heard when two notes are slightly out of tune with each other</term> <note>original: schwebend</note>. Then the B-natural ($h$) must be tested against the **tenth** $g$, and drawn quite purely. Following this, the **octave** $g$ and $\bar{g}$: These three **keys** <note>original Latin: Claves</note>, however—$\bar{g}$, $f^\sharp$, and $\bar{h}$—should be tuned quite purely against their **thirds**, such as $a$, $d$, and $e$. Although such things are always more precisely perceived against their **tenths** (as has been often mentioned), their **octaves** must afterwards be fully pulled into tune as well.

The **fifths** $c$ to $g$, and $h$ to $\bar{f}^\sharp$, must not be entirely "false" <note>out of tune</note>, nor yet entirely pure, but only to a certain degree; however, they should not <term>beat: vibrate with dissonance</term> as much as other **fifths**, so that when one plays in "foreign" **keys** or through the **semitones** <note>original Latin: Semitonia; the black keys</note>, it does not dissonate too greatly. Although some believe the **fifth** $c^\sharp$ to $g^\sharp$ must be entirely pure, in my opinion, this cannot be allowed to pass.

For this reason, the ancients called the interval $f$ to $g^\sharp$ the **Wolf** <note>original: Wulff; a notoriously harsh-sounding interval in early tuning systems</note>. This is because these two **keys**—whenever the <term>Second Mode: a specific scale or "key" in early music</term> <note>original Latin: Secundus Modus</note> happens to fall a tone lower on $f$, or if one must play <term>chromatically: using notes outside the standard scale</term> <note>original Latin: Chromaticè</note> through the **semitones**—produce a completely false **minor third** <note>original Latin: Tertiam minorem</note>. To help the situation somewhat, they "stole" a very small amount from all the other **keys** and stretched the **major third** <note>original Latin: Tertiam Majorem</note> $e$ to $g^\sharp$ so it was not quite pure, but a bit wider. This was done so the $g^\sharp$ would be a little higher and closer to $a$, but further from $f$, and thus could almost—though not perfectly—be used as a **minor third** in times of need.

Some do not want the $f$ and $g^\sharp$ to be the **Wolf**, but rather place the **Wolf** at $c^\sharp$, because $c^\sharp$ and $g^\sharp$ cannot be pure, which is proven on all organs. Others think the **Wolf** is in $c^\sharp$, $f^\sharp$, and $b$-flat to $e$-flat. I, however, let everyone keep their own opinion; it is best that the **Wolf**, with its unpleasant howling, stays in the forest and does not <term>disturb: throw into disorder</term> <note>original Latin: interturbire</note> our **harmonic concords** <note>original Latin: harmonicas Concordantias</note>.

The reason that $f^\sharp$, $g^\sharp$, and $c^\sharp$ must stand as they do is, among other things, because of the <term>cadences: the concluding formulas of a musical phrase</term> <note>original Latin: Clausulen</note> which are formed in these black **keys** or **semitones**. In $f$–$f^\sharp$, $g$–$g^\sharp$, and $c$–$\bar{c}^\sharp$, there is no "la fa" or "mi fa" <note>solfège syllables used to describe half-steps</note> as there is in $a$–$b$ and $d$–$es$. Conversely, in these **semitones** $b$ and $es$, one cannot <term>perform cadences</term> <note>original Latin: clausuliret</note> as in the others mentioned before. But if the black **keys** are doubled <note>referring to "split keys" where one key is divided into two to provide both a D-sharp and an E-flat, for example</note>, as can be seen in Part 2, Number 39, then one can have it however one wishes.

But more shall be said regarding this hereafter from the **consideration of the monochord** <note>original Latin: ex consideratione Monochordi; a single-stringed instrument used to measure musical intervals mathematically</note> and according to the **fundamental rules of proportions**, God willing. For here, it was intended only to be written and recorded in a good **organ-maker-like** and **organist-like** <note>original: Orgelmacherisch vnd Organistisch</note> fashion, so that even the simple-minded might understand it.

# ON THE DESCRIPTION OF INSTRUMENTS.

...remain in their proportions and are neither increased nor decreased. This is found in the human voice <note>original: *voce humana*</note>, as well as in trombones <note>original: *Posaunen*</note> and others where one can add or take away something with human breath. For the human voice naturally directs itself to the correct proportion of the intervals <note>original: *intervallorum*</note>, and adds to them where something is lacking, or takes away where there would be an excess.

But on instruments and organs, there is another consideration, for there are far too few keys <note>original: *Clavier*</note>; therefore, one must take something from certain consonances <note>original: *consonantiis*</note> <term>consonance: an interval or chord that sounds stable and harmonious</term> so that the deficiency does not fall on a single key <note>original: *clave*</note> alone.

## The keys <note>original: *Claves*</note> are thus:

| | | |
|---|---|---|
| **c** and **d** | are distant by a major tone | 9/8 |
| **d** and **e** | by a minor tone | 10/9 |
| **e** and **f** | are distant by a major semitone | 16/15 |
| **f** and **g** | by a major tone | 9/8 |
| **g** and **a** | are distant by a minor tone | 10/9 |
| **a** and **b** <note>original: *h*</note> | by a major tone | 9/8 |
| **b** <note>original: *h*</note> and **c** | by a major semitone | 16/15 |

If instruments were to be tuned according to these pure proportions, then from **d** to **f** would immediately become an imperfect minor third <note>original: *semiditonus imperfectus*</note>; for it is a minor tone combined with a semitone, and a whole comma <term>comma: a tiny musical interval (approx. 1/9th of a tone) that represents the difference between notes reached through different tuning paths</term> is missing. Likewise, from **d** to **a**, the fifth <note>original: *Quinta*</note> would also be missing a comma, which is far too much, and the ears cannot endure such a deficiency. Therefore, one should rightly have more keys <note>original: *Clavier*</note>, so that one had two different **d** keys, which were only a comma apart from each other.

But because this also happens with other keys <note>original: *clavibus*</note>, the number of keys—especially if the doubled semitones <note>referring to split keys used to play both D# and Eb, for example</note> were also added—would become far too many. Therefore, one must use temperament <note>original: *temperatur*</note>, which is as follows:

A half-comma is taken from the major tone; conversely, a half-comma is given to the minor tone. From this it is clear <note>original Latin: *hinc manifestum*</note> that nothing is taken away from the major third <note>original Latin: *tertia majori*</note>, which consists of a major tone and a minor tone, and it remains pure; and the other part, namely the minor sixth <note>original Latin: *sexta minor*</note> (so that the octave is completed), also remains pure. But one-quarter of a comma is given to the major semitone; from this it follows that now a fourth <note>original: *Quarta*</note>, which [consists of] a major tone and a minor tone, and...

...has a major semitone <note>original: *Semitonium majus*</note> / it is too coarse / because a quarter of a comma <term>comma: a very small interval, the difference between two near-identical notes in different tuning systems</term> has been added to the semitone.

Also, the Fifth <note>original: *Quinta*</note> has two major tones, one minor tone, and one semitone; because here a half-comma is taken from each major tone, and thus a whole comma is taken from both together / and in contrast only three-quarters of a comma are given back / it follows / that the Fifth in instruments cannot be perfect.

But because a Fourth <note>original: *Quarta*</note> and a Fifth make an Octave <note>original: *Octavam*</note> / which cannot be changed / it follows necessarily / when one part becomes larger / that the other becomes smaller / and it requires no further demonstration. <note>original: *Divide grossum in duas partes, sunt utrobique sex nummi: Si jam alterutri parti dabis septem nummos, necesse est, altera pars habeat tantum quinque nummos, si grossus integritatem custodire debet, & non minui aut augeri.*</note> Divide a groschen <note>a silver coin</note> into two parts; there are six coins on each side. If you then give seven coins to one part, it is necessary that the other part has only five coins, if the groschen must maintain its integrity and not be diminished or increased.

But when the organ builders <note>original: *Orgelmacher*</note> say / the Fourth **d g** beats <term>beats: 'schwebt', the audible pulsing sound heard when two notes are slightly out of tune with each other</term>: The minor Third <note>original: *Tertia minor*</note> **g b** <note>original: *b*, meaning B-flat</note> also beats: Therefore the minor Sixth <note>original: *Sexta minor*</note> **d b** is pure / etc. That is indeed somewhat after their own fashion / but it is not spoken correctly according to art and demonstration <note>original: *secundum artem & demonstrationem*</note> / rather, if I wish to demonstrate / that the minor Sixth is pure / I must say thus:

> A major Third and a minor Sixth constitute an Octave; But the major Third in temperament <term>temperament: the system of tuning where intervals are adjusted away from pure mathematical ratios to allow for playing in different keys</term> retains its true proportion; Therefore it is necessary that the minor Sixth also retains its own, and is legitimate. Thus the Fifth and Fourth constitute a double, or octave; and the Fifth in temperament is diminished by a quarter part of a comma: Therefore it is necessary that the Fourth, which is joined to it, be increased by a quarter part of a comma: And vice versa for the others. For it is necessary that the parts be judged based on the whole. <note>original: *Tertia major & Sexta minor constituunt Octavam... Necesse enim est, ut de partibus judicetur ex integro.*</note>

...must be tested with particular diligence. 4. Item: Regarding the stability and understanding of the designs of the internal structure, and other hidden defects (which should rightly be rejected and might be unknown even to those who consider themselves experts) that may be necessary to reveal and demonstrate. 5. And finally, how an organ <note>original: *OrgelWerck*</note>, along with the reed stops <term>reed stops: *SchnarrWercken*, pipes that use a vibrating metal tongue to produce a buzzing or 'snaring' sound</term> and all common instances of defects—those that do not arise fundamentally <note>original: *fundamentaliter*</note> or from the foundation—can be maintained in proper condition by an organist.

In reasonable consideration, nowadays even in small towns as well as larger ones, congregations spare no expense to have an organ built and installed for the honor, praise, and glory of the name of God the Most High; yet they are often very poorly guided. Thus, it often happens that such instruments require more repairs and patching from one year to the next than would have been caused by higher initial costs if a truly upright master had been contracted from the start.

For when some of these organs are made superficially <note>original: *obiter*</note> and not fundamentally <note>original: *fundamentaliter*</note> by their masters—be it out of greed, ignorance of the art, or out of a lazy reliance on assistants and the instability of all kinds of materials—and are also rushed (so that many may have the reputation of being able to finish sooner than others); then there immediately arises a host of defects. These flow from a poor foundation in the windchests <note>original: *Laden*</note>, or sticking and jamming in the linkage of the valves <note>original: *Ventilen*</note> and keyboards <note>original: *Claviren*</note>, or from the swelling and drying out of the wood in various places. Soon one register <note>a stop or set of pipes</note> pulls smoothly while another is stiff; one opens halfway, another fully; soon they stick entirely, or break and tear, resulting in great inconvenience. Soon the pipes sag because of their weakness and too-thin metal; soon they collapse entirely due to their top-heaviness and poor mounting, or they stand and hang across one another **as if drunken peasants were holding a church-fair dance among them.** Consequently, the intonation <term>intonation: the process of adjusting the tone and speech of a pipe</term> is hindered, the accord of the tuning vanishes, and a disgusting sound is produced. Soon the wind leaks here and there and vanishes, or it fails to reach its full power. Soon it is too strong in the winter and too weak in the summer. Soon one must hire two, then three bellows-blowers <term>bellows-blowers: *Calcanten*, the people who physically pumped the organ's bellows to provide air</term>, often because of the heavy treading required, and often because of the rapid pace of the playing, etc. And regarding the many faults and defects that arise from time...

### ON THE DESCRIPTION OF INSTRUMENTS.

...and one defect leads to another, appearing in even greater numbers. Because of these aforementioned recurring defects, an upright organist often becomes so anxious that he would much rather go to a barn to thresh grain than to go and play upon such an organ.

And although we humans cannot make eternal things in which no flaw would ever appear, experience nevertheless testifies that some organ works—when they have been crafted by experienced and diligent observers <note>original: *observanten*, meaning careful craftsmen</note>—stand for 50, 60, 70, or 80 years without needing any special revision. They remain so precise, without any fundamental defect in the windchests, pipes, bellows, internal structure, and all other moving parts, that they often far surpass new organs. For this reason, such a magnificent creation of God—into whose invention our dear ancestors put such great diligence—is highly praised, lauded, and written about.

However, in order to prevent all these problems in the best and most possible way, so that churches are not so wickedly burdened with expenses and many a good organist may be spared such heavy frustration with their instruments, it is not only highly necessary that the inspectors and churchwardens consult beforehand—before they even decide to build—with experienced organists who will not vacillate or play the hypocrite with the organ builders. In the presence of these experts, they should propose the "disposition" <note>The list of specific pipes and stops intended for the instrument</note> of the voices and the entire contract for the work to the organ builder. Furthermore, necessity requires that, as mentioned above, a certain little treatise be correctly composed and published in print regarding all these matters.

Therefore, I have with all diligence urged the aforementioned appointed <term>Orgel- vnd Instrumentmacher</term> <note>organ and instrument maker</note> to my gracious Prince and Lord, Esaias Compenius (who was very helpful to me in the preceding report and instruction on old and new organs), that he should compose such a little treatise and let it be released in public print for the benefit of churches, organists, and organ builders.

In this effort, I consider it my duty to be not only encouraging but also—according to my modest understanding and ability—advisory and helpful for the sake of the common good.

And such an <term>Opusculum</term> <note>original Latin: "little work"</note> and treatise shall follow soon, if God wills, as it was not entirely appropriate to attach it here at the very end.

->E N D E.<-
